item.title: The J.J. McCarthy saga: Why did Minnesota give up on him, and can he save the Giants?
item.description: Cast off in Minnesota, McCarthy is trying to resurrect his career in New York while also leading the Giants to a division title.
item.content:encoded:
Even by the standards of the "this has to be scripted, right?" modern NFL, J.J. McCarthy's story is a wild one. Drafted 10th overall, injured his entire rookie season, bouncing back and forth between the field and the medical tent in his second year, losing his job and getting traded away, then immediately setting a franchise record with his new team … every time his NFL saga seems over, it turns out he's on to a new chapter. 

Dealt from Minnesota to New York last month, McCarthy entered the Giants' Week 6 game against New Orleans and tied a franchise-record with 243 fourth-quarter passing yards. In start No. 2 with the Giants, he led New York to victory over Houston on the road, apparently cementing himself as the Giants' QB1 going forward. Yes, it was an overtime win over an unspectacular two-win team, but at this point McCarthy must take what he can get. 

The McCarthy era in Minnesota was a cascade of bad luck, bad timing and bad bets that are worth recounting just to get the story straight. Going into the 2024 draft, the Vikings had an eye on Caleb Williams, Jayden Daniels or Drake Maye, but so did everyone else; when those three went off the board, the Vikings traded up to get the 10th pick, and opted to use it on McCarthy over current Broncos starting QB Bo Nix. 

McCarthy started the season behind Sam Darnold and stayed there, tearing his right meniscus during the preseason and losing the entire season. Darnold led Minnesota to a 14-3 record in 2024 before an ugly flameout in the playoffs; McCarthy watched it all from the sidelines. 

Prior to the 2025 season, Minnesota then entered into a very costly game of quarterback musical chairs. They'd already let Kirk Cousins walk a year earlier; Cousins went on to have a couple decent, if strange, years with Atlanta and is now handling business in Las Vegas. They'd considered Aaron Rodgers; Rodgers ended up signing with Pittsburgh and leading the Steelers to one, and potentially two, playoff berths. They couldn't entice late-season practice-squad signee Daniel Jones to stick around; Jones chose a starting role with Indianapolis. They'd opted not to re-sign Darnold, who could only manage to lead the Seahawks to a Super Bowl win. 

Minnesota had a team that had won 14 games the prior season, a team that was one win away from the No. 1 seed in the NFC, a team primed to win right now … and they decided to hand the keys to an utterly untested, unproven quarterback. 

And for one game, it looked like a genius move. McCarthy, playing in his first game since leading Michigan to a national championship win over Washington in early 2024, threw for two touchdowns and rushed for another, leading Minnesota to a comeback victory over Chicago. But the very next game, he threw two interceptions in a loss to Atlanta, along the way suffering a high ankle sprain that kept him out of the next five games. Later in the season, he missed games due to a concussion and a hairline fracture in his throwing hand as the Vikings limped into the offseason. 

The McCarthy-Vikings saga seemed a classic, painful example of bad timing; Minnesota was ready to compete for a title immediately, but McCarthy simply hadn't developed enough to lead them there. Vikings head coach Kevin O'Connell presaged the entire debacle a year earlier in an appearance on the Rich Eisen Show. "I just think as a whole, there's not enough emphasis put on the organization's role in the development of the position," he said, "meaning, I believe that organizations fail young quarterbacks before young quarterbacks fail organizations."

Prior to the 2026 season, the organization finally decided it had seen enough out of McCarthy, bringing in Kyler Murray to leapfrog him on the depth chart. O'Connell still doesn't have a single postseason victory, and the window on elite performance out of both the defense and wide receiver Justin Jefferson is closing. Plus, the questions about McCarthy's development, maturity — see his premature Griddy celebration last year that he did in defiance of coaches — and ability to stay healthy became too loud to ignore.  

#Vikings QB JJ McCarthy on his walk in TD griddy celebration:

“I did it in practice and I was told not to do it. So me being who I am, it's like oh, now I'm more enticed to do it. I'll definitely get a minus for that one.”pic.twitter.com/vHYQ8Cv0WE

— VikingzFanPage (@vikingzfanpage) December 15, 2025

"We tried to do everything we could to collaborate with a plan for [McCarthy] among coaches, among everybody in this building to try to put him in position to develop and grow," O'Connell said in September. "And I do think, you know, I do think he did. I do think he did develop and grow."

But not enough; the Vikings officially ended the McCarthy Experiment after 10 games, 1,632 yards passing, and 11 touchdowns to 12 interceptions. Minnesota dealt him to the Giants for a 2027 fifth-round pick — a significant depreciation in less than three years even though the Giants were desperate for quarterback help. 

So what's next for McCarthy? He's still on his rookie contract, which made him an attractive trade target. And he still has game, as he evidenced Sunday with throws like this one to Malik Nabers:

J.J. McCarthy finds Nabers downfield!

NYGvsHOU on FOX/FOX One
Stream on @NFLPluspic.twitter.com/VZ5HPcZ4JI

— NFL (@NFL) October 25, 2026

Plus, McCarthy is still just 23 years old. For perspective, he's five months younger than Ole Miss quarterback Trinidad Chambliss. The easy comparison here is Darnold and Baker Mayfield, who both resurrected their careers after leaving situations that didn't fit their skillsets. In the Giants' run-heavy offense, McCarthy has an opportunity to thrive. And he's already giving motivational postgame locker room speeches:

J.J. McCarthy’s locker-room speech after beating the #Texans in his first start with the #Giants:

This team is fully behind him.

(📽️ @Giants) pic.twitter.com/4I88M5VjSS

— Ari Meirov (@MySportsUpdate) October 25, 2026

Most importantly for the Giants' purposes: The division is a flat-out mess. Philadelphia has basically ejected itself, Washington can't get out of its own way, and Dallas perpetually takes two steps forward and then two steps right back. McCarthy doesn't need to be a star in New York, he just needs to be more than an anchor. 

After Minnesota gave up on him, New York gives McCarthy an opportunity to rewrite his career. Put another way: If he's going to make it anywhere, he's got to make it there.

item.title: Most common players on eliminated teams from Week 7 in Yahoo Fantasy Death leagues — plus FAB waiver wire advice
item.description: Death Leagues have claimed more star players. Fantasy football analyst Scott Pianowski advises you on how to approach the waiver wire in Week 8.
item.content:encoded:
Every week I'll examine the most common NFL players on the teams eliminated in Yahoo Death Leagues, trying to figure out where the puck is headed. I will also offer some FAB advice ($1,000 cap is the Yahoo default), but please remember this area is highly context-sensitive and manager-specific.

Waiver strategy in Death Leagues

If you're new to this format, it's critical to understand that waiver strategy is significantly different in the world of Death Leagues.

You can often win a traditional fantasy league with modest help from the waiver wire, maybe a timely pickup or two. Sure, it's great if you crush the market and land the right guys — the best managers will always aim to be smart on the wire — but if your drafted team stays healthy and runs pure, some years that might be enough.

Immediate needs vs. playing the long game

In Death Leagues, the eventual winning manager will have assembled a MONSTER team at the end of the year, a juggernaut, a Pro Bowl-type of roster. And the way you build that beast is usually by having resources all season — not by using the majority of your FAB on a tantalizing early star. It's pivotal that you understand that the waiver wire should get stronger and stronger every week in Death leagues, because the eliminated manager is coming from a smaller and smaller league size every week.

Unless you have a draft touched by the fantasy angels, you are unlikely to win a Death League without a successful and careful waiver-wire strategy.

My Death League strategy is centered on the concept that I like my squad early in the year and I am confident I can beat at least one team per week while the field of opponents is large. Therefore, while I will dip my toes into the FAB market early, my primary goal is to keep major reserves in play for later in the year, when bye weeks hit and injuries are more prevalent — and the pool of opponents is smaller (so advancing is harder, in theory). Again, I urge you to remember: the waiver wire in Death Leagues gets stronger as the year gets deeper, a key reason to be judicious with your resources.

Not everyone will share my strategy, of course. If you want to chase major improvements and use the bulk of your FAB to load up quickly, then shoot your shot. Play the strategy you're comfortable with. Just understand that my recommendations are predicated on being careful early, and if you prefer something more aggressive, you'll have to jump the numbers up. You know your room better than an outsider does.

Keep in mind the bye weeks are here — the 49ers, Giants, Saints and Texans don't play in Week 8. When in doubt, we will prefer players with later bye weeks — if you survive deep in this format, your roster will be loaded in the money weeks (making byes less painful). October absences can be more difficult to negotiate.

Understanding FAB recommendations

I will offer weekly FAB recommendations in three buckets:

Proactive: This means you highly covet this player, perhaps might even need this player. I realize these offers might not win if someone in your league is lighting money on fire, but as described above, that's often a short-sighted mistake in this format.

Reactive: This means you desire the player but the offer has to make sense for your short- or long-term strategy.

Keep Them Honest: This is an offer that is not designed to win, but might surprisingly land a player if your opponents are distracted by other talent available or unexpectedly passive that week. I often compare notes with other experienced Death League players and we're surprised at how often the Keep Them Honest offers actually win (this is also a portable strategy for regular season-long leagues; you never know when strange market behavior will come about).

One last note: Understand that the FAB recommendations are with the assumption that you won't be making offers for every available player.

1. RB Kenneth Walker, Chiefs

Fantasy’s No. 1 right answer finally had an off game, as the Seattle defense provided the Kryptonite. Walker remains a set-and-forget star, so long as he can handle the heaviest workload he’s ever been tasked with. Keep in mind Walker's bye week has already come and gone.

FAB Recommendation:

  • $350 proactive

  • $175 reactive

  • $100 keep them honest

2. RB Derrick Henry, Ravens

Henry was limited to 2.6 a carry in Week 7 against the Bengals and he hasn’t had any touchdown deodorant for two weeks. The eventual Lamar Jackson return can only help, but for the first time in his career, Henry is starting to look like a player in decline.

FAB Recommendation:

  • $175 proactive

  • $100 reactive

  • $70 keep them honest

3. WR Garrett Wilson, Jets

Wilson saw his smallest target share of the year and made his displeasure known. The Omar Cooper Jr. emergence isn’t helping Wilson, but the squeaky wheel narrative should kick in soon. Bet on talent.

FAB Recommendation:

  • $150 proactive

  • $75 reactive

  • $40 keep them honest

4. TE Sam LaPorta, Lions

He’s one of the best tight ends around, but he’s always going to be the third or fourth option in Detroit’s offense. And when it’s a Jameson Williams week, it’s almost always bad for LaPorta. The Vikings are a nasty Week 8 draw, then the schedule gets better.

FAB Recommendation:

  • $110 proactive

  • $55 reactive

  • $20 keep them honest

5. WR Nico Collins, Texans

We normally think of Collins as a target hog, but the Texans have been spreading it out in their passing game. Of course, Houston has to ask itself some hard questions after a stunning loss to the Giants. The Texans don’t play in Week 8, so factor that into your immediate plans.

FAB Recommendation:

  • $150 proactive

  • $75 reactive

  • $35 keep them honest

6. RB James Cook III, Bills

Bye weeks are a fact of life, but sometimes the bench doesn’t step up for you. Even with Josh Allen’s goal-line party, Cook has a rushing touchdown in five straight weeks. He’s never seen as the best back in fantasy, but he’s played like a first-rounder all year.

FAB Recommendation:

  • $355 proactive

  • $185 reactive

  • $110 keep them honest

7. WR Tetairoa McMillan, Panthers

Just when we thought it was safe to trust Bryce Young and the Panthers, the offense threw up a stinker against Tampa Bay. McMillan is an undeniable talent, but we can’t ignore that his stats haven’t separated much from Jalen Coker when both are in uniform.

FAB Recommendation:

  • $185 proactive

  • $70 reactive

  • $35 keep them honest

8. TE Isaiah Likely, Giants

After a season of delicious volume, Likely was suspiciously quiet in the win at Houston. At least J.J. McCarthy played well in his first start, so the offense looks credible moving forward. But Likely can’t help you during his Week 8 bye.

FAB Recommendation:

  • $100 proactive

  • $45 reactive

  • $10-13 keep them honest

9. WR Jalen Coker, Panthers

Another casualty of Bryce Young’s poor game, and now Coker has a shoulder injury to boot. It’s looking like Coker will play Thursday against Green Bay, but grind those injury reports closely.

FAB Recommendation:

  • $100 proactive

  • $45 reactive

  • $10-13 keep them honest

10. RB Chase Brown, Bengals

Post-bye games are often reveal weeks, and the reveal wasn’t kind to Brown (15 touches, 58 yards); Samaje Perine stole a goal-line touchdown and Tahj Brooks had some clock-draining carries. Brown is too good to drop but not consistent enough to proactively chase.

FAB Recommendation:

  • $125 proactive

  • $55 reactive

  • $15-20 keep them honest

item.title: Jalen Carter, Riq Woolen decline to speak to reporters after loss to Cowboys
item.description: With all the focus on the injury issues for the Eagles' offense, the team's defense got manhandled last night by the Cowboys.
item.content:encoded:
With all the focus on the injury issues for the Eagles' offense, the team's defense got manhandled last night by the Cowboys. After the game, two key players declined to speak to reporters.

Both defensive tackle Jalen Carter and cornerback Riq Woolen passed on the league-imposed requirement to talk after each game.

Said Carter, via EJ Smith of PHLY Sports, “Nah, y’all have a good night. You get home safe.”

Said Woolen, also per Smith, "Appreciate you all, as always. Y’all have a good night, get home safely as well."

It's not uncommon for players to refuse to speak after games. Sometimes, it morphs into a confrontation with the league, which has fined players in the past. More often than not, it gets resolved with a conversation or a warning.

The reluctance to speak is not surprising. The Eagles gave up 204 rushing yards to the Cowboys. Woolen slipped and fell on what would have been a long touchdown catch by receiver CeeDee Lamb, if the throw had been more accurate.

Beyond that, the Eagles are 2-5. The season is slipping away. Frustrations may have emerged, if either or both had spoken.

Still, the league mandates it. Last night, they both failed to satisfy the obligation.

item.title: The McCarthy/Murray Discourse Isn’t Going Away
item.description: And there’s a reason for that
item.content:encoded:
When the Minnesota Vikings traded quarterback J.J. McCarthy to the New York Football Giants a month ago, a lot of Vikings fans seemed to be relieved because they thought they would likely never have to hear McCarthy’s name again. After all, after McCarthy missed his entire rookie season following a meniscus tear in the team’s 2024 preseason opener and then had an up-and-down first season as the full-time while dealing with multiple injuries, a significant portion of the fan base had decided that there was no chance he could possibly be “the guy” in Minnesota.

The return the Vikings received for the highest-drafted quarterback in franchise history was a fifth-round selection in the 2027 NFL Draft, and a disturbingly large number of people seemed to be fine with that. The thought was that McCarthy would go to New York, continue to struggle, and likely be out of the league before he got to a second contract, after which everyone would just forget about him.

But a funny thing happened on the way to McCarthy’s impending irrelevance, and all of a sudden the people who were so sure that McCarthy was the worst quarterback they’d ever seen just don’t want to talk about him anymore. Why? Because now people have questions.

In Week 6, after Jameis Winston put the Giants into a 34-10 hole against the New Orleans Saints, McCarthy entered the game, led the Giants to 17 unanswered points, and had them within 12 yards of a potential tying score before he ran out of time. In Week 7, after being named the starter, he led the Giants into Houston as a double-digit underdog against the Texans and led New York to a 27-21 overtime win. He also seems to have unlocked Giants star wide receiver Malik Nabers, who has 11 catches for 206 yards since McCarthy took over.

In the five quarters plus overtime that McCarthy has been running the Giants’ offense, that offense has generated six touchdown drives.

The Minnesota Vikings’ offense has generated four touchdown drives. . .since Week 3.

There was Jordan Addison’s 41-yard touchdown catch against Tampa Bay, Justin Jefferson’s 15-yard touchdown catch and Aaron Jones’ 8-yard touchdown run against New Orleans, and T.J. Hockenson’s 5-yard touchdown catch against Indianapolis. That’s it. If you want to count the drive where Hockenson slid down at the 1-yard line against Miami, fine, but five touchdown drives in four games really isn’t terribly impressive, either.

And let me be clear on something. . .yes, the Vikings are 6-0, and I’m positively thrilled that they’re 6-0. The Vikings are 6-0 because Brian Flores is out here every week turning water into wine and Will Reichard is some sort of kicking robot cyborg machine from another planet. The defense and special teams have dragged this offense, kicking and screaming, to 6-0.

For the last few weeks, we’ve heard about how this is going to be the week that the Vikings’ offense was finally going to get itself right.

  • Week 4: “Well, the Dolphins might be the worst team in the league. This is going to be a get-right game for the Vikings’ offense.”
  • Week 5: “Well, the Saints have given up the most points in the league so far. This is going to be a get-right game for the Vikings’ offense.”
  • Week 7: “Well, the Vikings are getting almost all their key players back on offense and the Colts just lost to the Titans at home. This is going to be a get-right game for the Vikings’ offense.”

And the Vikings’ offense just continues to. . .not get right.

Which brings us to Kyler Murray. The case for bringing in Murray to be the starting quarterback was that he was the sort of veteran who could get the ball to Justin Jefferson and help this offense push the ball down the field in ways that McCarthy, Carson Wentz, and Max Brosmer couldn’t in 2025. Now, because of injuries to both Murray and Jefferson, they’ve only played two full games together, so there’s still time for chemistry to develop, but the early results have not been great.

On Sunday, against a Colts defense that has been less than stellar this season, Murray completed 14-of-24 passes for 150 yards and a touchdown. That included four catches for 44 yards for Jefferson. Jefferson did not have a catch in the second half. He was targeted once in the second half. The Colts came into the game with star cornerback Sauce Gardner on the sideline and, by the end of the game, had none of their top three corners on the field due to injuries. I don’t know why this happened, but it’s precisely the sort of thing that people had complaints about last season with this offense.

Now, as many people have pointed out, the Vikings’ schedule gets significantly tougher. They head to Detroit this week, then it’s Josh Allen and the Buffalo Bills in prime time, then they travel to Green Bay before heading to Mexico City to take on the San Francisco 49ers. As good as the Vikings’ defense has been so far this season, it seems unlikely that point totals in the teens are going to be good enough going forward.

This shouldn’t be “training wheels” time for the Minnesota Vikings’ offense. This should be “put the ball into the end zone more than once a game and stop relying on Brian Flores and company to bail you out” time. And now Vikings fans are seeing a 23-year-old quarterback that their team sold for pennies on the dollar and had been dismissed as a complete flop performing at a significantly improved level for a team he’s been with for a month and, if the season ended today, a team that the Vikings could potentially see in the NFL’s postseason party.

So, yes, people are going to have questions. And the people who thought they had all the answers a month ago have, suddenly, found a lack of desire to approach the topic. Strange, that.

Put simply, the discourse about J.J. McCarthy and Kyler Murray isn’t going anywhere. It’s going to continue until at least one of those two parties puts forth enough compelling evidence to suggest that it shouldn’t continue.

To this point, neither of them has. And until one of them does, it’s only going to get louder.

There's just one more game to be played in Week 7. The Dallas Cowboys and Philadelphia Eagles will close out the week Monday night, as the division rivals play for the first time this season.

The game will cap yet another eventful week of football, one surprisingly devoid of major injuries … mostly.

Other than the devastating loss of Carolina Panthers offensive lineman Taylor Moton, most big-name players came through Week 7 pretty healthy. San Francisco 49ers running back Christian McCaffrey gave fantasy mangers a scare after missing time during the team's loss to the Atlanta Falcons, though was able to return and said he would be "alright" after the game.

With injuries out of the spotlight, the most interesting development from Week 7 may have come from the Las Vegas Raiders. Following the team's loss, Raiders coach Klint Kubiak seemed to hint that a quarterback change could be coming soon. Kubiak said the team would re-evaluate "everything," even though veteran Kirk Cousins has played well.

The Dolphins earned their first victory of the season on Sunday and Willis had his second straight quality fantasy performance — sandwiched around Miami's bye. 

After finishing as the QB13 in Week 5, Willis was the QB4 overall this week. That result is thanks to a three-touchdown day (two passing, one rushing), as well as 208 yards through the air and another 37 on the ground. He's now run the ball at least eight times in three of his last four appearances. 

The most exciting development for Willis has been the emergence of his skill position talent with Caleb Douglas, Malik Washington, Chris Bell, Greg Dulcich and Ollie Gordon II stepping up in recent weeks. 

While the Patriots make for a tough test, Willis will have a much softer stretch versus the Lions, Colts, Bills and Jets again coming up after that. With his rushing upside giving him a solid fantasy floor, Willis will be a streaming option every week and now we're seeing the ceiling to go along with that in better matchups.

There's a reason why I haven't stopped highlighting Coleman in this column all season. In his first game back off injured reserve, the rookie immediately led the Broncos' backfield in what is now a three-man committee. 

Coleman played nearly half the snaps, while RJ Harvey and J.K. Dobbins shared the other half. Coleman also led the team in scrimmage yards (69), touches (11) and routes run (11). Unfortunately, it was Harvey who scored a long touchdown and Dobbins who took a goal-line carry into the end zone.

item.title: Week 8 NFL Power Rankings: Have the 49ers have fallen from the top rank?
item.description: Are the Niners still the top dogs in the NFL?
item.content:encoded:
The San Francisco 49ers are undefeated no more, as they fell 29-20 to the Atlanta Falcons on Sunday, dropping to 6-1 heading into the bye week.

It was not a pretty game by any means for the 49ers, who dealt with too many penalties and turnovers that took the game out of their hands. Still, it was an outing where San Francisco was quite beaten up, even forcing them to play without the regular number of players on game day.

In the weekly power rankings, the 49ers have been mainstays at the top spot for weeks. However, after a loss, they’ve finally fallen from the top rank in some places.

Here are the Week 8 NFL Power Rankings and where the 49ers stand among the consensus.

ESPN

Interestingly enough, ESPN’s power rankings is one of the lone spots that kept the 49ers at No. 1, even after the loss.

The Buffalo Bills moved up one spot to No. 2 behind them. So did the Minnesota Vikings to No. 3, while the Kansas City Chiefs fell from No. 2 to No. 4 after losing to the Seattle Seahawks. Seattle, even at 4-3, rounded things out at No. 5.

Rounding out the top ten were the Jacksonville Jaguars, Chicago Bears, Denver Broncos, Cincinnati Bengals, and New England Patriots.

FOX Sports

After being at No. 1, FOX Sports’s Ralph Vacciano dropped San Francisco all the way to No. 5 in his latest power rankings.

“I admittedly feel a little bad about dropping the 49ers this far against a Falcons team that has been impressive at times over the past few weeks, especially since I still suspect this is the best team in football — you know, in those rare moments when they’re mostly healthy,” Vacciano wrote.

“But there’s no avoiding the reality that they are incredibly banged up, and they added RB Christian McCaffrey to their injury list with a calf injury. Mostly, though, I’m concerned about this: They’ve turned the ball over eight times in the past three games, including four on Sunday. They’re too good to be that careless with the ball.”

Ahead of the 49ers are the Denver Broncos (No. 4), Kansas City Chiefs (No. 3), Minnesota Vikings (No. 2), and Buffalo Bills (No. 1).

CBS Sports

In Pete Prisco’s power rankings, the 49ers dropped, but not too far, as they moved down to No. 3 after the loss.

“They lost for the first time this season at Atlanta, and it was four turnovers that did them in Sunday,” Prisco wrote. “They head to their bye in need of key players getting healthy when they return.”

Here, only the Minnesota Vikings, who remain undefeated, and the Buffalo Bills were ahead of the 49ers, while the Chiefs and Bengals remained behind San Francisco.

Yahoo Sports

Here, even with the loss, Yahoo Sports’s Frank Schwab still has the 49ers as the No. 1 team in the NFL.

“The bye is coming at a good time for the 49ers. One of the reasons Mike Evans, Deebo Samuel Sr., Nick Bosa and others might have been inactive Sunday was because the bye would give them an extra week of rest before their return. Niners tight end George Kittle was unwilling to use the injuries as an excuse for the loss to the Falcons.”

“It’s the NFL, injuries happen,” Kittle told NBC Sports Bay Area. “It’s just how much depth do you have, how many vets do you have that can stay healthy that can like continue to keep the elevation, like the standard of play up, you know, that’s all that really matters.”

Overall, the Niners are still considered, at worst, a top-five team with their rough loss on Sunday, and now get the bye week to regroup and regain some key pieces from injury.

item.title: Saints WR Barion Brown shines in Paris
item.description: The rookie made the most of his opportunities as both a receiver and return specialist.
item.content:encoded:
The New Orleans Saints struggled in Sunday’s loss to the Pittsburgh Steelers in Paris, but rookie Barion Brown provided one of the team’s few bright spots.

Brown made an impact in all phases of the game, showcasing his big-play ability as a receiver while also one special teams. The rookie hauled in all three of his targets for 57 receiving yards, including a 49-yard reception that gave the Saints a much-needed spark.

The former LSU Tiger also contributed in the return game, recording three kickoff returns for 77 yards with a long of 42 yards. He added another 20 yards on his lone punt return.

According to Pro Football Focus, Brown earned a 90.5 offensive grade, an 89.2 receiving grade and a 90.4 special teams grade, which highlight just how effective Brown was on Sunday.

While the Saints ultimately fell short against Pittsburgh, Brown’s performance offered an encouraging sign from a rookie who has proven he can contribute in several areas. His ability to generate explosive plays in the passing game and provide a spark on special teams could help him carve out a larger role as the season progresses.

item.title: NFL Power Rankings Week 8 Roundup: Chiefs drop after first loss
item.description: Let’s see where Kansas City is ranked for Week 8 of the NFL season.
item.content:encoded:
In Week 7 of the 2026 NFL regular season, the Kansas City Chiefs lost to the Seattle Seahawks in front of a primetime audience.

Let’s see how the national media reacted to itin this week’s sampling of power rankings:

ESPN: 4

(Down from 2)

Best offseason addition: RB Kenneth Walker III

Despite his disappointing return to Seattle on Sunday, Walker has perhaps been the biggest reason the Chiefs are atop the AFC standings. He is second in the league with 701 rushing yards; his production has made life easier for quarterback Patrick Mahomes, who has excelled at play-action passes. At this point last season, the Chiefs realized they didn’t have any explosion in their running attack. Now the Chiefs’ biggest strength on offense has been when Mahomes hands the ball off to his new teammate. — Nate Taylor

— Nate Taylor

The Athletic: 3

(Down from 2)

Something spooky: An offensive blip

That was the first time in Patrick Mahomes’ career that his offense didn’t reach the end zone in some fashion. And frankly, it could’ve been even more lopsided if not for a Sam Darnold interception in the end zone. Still, the Chiefs should be fine. That game probably said more about Seattle’s defense than it did about Kansas City’s offense.

— Chad Graff and Josh Kendall

Pro Football Talk: 5

(Down from 2)

They badly need help at receiver.

— Mike Florio

CBSSports.com: 4

(Down from 2)

They are just too limited on offense without a big-play threat receiver. They need to make a move to get Patrick Mahomes some help.

— Pete Prisco

Yahoo! Sports: 4

(Down from 2)

The Chiefs are allowed one bad game, in a hostile road environment against a great defense. They couldn’t get anything going in a 20-3 loss. But it was troubling how little Kansas City did on offense once Kenneth Walker III was taken out of the equation. Walker had 36 rushing yards. Nobody else made an impact; no other Chief posted more than 44 yards.

Rashee Rice was out and that affected the offense. However, the Chiefs still have to be considered a candidate to make a trade for a receiver before the deadline to alleviate their recurring issues in the passing game.

“So you got to feel it on that plane ride home and understand that it sucks. But then how can you build off of it?” quarterback Patrick Mahomes said, via Chiefs Wire. “The biggest thing is as we get back and get back to that film study on the Broncos, you got to see where you made your mistakes and how they’re going to try to execute, and then do stuff to combat that and play better. So, obviously, it sucks right now, but we’ll be full steam ahead, trying to do our best to find a way to win this next week.”

— Frank Schwab

USA Today: 6

(Down from 2)

They don’t get the benefit of the doubt San Francisco does, and this could be a generous ranking after the first game of Patrick Mahomes’ career in which he never took a snap in the red zone. The offense’s 213 yards was also a new low under the three-time Super Bowl MVP … granted Mahomes could use better blocking and some help at wideout, especially against a unit like the “Dark Side.”

— Nate Davis

Sports Illustrated: 6

(Down from 2)

What we saw on Sunday was the epitome of how incredible Kenneth Walker III has been over the first six weeks of the season. You can cover up a lot of question marks by rushing the ball for more than 130 yards a game. 

— Conor Orr

Sporting News: 3

(Down from 1)

The Chiefs met a frightening Seahawks defense on the road at night that gave Patrick Mahomes and Kenneth Walker III chills they hadn’t experienced together this season. It’s not often they look so flat and lost but it’s good to get some out of it out of their system ahead of a huge division clash in Denver.

— Vinnie Iyer

FOX Sports: 3

(Down from 2)

The Chiefs were bound to stumble at some point, but that was one ugly way to do it. Patrick Mahomes managed just 165 passing yards and an interception against the tough Seattle defense. And RB Kenneth Walker III was held to just 36 rushing yards by his former team. Given how bad that was, it’s probably worth noting that the Chiefs haven’t exactly played a tough schedule. They are now set up for a very interesting rematch this week with the best team they beat: the Broncos.

Stat To Know: During the 20-3 loss to the Seahawks, Kansas City never reached the red zone, the first time that has happened in a Patrick Mahomes NFL start, with Sunday being his 153rd career start, including the playoffs. 

— Ralph Vacchiano

item.title: Film study: The good, the bad from Lions offense vs. Packers
item.description: The Detroit Lions offense showed a lot of good and some bad against the Green Bay Packers
item.content:encoded:
The Detroit Lions battled self-inflicted adversity as it scrapped out a 20-17 victory over the Green Bay Packers to start the season 1-0 in the NFC North.

Not how the prognosticators drew it up, the Lions defense had its best game of the season, stepping up in critical situations to hold the Packers to just 17 points. Although, some had pointed out the Packers’ deep passing game is a paper tiger. Might want to bookmark that to revisit in Week 18.

While the final score was 20-17, the Lions were definitively the better team on the field for most of the game. By comparison of success rate, this was the second largest margin of play of the Week 7 slate.

Unfortunately, costly turnovers and a failed fourth-and-goal in the second half held the Lions offense back from hitting its normal 30+ points per game output.

For this week’s film study, I want to take a look at both the good things the Lions offense did, and then look at the bad to improve on moving forward.

The good

Always start with the good.

Designed for Jameson Williams

Below is my favorite schemed play of the game. Jameson Williams is a nightmare for defensive coordinators because he can take the top off the defense at any moment with his speed. But in the red zone, that vertical threat is mitigated by spacing. Here, offensive coordinator Drew Petzing does an awesome job designing a play for Williams using his speed horizontally.

Below, Williams is set in motion presnap into the box behind the offensive line. At the snap, he continues horizontally into the flat. His speed is already hard to keep up with, but when he is hidden and mixed with the traffic and movement of the play action fake, it is a near impossible assignment for the defense.

The other critical element of the play design is Amon-Ra St. Brown lining up at the wing slot, and inserting inside the B-gap with the run-action. Most safeties and/or linebackers have keys that read this action as a run principle resulting in the first steps of the play side linebacker and deep safety to be downhill at the B-gap. From there, it’s an easy pitch and catch for Jared Goff.

Not-a-statue Jared Goff for MVP

After another great performance, Goff is finally starting to get the national attention he deserves for his historic start to the 2026 season. Dan Campbell has been consistent in his praise for Goff and the consistent, elite quarterback play he is showing week-in and week-out.

Goff does all of the things presnap that go unnoticed in the mental and command elements of the offense, and he does them at a high level. His trained eyes in the play action game is being recognized as being elite.

But when it comes to MVP voting, it’s typically the highlight reel out-of-structure plays that win the day. Goff is never going to match Josh Allen, Lamar Jackson, or Caleb Williams in this part of the game, obviously. It is time, however, to dispel the narrative that Goff is just a statue in the pocket. An immobile pocket passer that once pushed off his spot, he’s in trouble.

Below I want to spotlight two plays where Jared Goff uses his legs to create two big plays while while throwing off platform.

The first one is the touchdown pass to Jameson Williams. While Penei Sewell sitting in the zone on the mesh concept has garnered the spotlight, take a moment to watch how Goff navigates the pocket, feeling the pressure and driving forward, stepping forward to complete the pass to Williams. Jameson even noted that it was a no-look pass from Goff.

  1. Goff extended the play with his legs
  2. Threw the ball off platform, across his body
  3. No-look pass while drawing defenders toward Sewell.

On the second play below, Goff immediately recognizes the creeping safety and blitzing linebacker to his right and exits the pocket to his left. Shuffling his feet, Goff backs an accurate throw to Amon-Ra St. Brown on a dig route going in the opposite direction as Goff’s momentum. The combination of both his mental processing as well as his athleticism to throw on the run rendered the Packers blitz moot, a huge component that will come in handy when the Lions match up against the Minnesota Vikings historically blitz-heavy scheme.

Strong signs from the offensive line

With center Cade Mays making his return and first start as a Lions, plenty of attention was given situation as backup Juice Scruggs had played well in his absence.

Below is a third-and-1 run resulting in a first down, a critical situational area of the game that also reared its ugly head in the fourth quarter (more on that later).

The key point I wanted to highlight here is the recognition and pickup on this outside zone run following the late presnap shift from the Packers defensive line.

The bad

While there were strong signals from the offensive line, there were also a handful of missed assignments leading to negative plays.

The first play here shows some missed assignment/miscommunication up front. With left guard Christian Mahogany combo-blocking the nose with center Cade Mays and left tackle Penei Sewell working up to the play side linebacker, the B-gap defensive tackle is left untouched to make the tackle behind the line of scrimmage.

These types of mistakes are self-inflicted, and should become far and few between as the season progresses.

The fourth-and-1

Let’s get to the big one. To start, I agree with the decision to go for it on fourth down here. Beyond the generic historical analytical models given the field position and time on the clock remaining, it’s important to consider the particular teams on the field. In most games, the Lions offense will likely be the single best unit on the field on either side of the football. The weight given to that part of the equation needs to be adjusted and considered above the generic historic analytical models. That is, take the generic historical analytical model and adjust the weights and parameters to get a personalized approach for each game context.

Now, while I approve of the decision from Dan Campbell to go, I do not like the play call from Petzing in this situation.

I will admit, there are advantages to the play design particular for this situation. The part I do not like is that it did leave the team vulnerable in the exact way that the Packers took advantage of.

Let’s break it down in detail.

First, the clip of the full play is provided below.

Diagrammed, the unique part of this run concept is that it appears to blend duo and power gap concepts. On short yardage, duo has the positive element of preventing penetration and displacing the defensive front. Combining this with power elements (the pulling right guard and fullback trap motion), the offense creates a numbers and angle advantage for critical play side blocks. On paper, this checks all the boxes for a critical short yardage play.

The flaw, in my opinion, is in the details.

Spotlighted below is the backside of the formation. The vulnerability here is the presentation of the cornerback as an active run defender at the line of scrimmage. If the corner starts the play at the snap where he was when the offensive line made its presnap line call, he is not an impact player in the success of this down-and-distance play call.

The other interesting note is that the inline tight end here is none other than wide receiver Isaac TeSlaa. First, credit to TeSlaa for sticking his nose in the play and taking on the edge player.

Putting TeSlaa down at the line is not my criticism of the play. My guess is that Petzing designed the play this way to hold the cornerback from blitzing the way he did at the snap. TeSlaa is a big threat the release on a play-action concept. My criticism is that when you have a quarterback that has elite command of the offense, I want to put the play in his hands to make adjustments. The snap took place with five seconds left on the play clock.

I’m making an assumption that could be wrong, but this play is not set up or is executed like they had two plays called in the huddle to check out of when that corner presents on the backside edge. Maybe the idea is to not give the blitzing defender predictable timing to jump the run, but the Packers aggression paid off.

In critical spots, give the on-field coach the opportunity to correct problems when the game is on the line.

The other element of this design that I do not like is the level of difficulty in assignment that is put on tight end Sam LaPorta. Below is the front side of the play. LaPorta is asked to reach and gain inside leverage on the edge defender Lukas Van Ness (90) on his inside gap. This is an insane block from LaPorta (pay the man). But I don’t like fighting against the natural leverage LaPorta already has. Instead of blending the duo and power concepts, sticking to a true power concept on critical downs puts less strain on the players.

This fourth down play call is one that I think adds up to perfection on the chalkboard, but in practice there are critical points where failure can break the dam.

Overall, the Lions offense was way more good than bad. And the bad is mostly self-inflicted mistakes that this young offensive line can continue to grow and learn from. The 2023 Detroit Lions leaned on a veteran offensive line to win in critical situations.

This 2026 offensive line has the potential to provide the same late in the season. The ultimate fate of the team likely depends on it.

item.title: NFL Power Rankings for Week 8: Denver Broncos somewhere up there
item.description: The Denver Broncos are hardest team to figure out among NFL playoff contenders. At least if you are a national media writer doing weekly power rankings.
item.content:encoded:
It’s been a few weeks since I’ve run a power rankings update, but after a three-game win streak it felt like a good barometer check for how the national media feels about these Denver Broncos.

The answer was that there is no consensus and they have Denver all over the map in these rankings. From the best spot at third in the NFL to the worst at twelfth. The consensus seems to be around the sixth or seventh spot if you take out the extremes.

That could all change this week is the Broncos take care of business at home against the Kansas City Chiefs. They will move into first place in the AFC West and put the Chiefs into ‘catch-up’ mode after being one of the only unbeaten teams in the NFL just two days ago.

Here’s how the Broncos are doing in this week’s power rankings around the web:

CBS Sports – 7th

The offense showed signs of life against the Cardinals. That’s progress. Maybe it took a long touchdown run for Bo Nix to get him going this season.

NBC Sports – 6th

Take that, Ryan Fitzpatrick.

ESPN – 8th

Rookie running back Jonah Coleman has played in only three games because of an ankle injury, and he might win the impact-per-snap-played quotient, but Waddle leads the Broncos in receptions (26) and receiving yards (276). His numbers would likely look better if he had not been caught up in the swirl of Denver’s passing struggles. Waddle left Sunday’s game because of an apparent shoulder injury, but if it’s not serious and the Broncos can simply get him the ball more, his output will improve along with their offense.

Yahoo Sports – 12th

It’s unfair to just eliminate three long plays for a team and judge it on the rest of its production. Those explosive plays are earned. And the Broncos got a 62-yard touchdown run from Bo Nix, a 52-yard touchdown on a short pass to RJ Harvey and a 47-yard catch to Marvin Mims Jr. that set up a touchdown.

On the Broncos’ other 53 plays, they gained only 216 yards. That’s a middling 4 yards per play. Still, Sunday was another win. The Broncos are 5-2 and the Chiefs’ loss on Sunday sets up a game that should frame the rest of the AFC West race as the Chiefs visit Denver in Week 8. The Broncos will have to find some consistency on offense and they have a few key injuries to track: receiver Jaylen Waddle has a chest injury, defensive lineman Zach Allen hurt his hamstring and cornerback Pat Surtain II has missed three straight games with an ankle injury.

USA Today – 3rd

Bo Nix looked like a functional quarterback Sunday in the team’s best offensive showing of the season. Next, he gets the opportunity to make up for Week 1’s disappearing act in Kansas City.

Fox Sports – 4th

The Broncos may have scored 30 points against the Cardinals, but this team still has a Bo Nix problem. He scored on a 62-yard run of his own and threw a short pass that RB R.J. Harvey turned into a 52-yard score. But other than that, the Broncos quarterback was once again unimpressive and downright shaky. Maybe this is just the way it’s going to be. The Broncos are just going to keep finding a way to win. But Nix is probably going to have to get it together at some point — like, perhaps, next Sunday against the Chiefs.

Bleacher Report – 6th

Finally, the Denver Broncos got a little juice instead of being held back by the quarterback position. 

Bo Nix opened up the Broncos offense with a 62-yard touchdown run. More importantly, the third-year quarterback began to push the ball downfield more against the Arizona Cardinals than he did during Denver’s previous six games. 

As a result, the Broncos built a halftime lead and continued to score on their first three second-half drives. 

The performance was a welcome change of pace after Denver struggled to get anything going during the first half of previous contests, which makes the Broncos a more complete team as the season progresses.

What do you think of these power rankings? Share in the comments section below!

item.title: Bill Belichick wants ACC to add more goal line cameras after controversial Syracuse finish
item.description: During much of his time in the NFL, Bill Belichick called for the NFL to spend the money necessary to install cameras that would make it easier to review plays.
item.content:encoded:
During much of his time in the NFL, Bill Belichick called for the NFL to spend the money necessary to install cameras that would make it easier to review plays. In his second season as a college coach, Belichick is banging that same drum.

Via Brian Murphy of WRAL, Belichick wants the ACC to add cameras at the goal line and along the sidelines to assist the replay officials.

The issue is particularly relevant because Belichick's North Carolina team lost to Syracuse on a controversial all-or-nothing two-point play in overtime. The ruling on the field was that Syracuse had successfully earned the decisive two points. The call was upheld via the available replay angles.

“If he scored he scored,” Belichick said Monday. “If he didn’t score, he didn’t score. Just put a camera there and get it right. That’s what I’m for. But based on what was called on the field, the views that the officials had, I don’t know how you could possibly overturn it. The view was from a long, long way away.”

At both the college and pro level, replay overturns the real-time ruling only if there is clear and obvious evidence to the contrary.

“From what the officials had to work with, it would be hard to tell,” Belichick said of the game-deciding play. “I think from what the fans showed — they had some good footage of it — that there are different views there that the officials in Charlotte, the headquarters there where they looked at reviews of the game, they didn't have those films. So the answer to the question is to put goal line and sideline cameras on the lines so that you have a good look at those plays.”

More official cameras would increase the chances of getting a decisive look.

"The ACC doesn't have goalline cameras," Belichick said. "They don't have sideline cameras, like the other conferences do, and that's something that I've always advocated when I was in the NFL for 20 years — sideline cameras, end zone cameras, like in tennis. Put on the sideline, put on the goal line, put on the end line. Those are the scoring [views], especially in college football, where you have the overtime rule, which is going to put you in the red zone. . . .

“All the other conferences have them. The ACC doesn't have them. I'm not sure why, but we've talked about that in league meetings. But for some reason, we don't have them, and I think it would be good for the game to get a definitive look at every play like that.”

He's right. Too much rides on these games to pinch pennies when it comes to the replay function. It's only as good as what the video evidence reveals. More video evidence is always better.

In the years since Belichick was fired by the Patriots, the NFL has implemented a Hawk-Eye system of stationary cameras in all stadiums that provides angles not provided by the TV broadcast, which has more or fewer cameras based on the window.

item.title: Jerry Jones: Troy Aikman working for Cowboys in future is "very possible"
item.description: Troy Aikman was in Philadelphia to call Monday night's game between the Cowboys and the Eagles and he took some time before it got underway to catch up with his first boss in the NFL.
item.content:encoded:
Troy Aikman was in Philadelphia to call Monday night's game between the Cowboys and the Eagles and he took some time before it got underway to catch up with his first boss in the NFL.

Aikman's conversation with Cowboys owner Jerry Jones before the Dallas win comes at a moment of professional uncertainty for Aikman. His contract with ESPN will be up at the end of the season and he recently said he would "have a hard time not taking a good look" at a chance to work for the organization that drafted him with the first overall pick in 1989.

Aikman has worked as a consultant for the Dolphins and Jones was asked on 105.3 The Fan on Tuesday if he's open to the idea of Aikman taking on a significant role in the organization. Jones said he "could and would" be open to that notion and called Aikman "certainly qualified" to take on that kind of job.

"He’s one of the hardest working, most focused people that I’ve ever been around," Jones said. "When you’re around each other, a part of that makeup can make it where you have your ups and downs. I think the world of him. I’ve seen his image and had it in my eyes since I walked in the NFL. He's outstanding. The answer is not necessarily that we're going to do something more direct with the team at this time, but don’t rule it out. It is very possible."

Very possible and definitely happening are far from the same thing, but smoke signals about a possible partnership could prove to be foreshadowing for what will take place when and if it becomes definite that Aikman is going to be looking for a new job come the end of the 2026 season.

item.title: Fantasy Football Kicker Streamers: The 3 best pickups for Week 8
item.description: A close look at which kickers should get plenty of field goal opportunities in Week 8.
item.content:encoded:
Kickers are creatures of game script.

In fantasy football that doesn’t make them any different than a lot of running backs and wideouts and tight ends. For those positions, as with kicker, opportunity evaporates with unfriendly game script.

The receiver or tight end sees a dip in routes and targets when their team gets out to a big lead and runs the rock in the second half. The running back ends up with ten carries instead of twenty because his team has to abandon the run as they chase points in a trailing script. In an opportunity-based game, this is something short of ideal.

That’s why we want kickers in our lineups whose teams have a good chance of seeing plenty of neutral or positive game script. Usually this means a team won’t forgo easy field goal opportunities in the second half, down by multiple scores. So there is a process to selecting kickers — even those off the waiver wire.

Fantasy Football Waiver Wire Week 8: Caleb Douglas breaks out, Omar Cooper Jr. stays hot
Omar Cooper Jr. stayed hot with another 100 yards and a touchdown in Week 7. Fellow rookie Caleb Douglas also broke out with two touchdowns of his own. Both players headline the list of best waiver wire targets for Week 8.
  • Kyle Dvorchak,

In this space I’ll highlight a few waiver kicker options who check the boxes of a viable play. Some, of course, will be better than others. Oh, and one more thing: Accuracy doesn’t really matter at all. We want opportunity.

Week 7 Results:

  • Andy Borregales: 7 points
  • Ryan Fitzgerald: 1 point
  • Jason Sanders: 4 points

They’re calling it a “rough week” for Rotoworld’s resident kicker bro. And it was, thanks largely to out-of-control game script in the Bucs-Panthers game that rendered Fitzgerald irrelevant for three quarters as Carolina faced a 200-point deficit. As for Sanders: The previously lifeless Dolphins showed signs of life in Week 7 and grabbed an early lead, which is never good for the kicker on the other side. So it goes.

Week 8 Kicker Options

Trey Smack (GB) vs. Panthers

Carolina’s defense has shown some serious cracks in recent weeks. They can safely be labeled one of the NFL’s worst run defenses, and their injury-riddled secondary isn’t going to stop Jordan Love and company. Maybe that’s why Green Bay is a seven-point favorite here.

That should put Smack in good position to try multiple field goals against a Carolina team that has given up multiple field goal attempts in four of its past five games. The Packers rank 30th in red zone touchdown rate this season. Maybe that will regress (positively) in the coming weeks, but against the Panthers, I like their chances of putting up a lot of points.

That Smack has missed five of his 16 field goal tries this season might make you queasy bordering on nauseated. That’s OK. Take an antacid and plug in Smack for Week 8.

Evan McPherson (CIN) vs. Titans

Fresh off a gaudy four field goal performance against the Ravens, McPherson now has multiple field goal attempts in three straight outings as the Bengals offense overcomes its annual early-season doldrums. Joe Burrow is finally awake and operating with swiftness and efficiency.

McPherson, available in more than half of leagues, should be considered a top kicker option for Week 8. The Bengals are averaging almost five red zone possessions per game over their past three games and the Titans -- as you can see -- allow the third most field goals on the season.

Jason Sanders (NYJ) vs. Raiders

We’re doing the Sanders Thing again because it was so much fun in Week 7 (it wasn’t). He’s in another good spot against a Raiders team giving up the league’s highest EPA per play and offensive success rate since Week 3. The Jets, meanwhile, are 1.5-point home favorites.

Look for another productive day for Geno Smith and his pass catchers here. They should be able to move the ball at will against Vegas’ marshmallow-soft defense. Vegas opponents are averaging four red zone trips per game, the fourth highest mark in the NFL. The Raiders are two weeks removed from giving up four field goals to the Bills. Sanders is most definitely in play.

item.title: Fantasy Football Backup RB Rankings: Jordan Mason's return in Week 7 shakes up Vikings' backfield
item.description: Fred Zinkie examines the best second-string backs for fantasy football heading into Week 8.
item.content:encoded:
Let's take a look at the backup RBs, who are listed in the order that they should be rostered, taking into account both their immediate fantasy football value as a flex option and their long-term potential to take on a larger role.

1. Braelon Allen, Jets (87% rostered on Yahoo)

Although Breece Hall missed a fourth straight game, the fact that his availability came down to game day suggests that he will return this week. Allen had another outstanding effort in Hall’s absence, gaining 104 yards on 17 carries and 30 yards on six catches.

At this point, there is no doubt that Allen will have a role when Hall returns. After all, Allen has averaged 5.0 yards per carry and 89 rushing yards per game over the four contests Hall has missed. There is even a chance that although Hall will return to his starting role, Allen will be the one to receive more carries. He’s a solid RB2 or flex option for a favorable home game against the Raiders, while we seek some certainty on the Jets’ backfield split.

2. Jonah Coleman/RJ Harvey, Broncos (35%/82%)

Well, that didn’t take long. In his first game off the IR, Coleman led the Broncos backfield in snap share, and his 30 snaps were as many as Harvey (16) and starter J.K. Dobbins (14) combined. Coleman not only played more than the veterans — he also played better. The rookie averaged 6.0 yards on his nine carries, in comparison to 3.8 yards per carry for Dobbins and 2.0 yards per carry for Harvey.

Coleman also factored into the passing game by gaining 15 yards on two catches. It was Harvey who made the big play in this area, with a 52-yard receiving touchdown. He had one other catch, while Dobbins was not targeted at all.

There is no doubt that Coleman is the Denver RB that fantasy managers want to have on their roster, as he’s the only member of the trio who could soon receive 15 touches per game. In PPR leagues, Harvey would be the second choice thanks to his consistent involvement in the passing game.

3. Kyle Monangai, Bears (77%)

Monangai has missed three straight games with thumb and toe injuries. The Bears have not put him in injured reserve, which suggests that they expect him to miss fewer than four games by returning this week. D’Andre Swift has assumed a workhorse role in Monangai’s absence, and while he has scored four times in his past three games, Swift has averaged 3.2 yards per carry over the past two contests.

With Caleb Williams at the helm, the Bears offense is among the best in the NFL. The return on Monangai will give the running game more power and explosiveness than Swift can provide, and there are plenty of analysts who see Monangai as the team’s best ball-carrier.

4. Blake Corum, Rams (82%)

The public complaints from Kyren Williams after Week 6 had no impact on the Rams’ backfield split, as the veteran logged a 53% snap share in Week 7 in comparison to a 47% share for Corum. The even split seemed to work, as Williams averaged 6.2 yards on 16 carries and Corum averaged 5.5 yards on his 17 rushes. Both players scored a touchdown on the ground and neither had much impact on the passing game.

While Williams remains the starter and preferred fantasy option, Corum is also having an excellent season by averaging 4.9 yards per carry and tallying three scores in seven games. The Rams should score plenty of points in the coming weeks, as their next three opponents are the Chargers, Commanders and Cardinals. Corum is easily a flex option for those contests.

5. Woody Marks, Texans (90%)

David Montgomery missed a second straight game, and in his absence, Marks was once again underwhelming but somewhat effective. The second-year pro gained 66 yards on 19 carries and caught one pass for 15 yards in an overtime loss to the Giants.

We have a good read on Marks at this point. He can grind out yards on the ground but isn’t especially effective and is averaging just 3.5 yards per carry this season. And although he is known to have some skills as a receiver, C.J. Stroud rarely opts to throw to his running backs. Marks is an uninspiring RB2 or flex option who can keep managers from taking a zero but is unlikely to score more than 10 points.

6. Aaron Jones Sr., Vikings (93%)

The return of Jordan Mason caused the Vikings to list their top-two running backs as co-starters on their official depth chart. For the purposes of this article, Jones will be treated as the backup after Mason received seven more carries in Week 7. Admittedly, Jones missed most of the fourth quarter after suffering a knee injury on a 17-yard run. But Mason was already leading the team in carries when Jones left the game.

The Vikings were clear last week that Mason was going to receive a heavy workload. Given that he is five years younger than Jones and has 75 fewer carries this season, it would make sense for Mason to be leaned on in the coming weeks in an effort to keep both players healthy. Jones is now a weak flex option whose case for lineup inclusion would be better if Kyler Murray threw more passes to his running backs.

7. Bam Knight, Cardinals (25%)

Although the Cardinals fell behind early and trailed throughout a 30-16 loss to the Broncos, Knight was a bright spot for a second straight week. The 25-year-old averaged 6.9 yards on seven carries after averaging 5.3 yards on 15 carries in the Cardinals’ Week 6 win over the Rams. He also caught three passes after tallying two receptions the previous game.

The coaching staff will likely highlight Jeremiyah Love when he returns from an ankle injury, which could happen as soon as this week. But it’s worth wondering if Knight is their best rushing option, given that Love is averaging 3.7 yards per carry in comparison to 6.4 for Knight. Given that Love is a skilled receiver who hasn’t done much in the passing game as a rookie, it may make sense to divide the carries evenly and give Love more work on third down.

8. Mike Washington Jr., Raiders (29%)

While the QB situation is the hop topic in Las Vegas, the RB workload likely deserves more scrutiny. Washington outperformed Ashton Jeanty yet again in Week 7, with the rookie averaging 4.5 yards on six carries in comparison to 1.9 yards on eight carries for Jeanty.

Jeanty continues to make a massive impact in the passing game, which included a beautiful TD catch in Week 7. But the supposed superstar has averaged less than 4.0 yards per carry in each of his past six games and has a season average of 3.1. Meanwhile, Washington is averaging 4.9 yards per carry, and looks faster and more explosive than Jeanty. Washington doesn’t yet have the workload to be a flex option, but he’s getting closer after tallying 15 carries and two catches over the past two games.

9. Tyjae Spears, Titans (17%)

Although Spears missed Week 7 with a knee injury, there were some developments that worked in his long-term favor. First, Tony Pollard was awesome (25-129-3), which increases his appeal to contending teams. Second, the Titans lost a close game to the Browns, which dropped them to 1-6 and increased the odds that they will opt to deal the 29-year-old Pollard by the Nov. 10 deadline.

To be clear, Spears has no fantasy value in his current role. But for the cost of stashing him for a couple weeks, fantasy managers could have a starting running back for the second half of the season.

10. Kaelon Black, 49ers (28%)

The combination of multiple WR injuries and a Christian McCaffrey hamstring ailment in Week 7 gave Black a bigger role in the offense. The rookie responded well to the added workload, averaging 5.3 yards and scoring a touchdown on his 12 carries. Black’s success was reminiscent of his Week 1 effort, when he tallied 65 yards on 14 carries in a win over the Rams. In between those two games, his role had been reduced.

The Niners head into their bye week with the hope of having McCaffrey and Mike Evans at full strength in Week 9. In the event that those players are out for an extended period of time, Black would be a viable flex option after the bye. At the very least, he’s an interesting player to stash for those who have bench space given McCaffrey’s history.

The best of the rest, factoring in current Flex value and long-term potential.

  • Samaje Perine, Bengals

  • Rico Dowdle, Steelers

  • Dameon Pierce, Eagles

  • Brian Robinson Jr., Falcons

  • Keaton Mitchell, Chargers

  • TreVeyon Henderson, Patriots

  • Tyler Goodson, Cowboys

  • Kendre Miller, Saints

  • MarShawn Lloyd, Packers

  • Chris Rodriguez Jr., Jaguars

  • Justice Hill, Ravens

  • Tyrone Tracy Jr., Giants

  • Pierre Strong Jr., Packers

  • Austin Ekeler, Commanders

  • Kimani Vidal, Chargers

  • Kenny Gainwell, Buccaneers

  • Jaylen Wright, Dolphins

  • Emmett Johnson, Chiefs

Injured backups to stash

  • Zach Charbonnet, Seahawks
