item.content:encoded:
You should never underestimate the power of The Dark Side.

As was the case back in the halcyon days of 2013, the Seattle Seahawks won their championship last year with defense. Back in Super Bowl XLVIII it was Richard Sherman, Kam Chancellor and the “Legion of Boom.” In Super Bowl LX, it was Ernest Jones IV, Leonard Williams and “The Dark Side.”

And in a year when so many highly-drafted defenses have disappointed (Looking at you, Houston. Looking…right…at…you.), the fourth defense drafted on average over the summer is doing their best to repeat last season’s success.
Sunday night against Kansas City, the Seahawks completely put the clamps on an undefeated Chiefs team. Patrick Mahomes and Co. managed just 213 yards of offense, three points and three third-down conversions in 11 attempts. There wasn’t much in the way of big plays—just one takeaway and a single sack. But all told, it was a solid performance.

The Emperor was pleased.

That has been Seattle’s MO so far this season. There haven’t been the explosive fantasy outbursts like the late-season surge that propelled the Seahawks to the top spot among defenses in 2025. But there also haven’t been any clunkers, and the Seahawks presently sit right where they were drafted—in fourth place.
Flash is fun in fantasy. But at a position that is as high-variance as defenses, Steady Eddie isn’t a bad friend to have—even if he insists you call him Darth Eddie.

Fantasy Football Waiver Wire Week 8: Caleb Douglas breaks out, Omar Cooper Jr. stays hot
Omar Cooper Jr. stayed hot with another 100 yards and a touchdown in Week 7. Fellow rookie Caleb Douglas also broke out with two touchdowns of his own. Both players headline the list of best waiver wire targets for Week 8.
  • Kyle Dvorchak,

▶ THE NO-DOUBTERS

Cincinnati Bengals (vs. Tennessee Titans)

In what is the most 2026 thing about 2026, the surest bet among fantasy defenses (or as sure as they get) in Week 8 may well be…the Cincinnati Bengals. Cincy’s offseason improvements on the defensive side of the ball have resulted in an AFC-high 21 sacks, a tie for the fifth-most takeaways in the league and the sixth-most fantasy points among defenses. The Bengals have had four good weeks and a pair of bad ones, and this week they host a Tennessee offense that ranks dead last in total offense and 31st in points per game. Good week incoming.

Jacksonville Jaguars (vs. Indianapolis Colts)

After a hot start to the season, the Jaguars have tailed off in recent weeks, with their loss in London two weeks ago being their worst defensive effort of the season. Now back in the States and coming off the bye, the Jags are in a prime spot to rebound against a reeling Colts team that appears headed toward a trade deadline fire sale. The Jaguars are leading the league in run defense for the second year in a row. The only reliable offense the Colts have is Jonathan Taylor—assuming he isn’t dealt. Get where I’m going with this?

Pittsburgh Steelers (vs. Cleveland Browns)

Not since these two teams met in the Wild Card Round in 2021 have the stakes been this big for a matchup between these longtime rivals in the Steel City. The Browns won that matchup, but the last time the Browns beat the Steelers in the regular season in Pittsburgh was 2003. The Steelers are third among all defenses in fantasy points and tied for third in sacks. The Browns lead the league in sacks allowed with 25 and have given up the sixth-most fantasy points per game to defenses. Can’t argue with math.

Denver Broncos (vs. Kansas City Chiefs)

The Broncos opened the season getting boatraced at Arrowhead by the Chiefs, and Denver’s inconsistent offense has put a lot of pressure on the defense to make plays. But the Chiefs team that won that Week 1 matchup wasn’t 13 kinds of banged up at wide receiver, and the injuries showed last week in Seattle. Since that Week 1 faceplant, only the Vikings have more fantasy points among defenses, and the return of edge-rusher Jonathon Cooper is a boost to an already formidable pass rush.

Green Bay Packers (vs. Carolina Panthers)

Despite being down their best pass-rusher and top two linebackers on the road against Detroit’s high-octane offense last week, the Packers held the Lions to 20 points and posted the sixth-most fantasy points among defenses for the week—the same spot they occupy for the season. No team in the league has turned opponents over more. And this week at Lambeau Field brings a visit from a Panthers team that just got hammered at home by the Tampa Bay Buccaneers while surrendering the biggest fantasy score of the week.

Cleveland Browns (at Pittsburgh Steelers)

This matchup has the potential to be quite the old-school brouhaha—a defensive battle where the first team to 17 wins. Someone forgot to tell Cleveland they can’t play defense without Myles Garrett—the Browns are seventh against the pass, sit second in the NFL with 20 sacks and have scored the eighth-most fantasy points among defenses, Meanwhile, the Steelers sit just outside the top-10 in points per game allowed to the position, and Aaron Rodgers has been dropped 22 times. The last time these teams met, Rodgers was sacked five times and the Steelers turned the ball over twice.

▶ STREAMERS OF THE WORLD, UNITE!

Los Angeles Rams (vs. Los Angeles Chargers)

This is where we are with the Rams defense. A team that was drafted as an elite fantasy option has so thoroughly disappointed through half of the fantasy regular season that they are a matchup play at best despite taking on the only thing at SoFi Stadium more depressing than they are—the winless Chargers. The Chargers are mired at the bottom of the league in many offensive categories and have surrendered more fantasy points per game to defenses than any team in the league. If the Rams can’t post a number here? Drop them.

New England Patriots (at Miami Dolphins)

It has admittedly been a rollercoaster ride for the Patriots defense this year. There have been highs, and there have been lows. Week 7 brought the latter, although they aren’t the first defense that the Chicago Bears have made look foolish in 2026. But the former should be in store this week—the Miami Dolphins have shown some signs of life on offense the past couple of times out, but we’re still talking about a one-win team that has allowed the sixth-most fantasy points per game to defenses this season.

Tampa Bay Buccaneers (vs. Atlanta Falcons)

Will the real Tampa Bay Buccaneers please stand up? On one hand, the Buccaneers are a two-win team that just played a game where they completed seven passes. On the other, the Bucs won that game by 30 points, because the defense has played at a high level all season long. The Buccaneers are second among all defenses in fantasy points after seven weeks, and perhaps most importantly this week, Tampa has the NFC’s best run defense. Atlanta is second in the NFC in fantasy points per game allowed to defenses. So there’s that, too. If the Bucs shut down Bijan Robinson and make Michael Penix throw to beat them, there’s some there there. So there.

Atlanta Falcons (at Tampa Bay Buccaneers)

The only team in the NFC allowing more fantasy points per game to defenses than the aforementioned Atlanta Falcons? Your Tampa Bay Buccaneers! If last week’s gameplan straight from 1958 is any indication, Baker Mayfield’s busted thumb isn’t close to 100 percent, and going run-heavy on the league’s fourth-best run defense isn’t going to be easy. Fresh off an upset of the unbeaten 49ers at Mercedes-Benz Stadium that included two sacks and four takeaways, the Falcons are a decent streamer play this week.

Washington Commanders (vs. Philadelphia Eagles)

From the “In Case of Emergency Break Glass” files, we have our weekly look at the bottom of the streaming barrel and the Washington Commanders. Is Washington’s defense good? Nope. Rookie linebacker Sonny Styles looks like the real deal, but the Commanders are 25th in total defense, 31st in scoring defense and 26th in fantasy points. But the Eagles have well and truly imploded—at this point the team is going to have to hold running back tryouts in the parking lot at Geno’s.

▶ CAVEAT EMPTOR, FOLKS

Seattle Seahawks (vs. Chicago Bears)

To be clear, fantasy managers who have rostered the Seahawks should just go ahead and start them—the team has shown they can at least slow down any offense, especially at home. But “slow down” may be about the best Seattle can hope for against Chicago’s buzzsaw offense—the Bears are third in the league in total offense and seventh in points scored without the services of Caleb Williams for multiple games. Their quarterback is healthy now though—and the offense is rolling.

Minnesota Vikings (at Detroit Lions)

It’s not hard to figure out why the Vikings are fantasy football’s No. 1 defense at the halfway point. Brian Flores is sending blitzers at a rate we haven’t seen since Buddy Ryan was punching Kevin Gilbride on the sideline in Houston—last week against the Indianapolis Colts, the Vikings’ blitz rate was north of 80 percent. But this week’s trip to Motown is the stiffest test the Minnesota defense has faced—on the road on a fast track indoors against the No. 2 offense in yards and the NFC’s top offense in points scored.

item.title: Fantasy Football: 5 big-name wide receivers on different parts of the panic spectrum heading into Week 8
item.description: Fantasy football analyst Ray Garvin explains why he's feeling a little antsy about some usually-productive wideouts.
item.content:encoded:
This week, we're going all wide receivers. Five different situations, five different receivers and one question heading into Week 8: who am I actually panicking about and who am I not tripping on?

Rome Odunze, Chicago Bears — SOME PANIC

I'm at some panic (with a dash of total panic) with Rome Odunze, and it has nothing to do with whether I think he's a good football player. He is. We've seen the flashes, we've seen the impressive catches and, when things are clicking, Rome looks like the receiver we thought he could become. The problem is everything happening around him in Chicago.

Luther Burden III has simply been better. He doesn't run nearly as many routes as Odunze, but when he's on the field, he's more explosive, more effective and hasn't had the same issues with drops. Then you've got Colston Loveland, whose involvement over the past couple of weeks has been outstanding. At this point, I'm starting to believe Burden and Loveland are the 1A and 1B in this passing attack. You can argue which one deserves the top spot, but I'm having a hard time making the case that Rome is anything other than third in the pecking order.

And that's before we account for how this offense operates. Chicago wants to run the football. Caleb Williams is going to extend plays and scramble, which takes away additional passing opportunities. There's only so much volume to go around, and the players making the most of their opportunities aren't named Rome Odunze.

His four catches for 69 yards against New England was encouraging, especially some of those late-game plays. But a few impressive catches aren't enough to change the bigger picture. I had much higher expectations for what Rome could become in this offense, and right now, I don't believe he's the first read or even the second. That's a problem for his fantasy outlook.

DK Metcalf, Pittsburgh Steelers — NO PANIC

I'm not panicking about DK Metcalf. This is just the DK Metcalf experience, and honestly, I think we know what we're getting at this point. He's basically a great-value version of Jameson Williams. You're going to have games where the explosive plays hit and others where you're wondering what happened to the production.

He caught just two passes for 56 yards against the Saints, but I'm not putting too much stock in one game overseas. Pittsburgh leaned on its running backs, the offense didn't need to throw a ton and Metcalf still had opportunities downfield.

The biggest reason I'm not concerned is Aaron Rodgers. Say what you want about Rodgers at this stage of his career, but he's still playing some damn good football. He's throwing touchdown passes, he's keeping this offense moving and he can still connect on those downfield shots that make Metcalf dangerous.

Metcalf saw 15 targets in Week 6 before dropping to six in Week 7. That's the kind of weekly volatility you're signing up for. I never expected him to be a high-volume possession receiver who catches eight or nine passes every week.

Would I love more consistency? Absolutely. But the quarterback play is good enough, the explosive opportunities are still there and nothing about this situation has me changing my expectations for Metcalf. No panic.

A.J. Brown, New England Patriots — TOTAL PANIC

A.J. Brown is one more bad game away from the Coping Corner. I'm already at total panic, and the only thing keeping him out of that final category is the volume he's still receiving.

I understand he missed four games with a high ankle sprain. You don't just come back from that kind of injury and immediately look like yourself. He's got to get back into football shape and find his rhythm with Drake Maye. I get all of that. But at some point, we have to acknowledge what we're watching.

Brown just doesn't look like the same explosive receiver he was a few years ago. He's not creating meaningful separation; he's leaving plays on the field and some of the bigger gains we're seeing are coming late in games rather than from him consistently beating defenders.

Since returning, he's caught six passes for 75 yards on 16 targets. Six catches! That's a lot of opportunities without much production to show for it.

And watching this offense, there are times when I'd rather see the ball going to DeMario Douglas or Hunter Henry. That's not something I expected to be saying about A.J. Brown heading into this season, but here we are.

The saving grace is that New England continues to target him. As long as he's getting those opportunities, there's still a path to fantasy relevance. But we're getting dangerously close to the point where volume alone isn't enough to justify keeping him in your lineup.

I'm giving Brown one more game to show me something. If the separation doesn't improve and these targets continue to turn into empty production, we're moving him straight into the Coping Corner and having a serious conversation about whether he belongs on fantasy benches.

Justin Jefferson, Minnesota Vikings — NO PANIC

I'm not panicking about Justin Jefferson, but I do think we need to have a conversation about what our expectations should be for him moving forward.

It's unfortunate because, since Kirk Cousins left Minnesota, we've really only seen Carson Wentz provide the kind of quarterback play that consistently supports the Justin Jefferson we're accustomed to watching. Right now, that connection just isn't happening with Kyler Murray.

Jefferson caught four passes for 44 yards against Indianapolis in a game where Murray threw for just 150 yards. That's not going to get it done for fantasy managers who invested an early first-round pick in Jefferson.

But here's why I'm not concerned about the player himself. Jefferson dealt with an ankle injury earlier in the season, and Minnesota's passing offense hasn't needed to carry this team. The Vikings are winning football games without asking Murray to throw it all over the field.

Unlike some of the other receivers on this list, there's nobody in Minnesota who's threatening Jefferson's position as the top receiving option. We're not watching another wideout consistently outperform him or take away his opportunities. The issue is the passing environment, not Jefferson's ability.

Now, do I think the elite weekly ceiling we've become accustomed to is still there? Probably not on a consistent basis, at least with the way this offense is currently operating.

But I'm confident Minnesota will figure out how to get its best offensive weapon more involved. The expectations might need to change, but I'm not selling Jefferson or panicking about his ability to produce.

Michael Wilson, Arizona Cardinals — SOME PANIC

I'm trying really hard not to move Michael Wilson into total panic, but he's making that decision more difficult every single week.

We're three weeks into this stretch where we keep looking around for excuses about why Wilson isn't producing the way we expected. And at some point, those excuses have to stop.

Marvin Harrison Jr. is gone. The Cardinals aren't winning football games. There should be plenty of opportunities for Wilson to establish himself as a reliable fantasy option in this offense, yet the production continues to disappoint.

He caught four passes for 55 yards against Denver, bringing his season totals to 37 receptions, 375 yards and one touchdown. That's simply not enough.

And the frustrating part is watching Trey McBride continue to produce. McBride caught 10 passes for 111 yards and a touchdown against the Broncos. He's getting the targets, he's finding the end zone and he doesn't seem nearly as impacted by Jacoby Brissett's struggles as Wilson does.

So how many more weeks are we going to blame the quarterback? How many more games are we going to point to the opportunities that almost happened instead of the actual fantasy production?

Wilson is getting involved. He's drawing defensive attention and there are certainly opportunities in this offense. But fantasy football is about turning those opportunities into points, and right now, that's not happening nearly enough.

I'm not at total panic just yet because I still believe there's a path for Wilson to produce with the role that's available to him. But we're getting close to that panic level. If McBride continues to dominate the valuable targets and Wilson can't find the end zone, it's going to be difficult to keep making excuses much longer.

item.title: Now comes the fall for the Eagles
item.description: Pride goes first
item.content:encoded:
Across various forms of the internet this season I have seen a common defense of Nick Sirianni, who has no answers to save a sinking ship. This defense comes in two versions of the same flavor: his team doesn’t quit/his players try hard.

First of all, so what? Players not quitting on their team is less than the bare minimum expected of a coach. 

The team is poorly coached. The game plan sucks, the play calling sucks, the in-game decisions suck, the post-game retrospect sucks. “They play hard” doesn’t have a lot of sticking power when it’s all you have. Dan Quinn is just down the road if you want a guy who brings nothing to the table other than effort.

Secondly, it looks like that ship has sailed. Jordan Mailata sowed seeds of doubts about that last week when he said the team didn’t play with “want to.” He was here for the 2020 season, he knows what a lost cause looks like.

Monday night was the same script as all season: hang around in the first half, then crumble in the second. They have the worst scoring offense in the second half, and the 6th worst scoring defense.

Even in their two wins the Eagles were outscored by Washington in the second half and tied the Titans in the second half. 

And over his career, Nick Sirianni is now 0-8 as a home underdog, and the Eagles are the only team to not win as a home underdog since 2021. He’s also never covered. Granted, half of those games the line was 3 points or less, but they usually don’t come close to covering, nor do they muck up the game.

Pride comes before the fall. When you no longer have “they played hard” as a fall back, what is left? Nothing.

The 2012 team was 3-1 then lost 8 straight. The 2015 team was 4-4, a month later the starting RB was complaining to the owner on the plane. The 2020 team was 3-4-1, finished 1-7. 

This season is over. All that is left is the shouting.

item.title: Commanders RB Rachaad White needs to elevate his game; can he do it? - Daily Slop

The Daily Slop – 27 October 2026

Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy!

Commanders links

Articles

Bullock’s Film Room (subscription)

Commanders Film Review: Under Center Struggles

[Note: the play described in the excerpt below can be viewed in the video embedded in the tweet]

[S]ix games into the season, we’ve yet to really see a huge shift in under center usage. It’s definitely gone up compared to the past two years, but they are still in the bottom three in the NFL for under center usage rates so far this season. Now, part of that is the game situation. The Commanders have been behind in a lot of games this year, which naturally leads to the offense having to pass more and using the shotgun as a result. But part of the reason for the lack of under center usage is also its effectiveness. The Commanders started off the season with some nice looks from under center, but as the season has progressed it’s become less and less effective.

So why is that and what can David Blough and the Commanders offense do to remedy that? Well first we need to look at what they were doing that worked at the start of the year. They entered the season with the intent to run the ball more from under center and lean into more of a wide zone run scheme. Early on, that had good results.

As they went into their second game of the season against the Cowboys, we started to see Blough use some nice sequencing to set up play-action passes.

[On] the run by White on the previous play, the Cowboys [kept] two safeties back deep. Their defensive coordinator comes from the Vic Fangio tree that likes to keep both safeties back deep when possible. However, due to the success of that run from that look earlier, you’ll notice on this play that while the Cowboys show two deep safeties initially, one of those safeties rotates down into the box late to help support the run. Keep that in mind as we dive into the passing concept now.

The Commanders run a play-action concept that is known as “Rider” in the Shanahan tree. On Rider, you have two main routes. To the left of the formation, Terry McLaurin runs a high cross, working to about 20 yards of depth as he crosses the middle of the field. On the other side, Treylon Burks runs a streak right down the seam. This combination is a great one to attack single-high safety coverages like the one the Cowboys play here. Remember my point earlier about how the Cowboys were forced out of their two deep safety structure with this look. It’s important now because this concept puts the single deep safety in conflict. Should he sink back and stay on top of the go route and risk giving up an easy throw underneath him, or should he attach to the high cross and risk giving up the shot over the top?

In most situations, the deep safety sinks back and takes away the deepest route, which is the correct thing to do. However, as Jayden Daniels drops back to pass, he reads the safety and spots him playing shallow and opening his body to McLaurin’s route, indicating he’s looking to take over that route and cut it off. So Daniels immediately knows he has Burks on the go route and pulls the trigger. Unfortunately, Daniels puts just slightly too much on the pass and despite Burks making a full diving effort, the ball grazes his fingertips and falls incomplete.

While the result might not have been what the Commanders would have wanted, that’s more down to the execution. If Daniels takes a yard off that throw, Burks has an uncontested 55-yard touchdown. The scheme was a good one from Blough and it was made even better by the set up. That’s what the best play callers do. They sequence their plays so they show a look early in the game, come back to it later to bait the defense into thinking it’s the same play, only to fool them with a twist.

Despite that promising start, the effectiveness of the Commanders under center game has dropped off significantly. I believe that is in large part due to its predictability. When the Commanders get under center, they almost exclusively run the ball or use a play-action pass. There’s no pure drop back passing game of any sort from under center. In the offseason, I wrote about lessons Blough could learn from Ben Johnson’s first year in Chicago.One of those lessons was incorporating some drop back passing game from under center, but easing the quarterback into it.

Commanders Roundtable

Three underperforming veterans need to deliver immediately

RB Rachaad White

With running back Jacory Croskey-Merritt placed on Injured Reserve, Rachaad White needs to step up in a major way, and so far, he simply has not.

Through five games, White has managed just 145 yards on 36 carries (4.0 yards per carry) with no rushing touchdowns, alongside just 83 receiving yards. The former Tampa Bay Buccaneer was brought to Washington to serve as a reliable dual-threat out of the backfield, but his impact in the passing game has waned over time. After averaging 8.6 yards per reception in 2023 and 7.7 in 2024, his efficiency dropped to just 5.4 yards per catch last season.

The offensive backfield struggles have been noticeable enough that the Commanders even brought back Austin Ekeler to help patch up the unit’s depth. While it is fair to acknowledge that White has been toughing it out through a shoulder injury, the expectation for a fifth-year veteran of his talent level remains much higher.

Ultimately, White has no choice but to elevate his game: with the depth chart stretched thin, he is currently Washington’s RB1.

To read more of this article, CLICK HERE

The Athletic (paywall)

Mailbag with Nicki Jhabvala

It’s starting to feel a lot like 2020. The NFC East is a mess (again) and the Washington Commanders sit at the bottom of the division with one win in six games.

And yet, they’re still in it — barely.

The next few weeks could have a significant impact on Washington’s meager playoff hopes; primetime wins over the Eagles and Giants could keep the Commanders in contention, while more losses could all but end their season and amplify calls for a coaching change.

(David) Blough is in over his head as OC. Wouldn’t it be wise to get an experienced offensive coordinator not working this year to help out? Even an out-of-work coach is better than this display of ineptitude. He has no clue in regard to misdirection, quick screens and blitz pickup to help (Daniels) out. Heck, bring back Joe Gibbs to give him some pointers on max protect and outlets for the blitz. — Gerald C.

An out-of-work coach would be better? You sure? I’m willing to bet there’s a reason (or multiple reasons) those coaches are out of work.

The offense certainly hasn’t blown me away, but I’m not sure I fully agree with your assessment, mainly because it’s impossible for outsiders to separate who or what is really at fault in many of these instances. It’s easy to run with a narrative, or an assumption that fits a narrative, but that doesn’t make it true.

There have been obvious moments when the play calling has been questionable. (I do wonder if the overtime gaffe against the Giants was the result of Blough getting the call in late.) But there are a number of other factors (see the earlier question about the roster) that go into an offense’s efficiency. Are the receivers running the right routes? Are they running them well enough? Is the quarterback moving through his progressions too quickly? Are the offensive linemen executing their blocks as they should? Have early deficits forced the offense to get away from the run game? Have breakdowns elsewhere led to repeated mistakes?

My primary issues with this offense are: One, it doesn’t seem to have enough answers. If something breaks down, if a defense sends heavy pressure, then what? And two, Daniels doesn’t seem to be playing as freely as he did in Kliff Kingsbury’s system. Some of that is to be expected. The transition to this offense was significant largely because of the huddling and relaying of plays, and Daniels not exactly playing behind one of the league’s best O-lines. But there’s a fine line between helping a young quarterback adapt to a new system that will benefit him and the team long term, and trying to fit a young quarterback into a system that takes away some of his unique abilities, or leaves him thinking too much.

That doesn’t mean it was a mistake to employ Blough’s system; there are a number of reasons most teams in the league use some version of this offense. But a big motivation for the change was to jumpstart the running game and give Daniels some help. That hasn’t happened, so additional change is necessary.

To read more of this article, CLICK HERE

Sports Illustrated

Three Changes Blough Should Make

I’d give Williams more of the early work, starting with crossing routes in the opening script. Pair those crossers with a route from Diggs or Okonkwo at a different depth, and give Daniels a defined place to start his read. If Baun jumps the throw to the back, Daniels needs an option behind him.

A few designed rollouts belong in that package, too, with a short receiving option on the side Daniels is moving toward. Protect the edge and give him somewhere to go with the ball if he has to throw early.

Then I’d use some tempo after a positive play. The first touchdown drive included an 11-yard Croskey-Merritt run followed by a 15-yard no-huddle completion to Diggs. Have the next call ready and give Daniels a chance to keep the group moving with a small menu of plays everyone knows well.

Washington was called for two delays of game and two false starts in the opener. Those are avoidable yards to give back against a defense that already makes moving the ball difficult. Getting the call in, getting aligned, and getting the snap off should be part of what the bye helped fix. “It’s not going to be a new system. It’s not going to be new plays, but I do think you’ll feel the systems be more precise,” Quinn said last week.

The short-yardage plan needs attention, too. White was stopped on third-and-1 in the opener, and Moro Ojomo blew up the final two-point shovel pass to John Bates. Washington also converted a fourth-and-one run and scored on Williams’ one-yard catch. There were different ways to get the yard.

To read more of this article, CLICK HERE

Sports Illustrated

Quinn Sees Bigger Role for Antonio Williams; Eagles Get Reinforcements | Burgundy Roundup

With Terry McLaurin out for the season, it looks like Antonio Williams could be getting more opportunities in Washington’s offense. Dan Quinn said Monday that he doesn’t expect Stefon Diggs’ workload to change much, instead pointing to Williams as someone who could see more targets. “I would say the natural progression is probably Antonio some more.” That doesn’t necessarily mean Williams will take McLaurin’s spot, with Treylon Burks and Dyami Brown also being considered for that role.

To read more of this article, CLICK HERE

Commanders.com

Chig Okonkwo reflects on injury, chemistry with Jayden Daniels

Okonkwo returned [from a Week 1 hamstring injury] in time for the Commanders’ Week 4 game against the Indianapolis Colts. Despite being a home game for Washington, the matchup was held at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in London, so Okonkwo had to wait an extra week to get a taste of playing at Northwest Stadium.

The wait was worth it, however, as Jayden Daniels was also making his home debut after missing two weeks with an elbow injury.

“That really is Game 1 for us as a duo,” Okonkwo said of playing with Daniels. “But it was nice to go out there and execute the plays, and, you know, show flashes of what I can do because it just lets things build up now and lets coaches just see what works, different things, and we can just keep on hammering in what our offensive philosophy is going to be.”

Okonkwo describes playing with Daniels as “very fun,” noting how elusive he is when avoiding defenders. In what ended up being a 27-27 tie against the New York Giants, the duo performed well. Okonkwo had four receptions for 60 yards, while Daniels completed 17 of 25 passes for 199 yards and added nine carries for 103 yards and two touchdowns to his stat line.

Commanders Expect Three Players Back at Practice, but Javon Kinlaw Needs More Time

Backup quarterback Marcus Mariota, defensive lineman Charles Omenihu, and receiver Treylon Burks will be returning to practice. Quinn didn’t like the bad news any more than anyone else: “Javon Kinlaw is not trending as fast as we had hoped, so he’ll continue to work, rehab with his knee.”

Omenihu couldn’t play against the Giants and 49ers while he’s been dealing with groin/ankle issues; getting him back is crucial to a defensive line that’s been dealing with some injuries. Kinlaw, meanwhile, will continue rehabbing his knee after Quinn acknowledged he isn’t progressing as quickly as the team had hoped.

The news on Burks is good after he left the 49ers game with an injury. With Terry McLaurin out for the season with a torn patellar tendon in his left knee, Washington is looking for a spark from somewhere on the roster. Quinn added this little nugget about Stefon Diggs: “Stef is doing well. Workload shouldn’t change as much; I think it’ll be others that would climb up more.”

Bullock’s Film Room (subscription)

Commanders Film Review: Pass Rush Issues

[Note: the play described in the excerpt below can be viewed in the video embedded in the tweet]

The Commanders hired Daronte Jones to bring across the ultra aggressive Brian Flores defensive scheme from the Vikings.

While Jones hasn’t been as aggressive as Flores, because nobody in the league is, Jones has blitzed at a higher rate than the vast majority of the league. Despite that, the Commanders rank in the bottom 10 for sacks and haven’t been able to consistently pressure opposing quarterbacks the same way that the Vikings do. So what can Daronte Jones and his defensive staff do to help turn that high blitz rate into higher pressure rates and sacks? First, let’s start with the things they do well that they can lean into more frequently.

Here we have a good example of a disguised overload blitz. The Commanders start off with five defenders on the line of scrimmage, two interior defensive lineman, two edge rushers and rookie linebacker Sonny Styles. Prior to the snap, you can see linebacker Frankie Luvu and safety Jeremy Reaves off the line of scrimmage and making calls to the rest of the defense. From this pre-snap look, the offense is likely expecting the four lineman plus Styles to rush, so they slide the protection to the right.

However, just before the ball is snapped, the real picture emerges. Luvu and Reaves charge up to the line of scrimmage, but it’s too late for the Giants to change their protection. The ball is snapped and the offensive line slides to the right, expecting Styles to blitz, but Styles and fellow rookie Joshua Josephs drop off into coverage from that side, leaving the Giants to slide their protection to just one rusher on that side of the line.

Meanwhile, the left side of the line is overloaded. Javon Kinlaw stunts inside to the A gap between the left guard and center, ensuring the left guard works inside to pick him up. Edge rusher Dorance Armstrong attacks outside of the left tackle, making sure the tackle works out to pick him up. That leaves a big gap between the left guard and left tackle. The running back steps up to try and fill it, but he’s left in an impossible position. Both Luvu and Reaves are blitzing in that gap. The back does the correct thing in picking up Luvu, as his blitz hits first, but Reaves comes flying in with momentum

Now, the scheme is good here and it ultimately results in a sack, but something that stands out consistently that is purely on the players is the ability to finish plays. Reaves comes flying in unblocked and misses a free sack. He allows the quarterback to spin out of his tackle attempt and escape. The quarterback avoids Reaves, but Dorance Armstrong is there to clean up, or so it appears. The quarterback manages to come out of his spin move to avoid Reaves and somehow also sidesteps past Armstrong. Fortunately, Daron Payne manages to clean up at the third time of asking, but there’s no way the quarterback should have gotten three lives there.

Commanders.com

Final thoughts | Commanders’ reset after bye-week

— Quinn said it was “awesome” to see Trey Amos back on the field against the 49ers. Amos has dealt with multiple injuries for the better part of the last calendar year, which Quinn said can take a toll on a player. There was no flinching, though, Quinn added, which was why he managed to have a larger impact than expected for a player who has barely practiced with his teammates.

— Quinn said there was “energy and optimism’ from the players to get started again after the break. There was certainly disappointment in how the season unfolded before the bye week, but everyone in the building is determined to get things back on track.

That’s what we’re chasing, and that’s what I’m certain we’re gonna get after [the bye week]. When we do that, beginning this week, I think that will really show what we’re made of.”

Metro Sports Page

Terry McLaurin’s Story Isn’t Over

A devastating injury has ended Terry’s season and cast doubt on his future in Washington, but after seven years of defying expectations, don’t count out No. 17 just yet

Before the season even started, there was talk about this being Terry’s last season in Washington. His three-year, $97M contract set up an out for the team after this season, allowing the Commanders to use a June 1 designation and recoup considerable cap space for next year (as much as $25M, according to Spotrac).

That is a lot of money, of course, but as I have said on Tuesday nights, if he was healthy and playing well, Terry McLaurin would have been worth keeping around. I mean, we basically pocketed that much for the 2026 season—Spotrac has us with $25M of available cap space right now.

Assuming Jayden and Terry were clicking, we would be asking Terry to continue his assault on the top of our career receiving list. I know I get overly sentimental about football, and that can result in wrong-headed decision-making.

Further, the injury he sustained (a torn patellar tendon) is very, very no bueno. The expected timetable for Terry’s return to the field is probably around 10–11 months, based on the historical average of almost 50 previous NFL patellar tendon tears. This means that contract decisions will be made long before he is cleared to practice fully.

I fully expect Adam Peters to leave the door open for Terry to return to Washington, but it is hard to believe that it wouldn’t be on a different contract. The injury itself isn’t career-ending, as about 60% of those aforementioned players returned to the field.

I don’t know what kind of miracle it would take for Terry to beat the odds in terms of his ability to produce at a high level again, but I do know that for that miracle to happen, it will take an insane amount of work. Terry excels at that part of the business, and nobody knows that better than our front office.

His 63% precise pass rate, measuring how often a quarterback hits his receiver in stride in the torso area, was the best figure McCarthy has posted in a single game as a pro.

As a quarterback who is reticent to throw over the middle of the field, McCarthy has to live throwing to the sidelines, where anything short of excellent ball placement risks a pick-six and any hesitation to throw the ball blows up the timing of a play. He was excellent on those throws in his first start with the Giants, going 8-of-13 for 169 yards on throws outside the numbers. Having Malik Nabers helps, but McCarthy looked more comfortable and effective throwing to Nabers and Malachi Fields than he did Justin Jefferson and Jordan Addison a year ago. It’s not proof that the Giants landed a steal with their in-season trade for McCarthy, but one impressive start is one more than a fair number of people would have expected from him in New York after his 2025 season in Minnesota.

item.title: Cowboys at Eagles Stock Report: Javonte Williams has a day
item.description: Here is our Stock Report for Monday night’s Cowboys win
item.content:encoded:
A win is a win.

To be clear Monday night was not that type for the Dallas Cowboys, but things have been so down as of late that even one road win against a hated division rival is likely not enough to bring some all the way back. That is fair.

But a win is a win as noted, and the Cowboys took a serious step forward by getting one on Monday night in Philly. Now awaits the true test in the Arizona Cardinals. If you know you know.

It was hardly a perfect effort from the Cowboys, but several key figures on the team really shined.

Let’s get to them in our stock report.

Stock Up: Brian Schottenheimer

There was really only one direction for Schotty to go.

Public approval was about as low as it had ever been for the Cowboys head coach, and while he still had some decisions on Monday that left us scratching our heads, he had the team ready for the challenge and everyone involved executed it. We are talking step by step, once more.

In all seriousness, Schotty did have the Cowboys ready to go from a head coach perspective and also was a man of his word as an offensive play-caller. He leaned on the ground game and saw a lot of success in that area. That shows a willingness to change and he deserves credit for that.

Stock Up: Javonte Williams

Speaking of!

Javonte Williams established a new career high in rushing with 155 yards, the most that any Cowboys player has had in a game since Ezkeiel Elliott back in 2016. What a throwback.

It is one thing for the head coach to commit to running the ball more. It is another thing for the running back to be ready for the challenge. Williams clearly was.

Stock Up: CeeDee Lamb

Over training camp, as people were fawning (rightfully so!) over George Pickens, it felt like CeeDee Lamb was getting a bit forgotten. He is so incredibly special.

Lamb is one of the most dynamic players in the entire NFL and sometimes it seems that he wills things into existence. This felt like the case during Monday night’s win.

Thankfully the Cowboys have both of their star receivers.

Stock Up: George Pickens

GP3 did not have the full statistical day that his counterpart did, but he had several incredible catches that were critical to the overall team succeeding. That is commendable.

What’s more, Pickens answered the call from his head coach to be more involved and help everything out. A rising tide and all that jazz.

Stock Up: Dak Prescott

Everything was moving and grooving for the Cowboys on offense and that certainly starts with the quarterback. Like his head coach and play-caller, Prescott had struggled over the last two weeks. He put that behind him, thankfully.

Of note, this was Prescott’s 80th career game with multiple passing touchdowns. He now has the most in franchise history as he broke a tie he had with Tony Romo at 79.

Stock Up: Tyler Goodson

While Javonte Williams rightfully got all of the headlines, Tyler Goodson is seriously earning a larger role on this team. Or at least he should be.

Goodson had the kickoff return touchdown called back due to penalty, but it seems like every time he touches the ball (however that is) he is doing so with extreme tenacity. He is making the most of those touches and you love to see that.

Obviously KaVontae Turpin was out for this game due to injury, but maybe the Cowboys should look to Goodson as an alternative option.

Stock Up: Shemar James

The Cowboys put a lot of responsibility on Shemar James’ shoulders and it sort of felt like a surprise that they did so. To be clear, his stock up is relative to that context because obviously there isn’t much to write home about for the defense at large.

Still, James kept things together in an overall sense. Given that the defense is really struggling to find any kind of stability out there that is a huge plus in his favor. So good for him.

Static Stock: Quinnen Williams

I’d like the record to show that I believe that Quinnen Williams rebounded a bit in the second half, but the first half was absolutely dreadful for him.

Williams committed two penalties early on in this game that cannot happen. These penalties cannot happen for anyone on your team, one was an encroachment that gave the Eagles new life after Dallas stopped them on fourth down, let alone from your defensive leader who you traded serious capital for and gave a massive extension to.

In the second half Williams was much more himself. He got a sack, and had three TFLs. That’s a pretty decent comeback for your star on the defense. He evened out his first-half mistakes.

Stock Down: Christian Parker

How is the defense still so consistently bad? And how are they committing so many penalties? Pre-snap penalties at that?

I recognize that Christian Parker’s stock cannot go down any further. But what is his “get right” game? It wasn’t Jalon Daniels. It wasn’t Tanner McKee. What circumstances does it take for his group to look proper or dare I say even good?

Stock Down: DaRon Bland

Like with a lot of things on defense, there isn’t a whole lot to say that hasn’t already been offered.

It is a little bit easier to see Bland’s struggles now that Joey Porter Jr. is a part of the fold, but this is such a serious point of weakness for the Cowboys. It might be their highest level priority in the offseason.

Sigh.

item.title: Best fantasy football waiver wire pickups: 8 players to add for NFL Week 8
item.description: With the fantasy football regular season now past the halfway point, it's time to make a playoff push and/or add pieces for a future title run.
item.content:encoded:
The fantasy football regular season has officially passed its midpoint, and by now, you should know whether or not you have a team that can compete for a championship.

That determination has a lot to do with your waiver wire decisions entering Week 8.

If you're on the fringe of contention, you're probably looking for players who can contribute immediately. As usual.

However, if you're in solid position in the standings, this might be a good week to see about possibly stashing players who could be more valuable later than sooner. Someone who could benefit if a higher-profile teammate is traded in the next couple weeks. Or what about a player who's going to be on bye this week and might be overlooked by your win-now leaguemates.

RB Kaelon Black (28% rostered), RB Tyrone Tracy (27%) and WR Malachi Fields (4%) might end up being very useful players after they return next week. (And as always, check out last week's waiver recommendations to see if those players might still be available.)

ON BYE: Houston, New Orleans, N.Y, Giants, San Francisco

Fantasy football players to add for Week 8

Due to the wide variance in types of leagues and individual team needs, the players listed here include their availability in Yahoo leagues, which may or may not match roster rates on other platforms. Suggested bid values based on $100 free agent acquisition budget (FAAB) for the season.

For customized waiver wire suggestions, synced to your league and subscribe to USA TODAY Sports Fantasy's exclusive tools.

RB Jonah Coleman, Denver Broncos (35% rostered)

Coleman is the prime pickup this week, especially in leagues where he couldn't be stashed on injured reserve while he was recovering from an ankle sprain that had kept him out since Week 2. The rookie fourth-round pick led the Broncos with nine carries for 54 yards and caught two passes for 15. Afterward, coach Sean Payton said the team needed to get Coleman more touches. Let's go! (Recommended FAAB bid: $21)

RB Seth McGowan, Indianapolis Colts (8% rostered)

Here's another rookie (7th round) who has a chance to make a major impact down the stretch. His snap counts have been gradually increasing, to a season-high 20 in Week 7. He also had his best day as a pro (at Minnesota, even!) with 11 carries for 46 yards on Sunday. But McGowan's real value could come if the Colts decide to trade star RB Jonathan Taylor before the Nov. 10 trade deadline. Stash McGowan now while he's cheap. (FAAB bid: $9)

WR Caleb Douglas, Miami Dolphins (10% rostered)

Like Coleman, Douglas hadn't played since Week 2 due to an ankle sprain. But he showed his big-play ability by catching a pair of touchdown passes from Malik Willis as the Dolphins won their first game of the season. Coincidence? Yeah, probably. But the Dolphins will be forced to throw a lot the rest of the way and Douglas may be their best downfield option. (FAAB bid: $8)

RB Samaje Perine, Cincinnati Bengals (12% rostered)

Perine continues to deserve a mention, and he may have fallen back into the player pool while the Bengals had their bye week. He didn't do a whole lot in Week 7 with four rushes for 16 yards, but one of those carries was from the 1-yard line. And he punched it in. If the Bengals are going to give Perine the red-zone carries over Chase Brown, he will have value. (FAAB bid: $7)

TE Chig Okonkwo, Washington Commanders

The Commanders were off in Week 7, but with the offense struggling to make plays, it's hard to find anyone under-the-radar to add. With top receiver Terry McLaurin out for the season and Stefon Diggs battling injuries, Okonkwo could emerge as an even bigger part of the passing game. With George Kittle, Isaiah Likely and Dalton Schultz all on bye, he makes an interesting dart throw. (FAAB bid: $3)

TE Mason Taylor, New York Jets (0% rostered)

We've already had Kenyon Sadiq hype week, but Week 3 now seems like a long time ago. And the rookie has caught a total of four passes since then. Taylor is now the man of the hour. He caught a pair of TD passes and added a 2-point conversion for good measure as part of a five-catch, 62-yard day. After missing Weeks 3 and 4 with a thumb injury, Taylor has 12 receptions in the last three games. (FAAB bid: $2)

QB Geno Smith, New York Jets (18% rostered)

Someone had to get Taylor the ball this past week, and Smith did a nice job of it. He completed 23-of-30 passes for 287 yards and three TDs, with the other score going to rookie wideout Omar Cooper Jr. If the Jets get RB Breece Hall back into the mix this week, it could be another solid week for Smith in a "revenge game" at home against his former team, the Raiders. (FAAB bid: $2)

WR Xavier Hutchinson, Houston Texans (1% rostered)

One last bye-week stash: The Texans are having trouble running the ball. And they have a wealth of options in the passing game. Maybe this past week was an anomaly; certainly Nico Collins needs to have more than two catches for 6 yards. But the team leader in targets (6) and receptions (3) against the Giants wasn't Collins or Marvin Harrison Jr. or Jaylin Noel or even Tank Dell. It was Hutchinson, who also caught a touchdown pass. With Houston off this week, take a shot if you have an open roster spot. (FAAB bid: $1)
