item.title: Nick Sirianni talks about the Eagles’ defensive struggles
item.description: The Eagles head coach addressed the team’s defensive struggles, and how they were able to have some offensive success.
item.content:encoded:
The Eagles lost another game in embarrassing fashion, and head coach Nick Sirianni spoke to reporters afterward about the defensive struggles, how they handled Saquon Barkley’s return, and how they were able to get things going offensively early in the game.

Sirianni was also asked about his message to the team, and it was about resilience and being grateful.

“We just talked about being the same version of yourself every single day. All that matters is we improve. I think back on the 2021 season, the way we finished that year — and I didn’t say this to them, but I’m thinking about it right now — The way we finished that year propelled us into the future Eagles way that we’ve been the last four years. Growth is important. We talked a lot about being the same version of ourselves regardless of the circumstances and that football is going to deal you some tough hands at times, but can you get up and keep fighting? Life’s going to deal you some tough hands at times. Can you get up and keep fighting? We talked about that. We talked about being the same guy every day. We talked about being grateful.”

Here’s what the head coach had to say:

On the defensive issues

“Obviously, it’s never just one thing when you give up a bunch of yards like that. We’ve got to do a better job coaching. We’ve got to do a better job executing, getting off blocks, tackling. We had a couple missed tackles, but it’s always going to be about block destruction, playing on their side of the line of scrimmage, and then us putting them in positions to succeed. I give them credit. They played a good game. Hats off to them.”

Sirianni didn’t want to get much into some of the missed tackling, but noted that they do look at each one, assess what the problem was, and then try to rep those corrections in practice and in drills. He explained that not only do they have to put players in position to succeed, but they also have to give them the tools and practice opportunities to do that.

The head coach credited the Cowboys offense for the lack of Eagles’ defensive pressure throughout the game. He said that they were able to stay ahead of the sticks quite a bit and had manageable third down situations – and they were able to keep the defense off-balance with the way they ran it and the play action game in those third downs.

“Again, there’s never just one thing. Again, when you’re not getting pressures, you’ve got to try to simulate them in some way. So again, it’s always a version of, how are we executing? How are we putting them in positions to succeed? Because all that matters is that it goes out onto the field and we try to give ourselves the best chance to win. In this game of football, just like anything, I think we always want to pin it on something, but there’s multiple things that contribute to it. We’ll look at that, look at some of the common themes and see what we need to do to get better.”

When asked specifically about the production from guys like Jalen Carter and Jordan Davis, Sirianni instead pointed to their contributions throughout the season, saying that everyone will want plays back from Monday night’s game, and with the struggles they had against the run, it’s never just one thing.

On Saquon Barkley’s return

“Obviously, you saw that [Saquon Barkley] was on a pitch count out there today. There was constant communication to see how he was feeling, see where he was, and obviously, he came out early in the second half. Again, when you go into something like that, you make sure that the player’s health is first and foremost. Is he ready to go? Do they feel ready to go? Do the doctors and trainers feel like they’re ready to go? We felt like that was the case today, but obviously wanted to keep a close eye on him, and he’s tough as heck. He wanted to be out there for his teammates, probably had to slow him [down] as far as — he’d be out there every play because of the person he is and the teammate he is and the player he is and the toughness that he has.”

Still, Sirianni went on to say that they tried to be smart with him, but it was good to have him back out on the field. He noted that the RB had a nice game and was very productive when he got the ball. The head coach also acknowledged that Barkley ended up playing less than they had planned for after he hurt his back on the first run of the game. 

On their offensive success

“I think when you’re able to be efficient in the run game and set yourself up on third down, we felt like we were able to kind of run some of the things, what we wanted to do coming into the game and coming into the season where we keep run, play action, stuff like that. We were able to get some tempo calls going into it. I think you just got to see a variety of things that we want to do because we weren’t behind the sticks and we have to keep up with that script. 

Obviously, we did a good job finishing in the red zone. Sometimes it was because some penalties extended the drives, but also being able to run it in down there was key, was obviously good for us. But I think it was just staying in phase, being able to hit explosives in the run game and being able to convert on third down. I’m not sure what we were throughout third down. I think it was over 40%, but we still even want to do better there. But yeah, we’ve still got a lot of things to correct and work on.“

On having to rely on depth players

“That’s life in the NFL. We feel good about our process of giving guys that maybe aren’t starters opportunities for developmental periods and things like that. But I think that’s the league. It is our job to bring depth in and it is our job to develop that depth. With that comes opportunity on my end, the opportunity to give them opportunities to grow with practice time, with how we review film with them, everything. But that’s life in the NFL. I’ll never use that as an excuse because at the end of the day, all that matters is if we won or lost and if we continue to get better, and we didn’t do that. No one’s going to feel sorry for us and our job is to get whoever’s on that field ready to play in the game that’s going to play every Sunday or Monday.”

Sirianni said that he is committed to helping players develop as leaders in the locker room, especially after losing several of their captains, and is always thinking about ways to coach them up in that regard.

item.title: Ravens to be without star rookie OG vs. Bills
item.description: Baltimore will be down its talented rookie guard vs. Buffalo
item.content:encoded:
With the 14th pick in the 2026 NFL Draft, the Baltimore Ravens selected Penn State guard Vega Ioane, and he’s been a rock-solid addition to the team’s offensive front in the first seven games of this season.

But the rookie blocker almost assuredly be on the field against the Bills in Week 8 after he suffered a knee injury in Baltimore’s Week 7 loss to the Bengals at home.

Fortunately for the Ravens, the injury isn’t considered to be a long-term ailment, per Ian Rapoport, but once can surmise from the report, Ioane won’t be on the field this week against the Bills.

The 6’4”, 320-pound blocker has only allowed eight pressures on 225 pass-blocking snaps to date and has been a road-grader for the Ravens run game in the first seven contests of this season. While Ioane is a right guard by trade, he actually manned the center spot in Weeks 4-6 for Baltimore.

It’ll either be veteran Andrew Vorhees or 2025 third-round pick Emery Jones filling in for Ioane during his absence.

Vorhees was a seventh-round pick in 2023 — he would’ve been picked higher but was selected with a torn ACL — and was Baltimore’s full-time starter at left guard in 2025 yet struggled mightily.

Jones is a 6’5”, 315-pounder from LSU who played 48 snaps as a rookie and has appeared on 228 snaps thus far in his second season in Baltimore. He’s allowed five pressures on 127 pass-blocking snaps to date.

item.title: Miami Dolphins Week 7 quick hits: Tuesday Thoughts With The Earl
item.description: Miami has the Dolphins, the greatest football team!
item.content:encoded:
SHHH!!!  Hey… you’uns hear that?  That’s the sound of… VICTORY!!! The Miami Dolphins got their first win of the season over the hated New York Jets.  It wasn’t a comfortable win by any means, but we will take any win we can get.  Especially over the Jets.  As The Miami Ute said in the reactions thread: “A victory versus the Jets is worth 10 victories over common opponents.”  I looked into it and that is correct; the math on that definitely checks out.  So what all went into this DUB?

THE OFFENSE CAME TO PLAY

But Duke… it’s just the lowly 2-4 Jets.  That’s correct.  But as Marisa Marino from DolphinsTalk tweeted, the Jets were a top 10 defense in just about every metric.  I pointed out some of those as well.  The Jets may now be 2-5, but they have only lost one game this season by more than one score, and that was just 11 points.  The Jets have held every team they have faced under their average passing yards per game… except the Dolphins.  Now, it doesn’t take much to get over Miami’s average, which was 31st entering the game.  But they exceeded that average nonetheless.  There were some hiccups in the second half, but they did what was necessary to win when it mattered most. 

They also scored 28 points, which is the 2nd most points the Jets have allowed in a game this season.  They are now off the bottom of the scoring average, nearly a full PPG ahead of the Titans and 1.3 PPG ahead of Mike McDaniel and the Captain If Justin Herbert led Chargers.  Whether they can maintain it is another question for another day.  But if they play like they did for the majority of this game, I don’t see why they can’t maintain it.  It’s also impressive that the Dolphins gained 360 total yards.  That’s the 4th most the Jets have allowed this season.  The teams ahead of the Dolphins are ranked in the top 10 in total yards this season.

But the most impressive thing the offense did Sunday: they got the ball with 3:24 left in the game.  The Jets had just scored 8 points to bring the game to within 3 points.  Outside of the explosive play to Douglas, the Dolphins had been quiet in the 2nd half.  This is big boy football time and if we are all being honest, we were all clinched up for this drive.  We have seen this FAR too many time, especially in the last regime, where the team just couldn’t put away an opponent.  NOT THIS TIME!!!  The Dolphins ran for a first down with a 14-yard run.  Then 3 runs for 9 total yards.  They were at midfield with a 4th-and-1 with 2 minutes left.  They went for it using their version of the Tush Push play.  And that was it.  They converted and entered the victory formation.  In the past, we have heard the talk about the Dolphins becoming more physical, but it was always nothing more than talk.  In that moment, the Dolphins were the more physical team and it showed up.

THE DEFENSE STILL NEEDS WORK

The pass defense is what it is.  The Dolphins still allow a ridiculously high completion percentage to opponents.  I somewhat expected this against the Jets as Geno Smith has been less reluctant to throw downfield this season.  Smith actually pushed the ball downfield this game and hit some explosives that resulted in TDs for the Jets.  This is stuff they’ll need to clean up from the film room and work on the communication.  Two big plays were busted coverages, and the other was a play that looked Dante Trader had a chance to intercept it.  Those 3 plays accounted for 153 yards, which is over half of the total passing yards.  Of course, we could do the same type of accounting for the Dolphins or any team really.  But 3 plays out of 30 passing attempts accounting for over half of the production signals outliers to me.  On 27 other attempts, the Dolphins allowed 134 yards, which tracks with the idea of the Jets keeping it short.  They still have issues with TEs although I’ll give them credit: both of Taylor’s TDs were contested catches.

The issue I’m going to take up is the run defense.  The Dolphins were top 10 in YPC allowed and overall yards allowed.  They held MVP candidate Kenneth Walker III in check a few games ago.  They allowed the Jets to run over them, especially late.  Braelon Allen ran for 104 yards on 17 carries, a 6.1 YPC average.  Allen has stepped up into lead back role for the Jets in the absence of Breece Hall and he is averaging over 4 YPC in games where he is the primary contributor.  But the Dolphins should have held their ground against him.  The game plan changed for the Jets in the 2nd half.  Of Allen’s 17 carries, 12 of them came in the 2nd half.  Allen had 5 carries for 23 yards in the 1st half.  The Jets, down 2 TDs, said they didn’t think the Dolphins could stop their rushing attack, and they were right.  The Jets are bad in the red zone, and the Dolphins got a goal line stand that resulted in a FG.  But the Dolphins will face much better RBs and better rushing attacks in the next few weeks.  I don’t know if they can fix the pass defense anytime soon, so the run defense needs to do their part.

THIS AND THAT

  • Malik Willis played exceptionally well this game.  The difference from what we’ve previously seen and that was night and day.  His stat line won’t blow anyone’s mind, but he was decisive, made smart decisions, and protected the ball.  As JUK pointed out, 5 bad games of Willis were not enough of a sample size to make a judgment on him, and neither is 1 good game. But this level of play could be the start of an upward trend.  Of course, we need to see this next week and then the next and so on.  But give credit where credit is due, he played very well.
  • Ollie Gordon continues to be refreshing part of a tough season with his aggressive running and fiery temperament – he’s gonna get a flag thrown on him with the way he’s chirping.  But that’s fine, because we need to see that fire from players.  Do you think Gordon is gonna be laughing on the sideline after making a mistake that effectively ends your season?  No.  He’s old school and I’m here for it. He’s currently 19th in rushing yards, which is wild considering he had 3 carries for 7 yards in the 1st 2 games this season.  In the 3 games since becoming the primary back, he has averaged 97 yards per game.  If he maintains that pace the rest of the way, he’ll finish with over 1400 rushing yards!  More importantly, he has scored a TD in all 4 games he has had be a heavy contributor.  That pace will be difficult to continue, but he has a chance to finish with double digit TDs.  There are too many AFC backs ahead of him and the Dolphins’ eventual record with be a deterrent, but he is on a Pro Bowl pace.
  • Bobby Slowik needs a shout out.  He finally listened to me (not really but let me feel important for a minute) and dialed up the short passing game.  Here are some interesting tweets about that here and here.  But what he was doing was working.  My favorite offensive stat: 41 rushing attempts.  Look, I grew up in the 80s on hard-nosed rushing attack football that was 3 yards and a cloud of dust.  The current NFL is flashy and pass happy and we saw all of that with McDaniel. I’m glad to see the return of “ground and pound”.  The Dolphins’ passing game was good against the Jets.  It will need to be better in future games.  But I’ll never complain about a dominant rushing attack.  Now… Willis rushed for 8 attempts.  3 of those were called runs for sure: the 2 kneeldowns and the tush-push.  On of the 2 sacks he took was actually a designed QB run play.  The others were pass plays, so we can assume 25 total dropbacks to 36 run plays called.  But still… if the Dolphins can dominate in the run game, they will be tough for anyone to beat.
  • Welcome back Caleb Douglas.  He was not a major factor in terms of volume, but both his catches went for TDs.  He is still a rookie and playing in only his third game.  He is still learning.  However, his mere presence will give the offense a boost.  The volume will get there. Also, watch the utter filthiness of this route.
  • I am going to continue to bang this drum, but… Chris Bell needs to work from the slot.  I’m not the only one who has thought this.  Bell has the size, strength, and speed to be an outside receiver.  But so far, he has struggled generating consistent separation.  What we HAVE seen, and saw against the Jets, was his ability AFTER the catch.  Against Cincinnati, he had a long run which shows what he can do with the ball in his hands.  Against NYJ, he had a WR screen play that gained 8 yards.  It should have been stopped for a loss or no gain.  But Bell was simply too physical and barreled ahead for 8 yards.  Folks… that’s slot WR type work.  If the Dolphins can use him as an underneath player that works for YAC, they have a monster on their hands.  The benefit to this thought process is Bell can still play outside.  He’s not LIMITED to the slot like other WRs may be.  But I think he can do the most damage there.  Stay with me here, because I’m gonna tie this together with the next few thoughts.
  • Greg Dulcich came out of witness protection to have a big game… on National Tight Ends Day of course.  He caught all 5 targets for 86 yards, including a fantastic catch-and-run that was an ankle tackle from being a TD.  We need to see more days like this.  My favorite play of his though?  On Miami’s second TD drive, Willis breaks the pocket for a 12-yard run on 3rd-and-9.  Dulcich effectively boxes out his defender to allow the 1st down gain for Willis.  It wasn’t a dominant block or anything.  But it’s one of those things that will never show up in the box score that helps the team succeed.  Had he not done that, his defender could have potentially tackled Willis short of the line to gain.  That early in the game, the Dolphins may have kicked a FG.  If so, that’s a 4-point swing in a game decided by 3 points.  All because Dulcich had the wherewithal to wall off a defender.  Smart football.
  • Last week, Kyle Crabbs of Locked On Dolphins did a podcast about how the Dolphins need to spend cash in 2027 to get close to the spending floor.  The part I’m interested in now is the names of players he listed.  The Dolphins will have the cash and cap to acquire 2-3 big money free agents (or 6-7 midrange players).  One of the names he mentioned was current Detroit TE Sam LaPorta.  LaPorta is a great receiving TE weapon that can play in line as well as off the line.  He would be a great addition to this unit.  I am also down with keeping Greg Dulcich, because he will earn an extension if he keeps playing the way he produced Sunday.  With LaPorta, Dulcich, and Kacmarek, the Dolphins could play 13 or 23 personnel and still have a quality passing attack.
  • This win is nice and I would love to see more.  But the reality is the Dolphins are still likely to finish with a top 5 draft pick.  With the QB class looking like it does, the Dolphins may be in position to get phenom Jeremiah Smith, who only has 984 yards, and 12 TDs in 7 games this season.  If Miami were to draft Smith, that would give them a true generational X-WR prospect that would allow Douglas to play the Z role and Bell can play in the slot (almost there).
  • Now for the payoff.  This is all contingent upon how Willis plays the rest of the season.  If he plays like he did on Sunday, the Dolphins will be in good shape.  With that in mind, imagine an offense featuring a backfield of Willis, Achane, and Gordon, a WR corps of Smith, Douglas, and Bell, and a TE group of LaPorta, Dulcich, and Kacmarek.  Is that too much to ask for?  Probably.  But we can dream, right?
  • Chop Robinson is playing better than you think.  He only has 2 sacks on the season and that’s the stat that gets paid.  But he is generating pressure better than anyone else in the league.  Per NextGenStats, he has a pressure rate of 23.4%, which is highest in the league.  Why aren’t they turning into sacks?  I don’t know.  But I do know I saw him used on stunts and got into Smith’s face on Sunday, but the ball was out quick.  I saw him rush from the interior a couple of times Sunday.  I also saw him force a jet motion pass play to go deeper into the backfield than desired and it resulted in a 3-yard loss.  He was also in a few run stops.  He had his fair share of losses.  Armand Membou is a good OT. But he’s not playing poorly, like some would suggest just because he doesn’t have the sack totals.  It also needs to be noted that the Dolphins have faced the 2nd, 3rd, 4th, and 7th ranked teams in order of sack percentage (SF, KC, LV, Cincy respectively). All 4 are under 5% and only Cincy is over 4%.  Those teams don’t give up sacks regularly.   Those teams are also 2nd, 10th, 1st, and 24th in pass block win rate respectively.  Cincy is low, but that’s all IOL.  Their 2 OTs are ranked top 20 in PBWR.  The next 3 opponents are 5th, 4th, and 14th respectively in PBWR and 14th, 11th, and 21st respectively in sack percentage. The next step in the development would be to win against the top OTs.  He will get his chance in 2 weeks as the Lions have 2 ranked in the top 20 in PBWR.
  • What is wrong with Jaylen Wright?  Every time he runs, he seems to get stopped for a loss or no gain.  It can’t be just on him, right?  Maybe there are some issues with vision and seeing the holes.  But something else has to be going on.  His 6 carries Sunday went for 2, 1, -3, 0, 6, & 2.  He has talent.  Is it the wide zone?  No clue what it is, but I hope he can get it turned around.  He has made some plays in the return game, so he has value there.  But he could be a trade deadline candidate.
  • Austin Jackson… I’m gonna let Coach Eric Smith handle this one.
  • Michael Taaffe may be a diamond in the rough.  His draft profile highlights his instincts and intelligence as positive traits.  He showed those off Sunday with the fantastic pick of Smith, where he recognizes the situation and breaks on the ball.  He has 2 INTs on the season, tied with 19 other players.  I have a hunch he’ll finish with a few more.
  • Kyle Louis and Julius Wood are key ST contributors.  Louis was always around the returner and Wood is a hard-hitting tackler.  I don’t know how much they’ll contribute on defense moving forward, but they will be ST aces and help settle that unit.
  • The Dolphins had not led a single second of a game this season.  In Sunday’s contest, they never trailed.

I SAID WHAT I SAID

Is this post a little longer than usual?  Yes.  Because wins deserve more discussion.  The Dolphins have a little time to enjoy this before turning their sites onto another divisional opponent.  We fans have had some hope this season, but they never materialized into wins.  This time, it did and while the actual team will be “On to New England”, we can bask in the radiance of a victory over the Jets.

item.title: Sean McVay: Poor kickoff coverage is "one of those deals that’s driving me crazy"
item.description: The Rams have made several changes on special teams over the last couple of years, but the team’s results have still been poor — particularly on kick coverage.
item.content:encoded:
The Rams have made several changes on special teams over the last couple of years, but the team’s results have still been poor — particularly on kick coverage.

Despite getting a win over the Raiders on Sunday, the Rams allowed a 36-yard return on the game’s opening kickoff, then allowed another 42-yard return later in the first quarter.

After that, Los Angeles had Brandon McManus send the ball to the end zone for a touchback.

It’s a continuation of an issue the team has had all season. It’s partially the reason Blake Grupe suffered a torn ACL, as he had to make a tackle to prevent an even longer return on a kickoff in Week 6.

Head coach Sean McVay told reporters in his Monday news conference that the coverage issues were the same.

“It was not good enough,” McVay said, via transcript from the team. "We've talked about this a lot, and it has to get fixed. It's not good enough, and we cannot allow ourselves to do that. That was a great return unit that we were going against. [Raiders Special Teams Coordinator] Joe ‘D’ [DeCamillis] and those guys did a really good job, but we have to be much better. You can't give up the first two times that you cover that field position.”

So what can the Rams do going forward?

“I have to figure that out,” McVay said. “It's one of those deals that’s driving me crazy. We have to figure it out, and we haven't yet.”

The Rams have notoriously under-invested in special teams in recent years, and it has continued to affect games. It’s likely to cost the team again in 2026 — unless and until the team can finally effectively cover a kick.

item.title: NFL Week 8 betting: 5 biggest storylines, including the undefeated Vikings being underdogs
item.description: The Vikings travel to face the Lions this week.
item.content:encoded:
Home-field advantage keeps disappearing in the NFL.

After the Dallas Cowboys won Monday night, road teams are 54-52-1 this season, according to Covers.com. The split gets even wider when the spread is involved. Road teams are 62-45 against the spread this season. Home-field advantage has been lessened through the years and through seven weeks this season, it really hasn't mattered at all.

Here are five betting storylines heading into Week 8 of the NFL season:

Vikings are underdogs

There's one undefeated team left in the NFL, and they're underdogs in Week 8.

The Minnesota Vikings are 6-0 and travel to face the Detroit Lions. If the Vikings feel like their great start is being disrespected, it won't get better once they see that the Lions are favored by a full field goal. The Vikings are undefeated straight up but not against the spread. They are 4-2 against the spread. Every team in the NFL has at least two losses against the spread this season.

Underdogs taking over

Road teams are doing well against the spread this season and so are underdogs. A surge by underdogs the past few weeks puts them at 58-48 against the spread this season. Road underdogs are a strong 38-25 ATS (60.3%) this season, via Covers.com.

That ATS record should even out as the season goes on, but to this point it has been smart to take the points.

Joe Burrow creeping up MVP board

Throwing for 249 yards and four touchdowns in a half, when your team outscores a major division rival 35-0, is going to get some attention. Especially when it's Joe Burrow.

The Cincinnati Bengals have taken over as the betting favorites to win the AFC North, and Burrow is making his move in the MVP race after he went nuclear against the Ravens in the second half on Sunday. Josh Allen is still the big favorite with +140 odds at BetMGM, but Burrow has slid into second place at +450.

Burrow's numbers are exceptional this season and the Bengals are having team success, which gives him a chance. Voters like spreading the award around, which worked in Allen's favor two years ago and could help Burrow this time. Burrow has a very favorable schedule the next few weeks, starting with the Titans in Week 8, so he should continue to cut into Allen's lead.

Bills favored over Ravens

The Lamar Jackson situation is making life complicated in Baltimore, and for oddsmakers too. The Ravens quarterback remained out last week with an ankle injury and Baltimore got blown out. Cincinnati covered the spread easily. We're probably in for another week of wondering if Jackson will return, which makes it tough to set a line on what is arguably the marquee game of the week.

The Ravens face the Buffalo Bills, and the Bills are 3.5-point favorites. That indicates that oddsmakers expect Jackson back, because a Tyler Huntley-led team wouldn't be that short of an underdog on the road, but the Ravens are still getting more than a field goal. That line could fluctuate a few times this week based on injury updates for Jackson.

Rams rebound in Super Bowl odds

The Rams' Super Bowl odds are fascinating. Oddsmakers don't want major exposure on the Rams if they turn it around, so after one good win against the Raiders last week Los Angeles moved back up the Super Bowl odds board. They are tied for fourth in Super Bowl odds at +1100. The only three teams with shorter odds are the 49ers, Bills and Chiefs. That's not a major move considering the Rams were fifth in the odds last week, but it's a trend that should continue.

The Rams have a soft portion of their schedule coming up, so they should improve upon their 3-4 record. And if they do, their odds will continue to get shorter. Their odds don't match the results so far this season, but there simply won't be a time in which the Rams' championship odds present fantastic value.

item.title: Cowboys coach has 4-word reply for Eagles fans in odd postgame comments
item.description: Cowboys coach Brian Schottenheimer's replies to questions after a "Monday Night Football" win over the Eagles were so odd he was asked if he was all right.
item.content:encoded:
Dallas Cowboys head coach Brian Schottenheimer had a simple reason for why Philadelphia Eagles fans' taunting had no effect on him.

After the Cowboys' dominant 38-21 win on "Monday Night Football" in Philadelphia, Schotteneimer held a post-game press conference that was shorter than most of his other media appearances. The brevity of the presser had everything to do with the brevity of the head coach's answers. His response to Eagles fans' jeers was just four words.

"I didn't hear it," Schottenheimer said, according to DLLS.

The Cowboys coach also explained that he gave a peace sign to "other people" and was not responding to fans in Philadelphia. He said he couldn't hear their taunts because he was wearing headphones.

NFL POWER RANKINGS: Who's No. 1 after 49ers, Chiefs lose first games?

Most of Schottenheimer's answers were similarly concise, with few constituting more than a few words or a couple of sentences. Quarterback Dak Prescott told reporters in his own post-game media availability that Week 7 brought out a "definitely hungry, pissed off version of Schotty" because of "some noise about him," ostensibly generated by the media.

Asked directly if he was all right, Schottenheimer said, "I'm great. Excited for our guys."

The head coach's offense was a main reason for the Cowboys' Week 7 win as it generated 416 total yards and 38 points – the most points scored by any team besides the Tampa Bay Buccaneers this week. The win moved Dallas to 3-4 and 1.5 games behind the New York Giants (4-2-1) for first place in the NFC East.

item.title: Ex-Seahawks Boye Mafe, Riq Woolen trending in opposite directions with new teams
item.description: Boye Mafe is thriving in Cincinnati, whereas Riq Woolen appears to be wearing out his welcome in Philadelphia.
item.content:encoded:
The Seattle Seahawks defense is still as fearsome and suffocating as ever, even though they lost three key contributors in free agency. Cornerback Riq Woolen went to the Philadelphia Eagles on a one-year deal, edge rusher Boye Mafe inked a three-year contract with the Cincinnati Bengals, and safety Coby Bryant signed his own three-year deal with the Chicago Bears. With Bryant shelved for potentially the entire season due to a knee injury, that leaves Mafe and Woolen as the notable ex-Seahawks from the Super Bowl defense who’ve been getting snaps on other rosters.

Through the first two months of the regular season, Mafe and Woolen’s teams are trending in opposite directions, and their respective performances match the trends.

If Mafe was thought to be a solid pass rusher whose sack productivity was not consistent in Seattle, he’s making his presence felt in a revamped Bengals defense. Here’s a report from Cincy Jungle’s Jason Garrison following the Bengals’ blowout win over the Baltimore Ravens.

Boye Mafe

In a matchup that was set up as a “Trey Hendrickson Revenge” game, it was Boye Mafe who made all the noise. The Bengals did a good job of keeping Hendrickson away from Burrow, often lending Orlando Brown Jr. help. The Ravens, on the other hand, were incapable of keeping Mafe out of the backfield. He ended up with two sacks, but was chasing Huntley around often.

Mafe has 4.5 sacks, six quarterback hits, a forced fumble, a fumble recovery, and (per NextGenStats) a career-best 17.6% pressure rate. His 14 quick QB pressures—these are pressures inside of 2.5 seconds—matches his 2025 total and in almost half the snaps of his final season in Seattle. The Bengals are 4-2 and have a super favorable schedule to return to the playoffs. Cincinnati’s defense may not be elite yet, but it’s no longer a laughing stock, which goes a long way toward helping Joe Burrow and the Bengals offense. Mafe has been a major contributor to the turnaround.

The same cannot be said for the Philadelphia Eagles and Riq Woolen. Philadelphia’s once elite defense has sharply fallen, and Monday night’s 38-21 loss against the Dallas Cowboys exemplified the collapse of Vic Fangio’s unit to (at best) mediocre. Philadelphia’s secondary is collectively struggling, and after a strong start to the season, Woolen’s “prove-it” deal is steadily turning south.

From Bleeding Green Nation’s Joseph Santoliquito:

Riq “Reek” Woolen had himself a game. He completely lost CeeDee Lamb with 12 seconds left in the first half for a 30-yard completion to the Eagles’ nine-yard line. Woolen was fortunate Lamb lost his balance and had to crawl out of bounds. The Cowboys had to settle for an Aubrey 27-yard field goal (3 points thanks to Woolen). The Cowboys scored on four of five drives in the first half. Woolen ran away from adversity, he declined to speak after the game.

Woolen did not have a good game. On a third-and-nine on the Cowboys’ first drive of the second half, he was flagged for holding, giving the Cowboys a new set of downs. He was later burned on the same drive by Ryan Flournoy for a 16-yard completion on a first-and-10 to the Eagles’ 27. On the same drive, Woolen was smoked by Lamb in the corner of the end zone for a 16-yard touchdown and a 28-21 Cowboys’ lead with 1:30 left in the third quarter (11 points thanks to Woolen after Prescott’s two-point conversion).

Woolen was “credited” with 111 yards allowed when targeted, one of the worst performances of his career.

Woolen only allowed five catches for 45 yards in Weeks 1-3. Over his last four games he’s given up 17 catches (on 27 targets) for 296 yards and 2 touchdowns. And lest you think his issues with penalties have subsided, he’s been flagged six times for pass interference, illegal contact, or defensive holding. Woolen leads the Eagles in penalties committed.

We’ve discussed to death the impact of Kenneth Walker on the Kansas City Chiefs, but on the defensive side of the ball we’ve seen that the performance of the cornerback room has not dropped off since Woolen’s departure. The edge rushing group probably could use Mafe right now given how much has been put on the plates of Derick Hall, DeMarcus Lawrence, and Uchenna Nwosu this season, but at $20 million/year he was highly unlikely to be retained.

While Mafe is prepping for a playoff push in Cincinnati, the Eagles could face a fire sale, and it wouldn’t be surprising at this point if Woolen is a potential trade piece as their disastrous season shows no signs of being recoverable.

item.title: Winners and losers from Ravens’ Week 7 loss to the Bengals
item.description: Plenty of Ravens share the blame for Sunday’s second-half collapse against the Bengals.
item.content:encoded:
The Ravens dropped to 4-3 with their second loss in a row to a divisional opponent in Week 7. There is plenty of blame to share after Baltimore was outscored 35-0 in the second half by the Bengals, but still a few positive performances to highlight. Let’s get into the winners and losers from Sunday’s game:

Winners

Zay Flowers: Flowers’ monster season continued on Sunday as the Bengals seemingly had no answers for stopping the Ravens’ top receiver. Flowers’ first catch of the day went for a 48-yard touchdown on a screen pass on the opening drive. He added another 89 yards on seven more catches throughout the rest of the game, finishing the day with eight receptions for 137 yards and a touchdown. Flowers’ production should only increase once Lamar Jackson is back under center.

K’Von Wallace: Wallace played 17 snaps on Sunday with Jaylinn Hawkins out with a knee injury. While his day was not perfect, the veteran safety made enough plays to stand out. Wallace ended Cincinnati’s second drive of the game with a pressure on Joe Burrow that forced an incompletion on second down and a tackle on Chase Brown short of the sticks on third down. Wallace then forced a fumble on a kickoff return, but the Bengals were able to retain possession of the ball. Wallace could make the decision to go back to Hawkins a difficult one if he can continue to make plays in his absence.

Cam Jurgens: Jurgens made his debut for Baltimore in Week 7 and appeared to provide a stable presence at center after much turnover at the position to this point. According to PFF, Jurgens allowed just one pressure against Cincinnati. Vega Ioane unfortunately left the game early on with a knee injury after moving back to right guard, so the Ravens are still waiting to see their projected starting offensive line play together for any significant stretch of time.

Travis Jones: Jones finished the game tied for the team lead in pressures with three, according to PFF. He has had a tackle for loss on a run play.

Losers

Tyler Huntley: Huntley came out of the gate hot against the Bengals, leading to a 13-0 lead heading into halftime. The second half was a completely different story for the backup quarterback as the offense struggled to move the ball, failing to score another point for the remainder of the game. Following a touchdown that put Cincinnati up 28-13 in the fourth quarter, Huntley threw an interception on the first play of Baltimore’s drive. The Bengals capitalized on Huntley’s error with another touchdown on a short field to go up 35-13 with just over six minutes remaining. For as admirable as Huntley is in a pinch, the Ravens desperately need their MVP quarterback back under center.

Roger Rosengarten: Rosengarten was beaten cleanly by Boye Mafe for a sack on third down on Baltimore’s second drive of the game. He was later flagged for a false start on another third down.

John Simpson: Simpson allowed a team-high four pressures while also being flagged for holding on a play where Huntley ran for seven yards to move the chains on third down.

Derrick Henry: Through a combination of factors, the usually dominant Hall-of-Fame back has struggled in several games this season. Henry was held to just 45 yards and 17 carries against Cincinnati — a measly 2.6 yards per carry. Blocking has been an issue, as Henry has been hit near the line of scrimmage too often, but it is fair to wonder if age is finally becoming a factor for the 32-year-old workhorse. Over the past two games against divisional opponents, Henry has been held to 103 total rushing yards while being kept out of the end zone.

Kyle Hamilton: It feels wrong to ever put Hamilton in this section, but his play on Sunday left a lot to be desired. Hamilton missed three tackles, including on a touchdown run where he had a chance to stop Samaje Perine in the backfield. He was also credited by PFF with giving up a touchdown to Tee Higgins, though it’s hard to know what his responsibility was on the play.

Marlon Humphrey: Humphrey, one of the longest-tenured players on the team, has been a source of scrutiny over the years, due to both on- and off-field behavior. According to PFF, Humphrey allowed 60 yards on three receptions while missing two tackles. The veteran cornerback has now allowed the most receiving yards in the fourth quarter this season with 176, according to Next Gen Stats.

Nate Wiggins: Wiggins struggled against the Bengals as well, allowing 80 yards and a touchdown on six catches while also being flagged for defensive holding, though the penalty was declined.

Jesse Minter / Anthony Weaver: While a large portion of the blame deserves to fall on the players, as the trend of defensive meltdowns has now lasted through multiple defensive coordinators and two head coaches, Minter and Weaver still have to face criticism as well for their unit’s horrendous second-half performance on Sunday. Minter’s decision to go for it on fourth down from the 12-yard line while trailing 14-13 instead of going up 16-14 with a field goal has been questioned, but it ultimately proved to be the right decision, as his defense was unable to stop Cincinnati’s offense from scoring touchdowns on the following three drives.

Declan Doyle: For all the good Doyle has done in his first season calling plays at the NFL level, he still has room to grow. The Ravens’ offense has been shut out in the second half of the past two games after strong starts in the first two quarters. Doyle has yet to figure out a consistently effective approach to short-yardage situations either. It feels harsh to judge Doyle too much without Jackson at quarterback, but he still has to be better at adjusting once opposing defenses begin to catch up in games.

item.title: Green Bay Packers News: Packers’ running game continues to struggle
item.description: Can the Packers ever find success on the ground?
item.content:encoded:
The Packers cannot get their ground game in gear.

They cannot run with MarShawn Lloyd. They cannot run with Chris Brooks. They cannot run with Pierre Strong. They cannot run with Kaleb Johnson, a healthy scratch this week despite the Packers giving up a draft pick for him.

They can’t even run with Josh Jacobs, who returned from his not-suspension against the Lions to grind out 36 yards on 11 attempts. 10 of those 36 yards came on one carry, meaning he averaged a paltry 2.6 yards per attempt on his other runs. Not great!

Will it ever get better? All signs point to no at this point, but who knows? The Packers’ 2026 season has been anything but predictable, and they’ve been able to figure out some of their issues on the fly. Maybe the ground game will miraculously improve.

It feels like it would take a miracle at this point. Maybe Kevin Zeitler finally gets into the lineup and ignites a change in fortunes. Maybe Josh Jacobs discovers the fountain of youth. Maybe MarShawn Lloyd figures out how not to get lost between his backfield position and the line of scrimmage. Maybe Jordan Love turns into a dual-threat savant. A lot of things could maybe happen!

I’m not hopeful, though. Even when the Packers have faced some of the league’s worst run defenses, they haven’t been able to get it going on the ground. They peaked at 86 rushing yards against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, and that included 58 yards on two carries from Kaleb Johnson and Chris Brooks. Unless the Packers can figure out a way to rip off a couple of big runs — or maybe fall into one by accident — it’s hard to see a big week of rushing output on the horizon this year.

But who knows? Anything can happen. Maybe the real ground game has yet to be discovered.

item.title: NFL Panic Meter: Chiefs have to address their offensive issues now, before they regret it
item.description: The Chiefs had a rough night in a 20-3 loss to the Seahawks on Sunday night.
item.content:encoded:
The Kansas City Chiefs are 5-1 with only a road loss to the Seattle Seahawks. Overall, they're fine.

Yet, Sunday night had to be an unnerving performance. The Seahawks were the first team to shut down Kenneth Walker III, and the Chiefs offense melted. They had the fewest points (3), yards (213) and first downs (11) in any start over Patrick Mahomes' career, according to NFL researcher Tony Holzman-Escareno.

The Seahawks defense can do that to teams. But for the Chiefs, it renewed the worry about the weapons around Patrick Mahomes. Nobody made plays on Sunday night. Kansas City's leading receiver had 44 yards. And while Walker will not have many games in which he has just 36 rushing yards, he has never been asked to carry an offense over a long season. He had 14.2 carries per game through four seasons with the Seahawks and this season he's at 20. That's a lot of extra carries for a running back over a full season. There has to be concern about putting so much pressure on him over 17 games and then a postseason.

Rashee Rice's absence hurt on Sunday night and when he's able to return from hamstring and knee injuries, maybe everything will look better. Xavier Worthy can drop down from a featured role that he probably can't thrive in, Travis Kelce can be more of a secondary piece at his age as well and others can play in smaller roles. Realistically, even if Rice comes back healthy, the Chiefs probably do need some help.

There aren't a lot of difference-making receivers available at the trade deadline, but there could be some. Jacksonville's Brian Thomas Jr., Cleveland's Jerry Jeudy, Tennessee's Calvin Ridley and Minnesota's Jauan Jennings are among those who could be available. The Chiefs have to look into all possibilities to make sure they're not stuck short on offense late in the season or the playoffs. Right now too much is on Walker's shoulders. It will eventually have to shift back to Mahomes. And he'll need more help.

Panic meter: Nothing too high for a very good team, but they can't ignore needs.

Texans done?

When you start 0-4, you can't afford a big loss. Certainly not one as a 10-point favorite at home.

The Houston Texans are 2-5 after losing in overtime to the New York Giants. It's hard to completely bury them, because the talent is still there. But now a team that couldn't even beat J.J. McCarthy at home has to go 8-2 at least to realistically be in the wild-card hunt. The defense is way worse than anyone was expecting, and the offense isn't good enough to overcome that. If it weren't for the Chargers, this would be the NFL's most disappointing team.

Panic meter: Still a sliver of hope at a rebound, but let's not waste any more time thinking about the 2026 Texans until they're back to .500.

Panthers meltdown

The Panthers trailed 43-6 at home on Sunday to a Tampa Bay Buccaneers team that was 1-5 coming in. Even if anyone was wondering if the Panthers were playing over their heads at 3-2, nobody expected that.

The score was 33-6 at halftime and everything was bad.

"I mean, it's a shock," Panthers coach Dave Canales told the media after the game. "For me to be able to move on from it, because I've literally never been a part of a half of football like that. To experience it in all phases: blocked kick, sack-fumble, interception, blocked punt and the defensive side not getting off the field in different ways. It was so crazy and so egregiously different than the ball we're used to playing."

No matter how bad the game was, the Panthers are allowed one ugly loss. They had looked good during a 3-2 start, particularly Bryce Young having a breakout season at quarterback. But next up is a game at the Packers and then a home game against the Broncos. We're about to find out if Carolina has staying power.

Panic meter: The Panthers are on notice after whatever that was on Sunday.

Is Kellen Moore's seat hot?

It was a bit strange for Saints owner Gayle Benson to seemingly put coach Kellen Moore and general manager Mickey Loomis on notice last week, saying she will "not accept this level of performance," according to the Associated Press. The Saints were seemingly on the right track late last season, although they were off to a 2-4 start this season. Then they had an ugly 16-10 loss in Paris to the Steelers, which can't help anything.

"Mrs. B's great," Moore said last week according to the AP, before facing the Steelers. "We all want better results, and that's how this business is."

The thought of Moore being in any trouble after a good finish to last season, his first as coach of the Saints, was far from anyone's mind. Until Benson sounded upset at the way the season is going. Then it got worse.

Panic meter: Probably nothing to worry about yet, but Moore might want to quickly win some games just in case.

Ravens' playoff hopes dipping

The Ravens have a very talented team and are no longer better than 50% to make the playoffs, according to DVOA.

The Ravens' odds dipped to 41.4% via DVOA after a bad loss to the Bengals in which they were outscored 35-0 in the second half. The problem is the Ravens face the toughest remaining schedule in the NFL, via DVOA. Lamar Jackson didn't return last week from an ankle injury and that's becoming a point of contention. The Ravens simply need him back if they're going to survive a rough schedule, and that includes their next two games against the Bills and Jaguars. For a 4-3 team, there should be a lot of concern in Baltimore. And if this season ends up with no playoff berth, who knows what changes might come next.

Panic meter: With Jackson back, maybe it will be OK. If he doesn't return soon, the season is probably headed downhill fast.
