item.title: Film review: J.J. McCarthy looked like the real deal vs. Houston
item.description: McCarthy was excellent on the road in his first start as a Giant. Here are several high level throws.
item.content:encoded:
The New York Giants traveled to Houston to defeat the Texans 27-21 in quarterback J.J. McCarthy’s first start as a New York Giant. McCarthy went 20 of 28 for 252 yards, while suffering three sacks. He was calm, poised, understood where to go with the football, and his arm talent shone in the Lone Star State.

McCarthy didn’t use his legs, but the threat of his legs allowed Matt Nagy to effectively run concepts out of different formations that made McCarthy’s athletic ability a threat to the defense. Read defenders had to remain disciplined off the zone-read, lest McCarthy break contain with his speed and burst. The Giants’ run game, also, was much more physical at the point of attack, and the overall rushing attack accepted and thrived when challenged by John Harbaugh last week.

Nevertheless, McCarthy’s presence helped make the offense multidimensional, allowing them to total 420 yards of total offense. McCarthy had two 40+ yard plays in the first quarter, and his velocity, ball placement, and ability to access all areas of the field were massive assets for Matt Nagy and the Giants’ offense.

McCarthy had several high-level throws in the game. Here are six of them below.

Q1, 6:59, First-and-10

The Giants got aggressive after picking up a crucial fourth-and-short on a Darnell Mooney jet sweep at the Houston 47 yard line:

via GIPHY

via GIPHY

The Giants confirm the middle-of-the-field-closed, Cover-1 look post-snap, and McCarthy rips a beautifully placed back-shoulder pass to Malik Nabers outside the numbers. McCarthy held the safety in place well, creating an easy one-on-one matchup post-snap. Still, the outside ball placement allowed the elite receiver to adjust his body, locate, and secure the pass, which set up the Tyrone Tracy Jr. touchdown.

Q1, 4:05, Second-and-17

On the first play of the next drive, J.J. McCarthy (18) drove a dime to Malachi Fields (88) that the rookie receiver took for 47 yard:

The ball jumps out of McCarthy’s hand with excellent velocity and ball-placement; he hit Fields in stride and allowed the big receiver to walk the tightrope up the sideline. It appears to be quarter-quarter-half coverage and Fields pressed to the midline of the numbers before exploding outside. The cornerback does a solid speed turn, but the ball placement and timing were too perfect from McCarthy. 

Q2, 6:52, Second-and-10 

via GIPHY

via GIPHY

McCarthy found Nabers for 17 yards after evading a free rusher in the pocket. I appreciate how the young quarterback navigated the pocket but kept his eyes downfield to find Nabers on the dig route. Space was cleared by Darnell Mooney (17) and Jalin Hyatt’s (81) vertical routes vs. Cover-4.

The dig was open in the middle of the field, but the vertical routes were both isolated in single coverage, both with a leverage advantage. It was a great call by the coaches, but McCarthy’s movement, throw, and ability to rip it off platform are all noteworthy.

Q2, :29, First-and-10

McCarthy gets the Giants in field goal range with an elite throw. This throw, however, was with an expiring clock at the end of the first half:

McCarthy was under pressure but fired the deep corner route against man. The accuracy was so precise that it allowed Nabers to secure the 27-yard pass and get out of bounds. Houston ran a successful T/E twist that got pressure but McCarthy stood strong in the pocket and delivered a pass that got the Giants into Houston’s part of the field. Zvada attempted a 44-yard field goal that was missed.

Q3, 12:42, Third-and-4

This is an exceptional play by McCarthy that went for 20 yards to Fields along the sideline. Nagy dialed up a high-low with Devin Singletary (26) and Fields, and McCarthy held the underneath defender with his eyes before delivering a 20 yard pass to Fields along the sideline. His eyes allowed his arm to make this throw.

Q4, 9:36, Third-and-9

This was an exceptional conversion by J.J. McCarthy, who delivered a far-hash rocket to Fields for a first down. The Texans paid attention to Isaiah Likely (9) on the underneath play, and the Cover-3 leverage was off and slightly to the inside. Fields ran a route and McCarthy delivered a good pass that hit the outside hip of Fields – move the sticks!

Bonus play

This is just an unreal arm talent throw by McCarthy, who recognized the lapse in coverage and gave Darnell Mooney a chance from the far hash to make a play. Mooney is open a lot; it’ll break right for him soon, but securing footballs like this would be an excellent start. 

Here’s a highlight reel from McCarthy, including a few plays that were not elaborated on above:

Final thoughts

The Giants were 10.5 point road underdogs with a young – new – quarterback, who was labeled a bust by his previous team. Yet, J.J. McCarthy answered the call and helped the Giants win an important game before the BYE week. The NFC East is up for grabs and the Giants sit in first place. Moving to McCarthy seemed to unlock the Giants’ ability to play multifaceted on offense, while giving the team a much higher ceiling than Jameis Winston. There’s an excitement around the Meadowlands – and it’s understandable!

item.title: Week 8 NFL Power Rankings: Grading Each Team’s Quarterback Situation
item.description: In Week 8’s installment of @AaronLemingNFL’s NFL Power Rankings, we take a look at each team’s quarterback situation.
item.content:encoded:
With the conclusion of Week 7, we are quickly inching closer to the midpoint of the season. While there’s still plenty of season left to be played, certain teams have separated themselves, while others are experiencing plenty of adversity through the way of injuries. The playoff picture has yet to take shape, but with the trade deadline just weeks away, the league’s dynamics will start to shift in the coming days/weeks. Before we turn the page ahead to Week 8, let’s dive into our updated Week 8 WCG NFL Power Rankings, reflecting on the week that was, headlined by each team’s quarterback play through seven weeks. 

1. Buffalo Bills (5-1)

Quarterback Progress Report: Josh Allen (A)

Josh Allen is an alien, and even when things aren’t perfect around him, there might not be a better quarterback in the league. Although his numbers aren’t otherworldly so far, he’s the primary reason why the Bills are sitting at 5-1 after their bye week. Assuming receiver D.J. Moore gets back healthy at some point soon, his numbers should increase. Either way, the Bills are one of the best teams in the AFC yet again; we’ll see if their defense can hold up their end of the bargain this season. 

2. San Francisco 49ers (6-1)

Quarterback Progress Report: Brock Purdy (A)

By the numbers, Purdy should be considered a front-runner in the MVP race so far this season. His hot start has been impressive, although I would argue that his last three games have been a bit of a “come back to earth” type of situation. That’s not meant to take away from what he’s done, but the decision-making is becoming shaky, and it needs to be mentioned. Overall, he’s playing at a high level, but he needs to course-correct a little bit for the 49ers to maintain their high level of play. 

3. Minnesota Vikings (6-0)

Quarterback Progress Report: Kyler Murray (C-)

Quarterback play was a big issue for the Vikings last season, but all of that bad luck they experienced in 2025 seems to be overcorrecting so far this season. What’s funny about this situation is that the quarterback play hasn’t been noticeably better, whether that’s Kyler Murray or Carson Wentz. Then again, does it really matter with this defense? Murray has been OK, but he’s also left a lot to be desired. We’ll see what shakes out over the final 11 games of the season, but so far, he’s been “good enough” but nothing more. 

4. Kansas City Chiefs (5-1)

Quarterback Progress Report: Patrick Mahomes (A)

Overall, there was a rush to judgment about the Chiefs’ 2025 season. Even if Mahomes hasn’t been playing at the MVP level lately, the way he’s come back from a torn ACL (among other issues) in such a short time is nothing short of impressive. The numbers haven’t been gaudy, but looking at the offensive depth chart, I’d say he’s playing well above what he should. The Chiefs appear to be back, and so does Mahomes. Considering the injury he suffered at the end of last season, his “comeback” has been extremely impressive. 

5. Jacksonville Jaguars (4-2)

Quarterback Progress Report: Trevor Lawrence (A)

The resurgence of the former No. 1 overall pick in 2021 has been quite the sight to see. Head coach Liam Coen has unlocked a level of consistency we haven’t seen since Lawrence entered the league. The offensive line has outplayed expectations, and even without Brian Thomas Jr. being a factor, this offense is humming. While I’m not sure I would categorize Coen’s hiring as a “career-saving” move, it was pretty damn close. 

6. Detroit Lions (4-2)

Quarterback Progress Report: Jared Goff (A+)

No matter who the offensive coordinator has been in Detroit, it hasn’t seemed to matter a whole lot for Goff. Under Drew Petzing, Goff has been damn-near perfect, especially in the touchdown-to-interception ratio at an impressive 14-0 through six games. His completion percentage is slightly down from the 70% he posted in 2024, but it’s right on par with what it was last year. He’s targeting the middle of the field and going deep often, and still doesn’t have an interception. That’s about as good as you can ask for, and it’s probably about time for him to be included in the MVP conversation. 

7. Chicago Bears (5-2)

Quarterback Progress Report: Caleb Williams (A)

The marriage between head coach Ben Johnson and Williams has gone about as well as hoped through a season and a half. In Year 1, Williams made plenty of big leaps, but through four starts in Year 2, he looks like a Top 5-7 quarterback. He’s continued to limit turnovers while taking more of what the defense gives him. That has led to a completion rate over 70%, yet he’s still taking plenty of accurate shots downfield. There’s still growth to be had, but he’s been night and day from what we saw in his rookie campaign. 

8. Seattle Seahawks (4-3)

Quarterback Progress Report: Sam Darnold (D-)

Little did we know that when Darnold went down in Week 1, it wouldn’t be a season-ending injury, but instead an eye-opening experience in which backup quarterback Drew Lock has severely outplayed Darnold this season. This has kind of been the story of Darnold’s career, but he’s put enough good football on tape to make many believe he can bounce back. That said, if he doesn’t soon, they might need to change the quarterback to salvage the season. Either way, Darnold has been brutal, and it’s simply not something Seattle can afford to live with. 

9. Denver Broncos (5-2)

Quarterback Progress Report: Bo Nix (D-)

Broncos fans will hope Sunday’s blowout win over the Cardinals was a “get right” game for Nix and this offense. So far, it’s been a jumbled mess, and no matter who the play caller is, Nix has struggled coming back from his ankle surgery. Mobility is a big part of his game, but the continued peppering at or behind the line of scrimmage on throws has been a big red flag. Denver is a very good team, but they’ll need their offense to do its part if they hope to contend for a Super Bowl again in January. 

10. Cincinnati Bengals (4-2)

Quarterback Progress Report: Joe Burrow (A-)

The Bengals have been relatively inconsistent through the first seven weeks of the season, including on Sunday when they trailed 13-0 heading into the half against the Ravens. Then they figured it out and scored 35 unanswered en route to a convincing victory to overtake Baltimore in the division. Joe Burrow was responsible for four touchdowns, bringing his total to 15 on the year through six games. If the defense continues to play as they did in the second half, this will be a tough team to beat down the stretch. 

11. New England Patriots (4-3)

Quarterback Progress Report: Drake Maye (B+)

It’s clear that Maye is bordering on elite territory, but a slow start to the season has kept his grade down for the season. Thursday night’s showdown with Williams was a great glimpse into two of the top drafted quarterbacks from the 2024 class, and the matchup did not disappoint. As A.J. Brown and the offensive line get healthier, Maye’s play should improve. He’s unlikely to be as high in the MVP conversation this year, but it’s clear that his yips are out of the way, and he is indeed a very good quarterback with plenty of ceiling still to chase. 

12. Green Bay Packers (4-3)

Quarterback Progress Report: Jordan Love (A)

For the first time in his career, his offensive line has not been ideal. While it has improved in recent weeks, several reserves have been taking real snaps, creating issues. Add in a non-existent run game, and Love has been set up to fail. The start of the season wasn’t great, but over the last month, he’s been a completely different quarterback. Although his completion percentage has dipped and his interceptions have risen a bit, he’s taking way more deep shots and, overall, looks like a big-play hunter. All things considered, he’s had a helluva year so far. 

13. Pittsburgh Steelers (5-2)

Quarterback Progress Report: Aaron Rodgers (B)

All things considered, Rodgers, in his age 43 season, has been pretty dang good. He’s shown signs of looking his age, but as of late, he’s been playing a lot better. There are still a lot of questions about this team’s overall ceiling, but the offense has been playing better, and a lot of that is because of Rodgers. The key to his and this offense’s success is establishing the quick game, but ultimately, he cannot be afraid to take shots downfield. 

14. Baltimore Ravens (4-3)

Quarterback Progress Report: Lamar Jackson and Tyler Huntley (B)

When Lamar is on the field, the Ravens are a dangerous team. The bigger issue is that he’s missed a bulk of games three or more games in four of his last six seasons. Huntley has done a good job in relief, but for the Ravens to reach their ceiling, Jackson needs to be healthy and playing. The biggest concern for this team is its defense, but hopefully a more productive offense will help balance it out. 

15. Cleveland Browns (5-2)

Quarterback Progress Report: Deshaun Watson (B)

Watson has played considerably better than anyone could have expected coming off back-to-back torn Achilles. Frankly, his improved play has been a big reason why the Browns found themselves in first place heading into Week 7. That said, there are still plenty of bad stretches, and that’s probably to be expected. The Browns are firmly in that spot where they can beat most teams, but they can still lose to just about everybody. With a pair of first-rounders in April, it will be interesting to see what they choose to do at the conclusion of the regular season. 

16. Los Angeles Rams (3-4)

Quarterback Progress Report: Matthew Stafford (C-)

Last year’s MVP, much like the rest of the offense, is off to a slow start in 2026. Yet, somehow they are still surviving, and I don’t think you’ll find anyone ready to count them out, despite their injuries. Stafford’s seven interceptions are just one short of how many he threw in both 2024 and 2025. The touchdown production is still there, but overall, things just haven’t looked the same. As the team gets healthier, it’s fair to expect the offense and Stafford to get better, but this has been an uncharacteristically slow start so far. 

17. New York Giants (4-2-1)

Quarterback Progress Report: Jaxson Dart, Jameis Winston, and J.J. McCarthy (B+)

Offensive coordinator Matt Nagy was passed over for multiple head coaching jobs last offseason, including Tennessee. Despite major adversity from quarterback injuries, all three quarterbacks have flashed impressively. Dart looked good before going down with a season-ending knee injury, Winston had flashes, and McCarthy has looked like a new quarterback during his two games so far in New York. The Giants are in a weird but nice spot with a horrible division. They started hot, and despite their injuries, they are in prime position to win the NFC East. 

18. Carolina Panthers (3-3)

Quarterback Progress Report: Bryce Young (A+)

Every quarterback is allowed to have a bad game, which includes Young. Let’s be real here- nobody, and I mean nobody, had Young reviving his career quite the way he has. The Panthers are an inconsistent team that will be prone to some bad days at the office like they had on Sunday, but Young has made a huge leap in Year 4, which should make the front office and fans alike feel like they have a franchise quarterback. There are some limitations to his game, but those haven’t shown up much this season. Coaching matters, but Young deserves a lot of credit for an almost unheard-of turnaround.

19. Atlanta Falcons (3-4)

Quarterback Progress Report: Michael Penix (A-)

Atlanta looked like a complete disaster at the start of the season, when they started 0-2 and didn’t reach the red zone. Then Penix returned from his third torn ACL, and the offense has looked like a completely different unit ever since. Although he has clear flaws to his game, his arm talent is impossible to deny. The same could be said about his overall impact on the offense and the overall team. Despite the slow start, the Falcons are far from out of it, and with the talent they have on offense, Penix could be the difference-maker. 

20. Las Vegas Raiders (3-4)

Quarterback Progress Report: Kirk Cousins (B)

The Raiders’ impressive 3-0 start is no more, and despite a few close games to contenders, it feels like the bottom might have fallen out. Cousins has been much better than expected, but it’s also worth wondering if maybe it’s time to give this year’s No. 1 overall pick to the offense. Fernando Mendoza will start at some point, and most of that will be circumstantial. Cousins has shown he still has some juice left, but the Raiders’ offense was always going to be a project.

21. Dallas Cowboys (3-4)

Quarterback Progress Report: Dak Prescott (C-)

Since 2020, Prescott’s even-year experience hasn’t been good, and so far in 2026, it’s been more of the same. That’s not to say that Dak has been bad by any means, but he’s not nearly as effective as he was last year, despite having similar problems on the defensive side of the ball. Even with a 2:1 touchdown-to-interception ratio, the offense just has not looked the same most of the season, despite having some elite weapons at his disposal. Sometimes you have to grade players on a curve, and because we know how good Prescott can be, he’s being graded with that in mind. 

22. Houston Texans (2-5)

Quarterback Progress Report: C.J. Stroud (A+)

The start of 2026 has been a nightmare start for the Texans, but there’s no way you can include Stroud in that conversation. Not only is he avoiding those mistakes that plagued him in the playoffs last year, but he’s showing athleticism to extend plays that we haven’t seen from him at the NFL level. Simply put, he’s more than proven he’s “worth” a high-dollar extension. Now we’ll see how they finish out the season, because things look grim, even after digging themselves out of a 0-4 hole. 

23. Tampa Bay Buccaneers (2-5)

Quarterback Progress Report: Baker Mayfield (D-)

The start of the season has not gone as expected, but following Sunday’s 43-13 victory against the Panthers, the Buccaneers find themselves hanging onto their season for dear life. Mayfield’s injury has hurt, but frankly, the drop-off in play between him and Jaylon Daniels wasn’t that big. Mayfield’s return wasn’t anything to write home about, but a win is a win. That’s what happens when a team forces four takeaways. Mayfield has plenty to prove, even though he was recently extended. We’ll see if he can get on track over the final 10 games of the season. 

24. New Orleans Saints (2-5)

Quarterback Progress Report: Tyler Shough (B-)

The Saints are off to a disappointing start, and owner Gayle Benson has put the heat on their second-year coaching staff. Typically, switching coaching staffs after two years doesn’t exactly serve a quarterback well, but Shough has proven to be an above-average quarterback with enough ceiling to build around. He’s been atop the league in yards and touchdowns, but interceptions have been an issue. Considering where he was drafted, this can be classified as nothing short of a success story, but things just haven’t clicked in Year 2 like most expected for this team. 

25. Indianapolis Colts (2-5)

Quarterback Progress Report: Daniel Jones (F)

In some ways, I get it. When you don’t have a quarterback, you’ll do anything you can to “find” one, even if it’s forcing the situation. Couple that with missing badly on a No. 3 overall pick, and it’s a dire situation. The issue is that the Colts didn’t learn from the Giants’ mistake and did it all over again, which led to general manager Chris Ballard being fired this past week. Jones had a nice stretch last year, but even before his injury, he was coming back down to earth. This year has been nothing short of a disaster so far. We’ll see what Indy does this offseason, but it’s hard to envision many scenarios where Jones is on stable ground heading into 2027. 

26. Philadelphia Eagles (2-5)

Quarterback Progress Report: Jalen Hurts (INC)

When healthy, Hurts is a quality quarterback, even if he has struggled to get this offense over the hump the past two seasons. Simply put, the minute he was placed on Injured Reserve due to the blood clots in his lungs was the minute the Eagles’ season ended. Obviously, the primary focus is on Hurts’ long-term health, and all reports are good on that front. Without a complete picture, it’s almost impossible to give Hurts or the Eagles a grade. Again, the most important thing is that Hurts appears to be going to be OK. The rest comes secondary, even in a lost season. 

27. New York Jets (2-5)

Quarterback Progress Report: Geno Smith (B+)

The Jets are a better team than they were a year ago, and a big reason why is that they finally have some certainty at the quarterback position. Things might not have gone well in Geno’s first stint in New York, but it’s been much better this time around. The bigger issue is that the Jets still lack talent, and even though Smith is a much better quarterback in Round 2, he’s on the tail end of his career. Losing to the Dolphins is going to sting, but this is a rebuilding team in need of another offseason or two. 

28. Washington Commanders (1-4-1)

Quarterback Progress Report: Jayden Daniels (B)

It’s funny to wind back to 2024 when RGIII said the Bears were in danger of ruining Williams’ development because of the support system around him. While he wasn’t wrong about some of that, Daniels simply hasn’t been the same since his breakout rookie season. So far this season, he has looked pretty good, but the support system around him has been an issue. On top of that, first-year offensive coordinator David Blough’s inability to force Daniels under center continues to be a big issue in his development. Durability will always be a concern, but Daniels’ ceiling as an NFL quarterback will be limited unless a play-caller can force him to play a more versatile style. 

29. Arizona Cardinals (2-5)

Quarterback Progress Report: Jacoby Brissett (D)

To nobody’s surprise, Brissett has been nothing short of replaceable after getting a bump in pay during the preseason. The good news for Arizona is that they’ve never seen the veteran as a long-term option. The bigger issue is that they are two wins ahead of the Chargers, and one ahead of the Titans. Finding a quarterback isn’t easy, but the result of this season needs to be getting them into a position to be able to draft their long-term answer. 

30. Los Angeles Chargers (0-6)

Quarterback Progress Report: Justin Herbert (F)

I know everyone wants to keep making excuses for Herbert, and to a certain extent, some are valid. The offensive line has been a disaster since Jim Harbaugh’s first year, but it’s impossible to ignore how bad he’s been late in games. Things can change from preseason expectations, but this was a front-runner for MVP coming into the regular season. Having more interceptions than touchdowns is never acceptable for a veteran quarterback, so maybe it’s time to stop moving goalposts here. Simply put, they need a helluva lot more from Herbert than they’ve gotten. 

31. Tennessee Titans (1-6)

Quarterback Progress Report: Cam Ward (D-)

In my preseason quarterback rankings, I ranked Ward much higher than the consensus. Even though I was skeptical of hiring a defensive-minded head coach, I thought Ward had the talent and mental makeup to overcome it. Clearly, I was wrong. The start of his second season has been nothing short of a disaster, and even though head coach Robert Saleh has been against benching him, they might need to revisit that conversation soon. It’s been a disaster season so far in Tennessee, which is a shame. 

32. Miami Dolphins (1-5)

Quarterback Progress Report: Malik Willis (D)

Up until the first quarter of Sunday’s game, the Dolphins had not led in a game this season. Miami is in the early stages of a rebuild, which has produced one of the league’s worst receiving corps, but Willis still has a lot to do. He’s averaging well under 200 passing yards per game, and came into Sunday with more interceptions than touchdowns. That last part has since evened out, but this was always an upside gamble with a low floor. All things considered, it’s trending toward the Dolphins using that first-round pick for a quarterback in April.

item.title: Future Hogs Week 8: College football players who could help the Commanders
item.description: Scouting college prospects for the Washington Commanders in upcoming NFL drafts
item.content:encoded:
Much like Week 7, several of the top-10 teams in college football suffered losses or close calls. After defeating Notre Dame and rising to #2 in the AP Poll, BYU lost on the road in overtime to UCF. Ole Miss fell from #7 after they could not pull off a comeback against #19 Texas. The #8 team in the country, Texas Tech, couldn’t keep up with Cincinnati, ultimately suffering a loss. In a ranked-on-ranked matchup, #10 Utah prevailed at home over #14 Houston. After the weekend, the only undefeated teams in the Top 25 are Miami, UCLA, and Utah.

Week 9 will see the top four teams in the AP Poll in action. #1 Miami will face Bill Belichick and UNC, #2 Ohio State will go on the road to face USC, #3 Georgia will host #17 Florida, and #4 Indiana will play Minnesota. Now ranked #6, Utah will try to avoid being upset by Cincinnati while #13 Texas Tech will be tested again by #22 Arizona.

Here are a few players who had a good week and might be able to help out the Commanders. Let me know. what you think about these prospects and feel free to post players that stood out to you.

Keyone Jenkins | QB | Senior | UCF

Keyone Jenkins picked a great time to have his best game of the season. Jenkins is a small quarterback at 6’, 200 pounds, but he put quality throws on tape in the Knights’ win over BYU. Jenkins threw with touch and layered throws over defenders. On a few of his passes in the end zone, Jenkins placed the ball where only his receivers could catch it. Generally, the ball came out on time, but he kept his eyes downfield and found receivers when it didn’t. Jenkins is a developmental quarterback prospect who needs to become more consistent with his mechanics in order to stick around at the next level. Against BYU, Jenkins went 25 of 41 for 293 yards and three touchdowns and added a touchdown on the ground.

Caleb Komolafe | RB | RS Junior | Northwestern

Northwestern continued its winning ways against Rutgers, and Caleb Komolafe was a major reason why. He’s 5’11”, 210 pounds, so enough size to play at the next level. Northwestern appears to use more zone-scheme run plays than gap scheme, but Komolafe plays well in both. His best attribute might be his ability to find holes and squeeze the most out of runs when much isn’t there. He can anticipate where holes will open on zone runs, then bursts through them. He has above-average vision and breaks off long runs, but I’m not sure he has the long speed to do this in the pros. Komolafe rushed 13 times for 150 yards and a touchdown in the Wildcats victory over the Scarlet Knights.

Ryan Wingo | WR | Junior | Texas

Ryan Wingo was busy early against Ole Miss, helping the Longhorns gain a lead that Ole Miss could never overcome. Wingo is 6’2”, 214 pounds, so he has the size of an NFL receiver. Wingo’s best attribute is his speed. He uses it to get past defenders downfield or run by them after short receptions. My biggest concern with Wingo is, while he can rely on that athleticism in college, it might not be enough in the NFL. He needs to improve his route-running and clean up focus drops to have a long career at the next level. He showed improvement in these areas against Ole Miss as he had seven catches for 111 yards and a touchdown.

Kari Ashley | TE | Senior | TCU

Kari Ashley had a unique path to starting tight end for the Horned Frogs. His career began as a linebacker at Georgia Tech, but an injury led him to being medically disqualified. He became a standout tight end at a JUCO school, impressing TCU. He’s now their leading receiver thanks to his sheer athleticism which Bruce Feldman noted in his College Football Freaks List 2026. Ashley is very small for a tight end at 6’4”, 225 pounds. You’d never think Ashley played defense given how easily he catches passes and runs after the catch. While his athleticism is impressive, he still has a long way to go to become a better blocker and all-around tight end. In a loss to West Virginia, Ashley made six catches for 118 yards.

Braelin Moore | C | Senior | LSU

LSU had no problem defeating Auburn, even though the Tigers were fresh off an upset of Georgia. Sam Leavitt had one of his best games and LSU rushed for over 165 yards. Braelin Moore manned the middle of the offensive line, his second year starting for LSU after three years at Virginia Tech. Moore is a little small at 6’2”, 300 pounds, but he is quick getting from snap to hands on a defender. His smaller size helps him to be light on his feet and mirror defenders. Where his size works against him is anchoring against rushers. He can get pushed back towards the quarterback, but he loses the rep slowly which allows the quarterback time to get rid of the ball. This also means he doesn’t move people in the run game, but he understands blocking angles and will find defenders in space. Moore would be a fit for a team with a zone running game and gets the ball out quickly.

Dylan Stewart | EDGE | Junior | South Carolina

There’s a good chance the first pass rusher taken in the 2027 NFL Draft will be Texas’s Colin Simmons or South Carolina’s Dylan Stewart. After missing games to start the season due to injuries, Stewart might finally be hitting his stride after back-to-back weeks with a sack. He has the length NFL teams desire at 6’5” and 250 pounds. Initial quickness on the line allows Stewart to beat tackles around the edge or convert speed to power and bull rush blockers. As a junior, he needs to improve his strength and hand usage to disengage from blocks. While there are areas for improvement, the upside of Stewart is easy to see. He helped the Gamecocks beat Tennessee with two tackles, a sack, and a forced fumble.

Ethan Wesloski | LB | RS Senior | Oklahoma State

Quarterback Drew Mestemaker isn’t the only productive player for Oklahoma State. The 6’1”, 234-pound linebacker Ethan Wesloski has been putting up big numbers this year. Earlier in the season, he had back-to-back games with 17 tackles. He makes so many plays by being instinctual and having a high motor. Wesloski is willing to fight off blocks and always hustles to the ball to make plays. I need to see more from him in coverage to get a better sense of how good a linebacker prospect he can be, but the other aspects of his game are solid. For the Cowboys’ homecoming win over Colorado, Wesloski had eight tackles, two sacks, and a PBU.

Zeke Berry | CB | Senior | Michigan

Calling the game between Indiana and Michigan a defensive battle would be an understatement. The only touchdown scored was in overtime by the Hoosiers to secure the win. Zeke Berry was one of the Wolverines’ top defenders. Keeping Nick Marsh and Charlie Becker, both potentially first-round picks, is no easy task. At only 5’11”, 188 pounds, Berry surrendered size to the duo but not skill. Berry has quick feet and fluid hips that aid him in changing direction to stay with receivers throughout their routes. Berry has quickness and speed that he uses to break on the ball. He has no issue making hits, but I’d like to see him wrap up and form tackle more consistently. Berry helped the Wolverines cause in the loss to the Hoosiers with six tackles, a PBU, and an interception.

MJ Cannon | S | Senior | Cincinnati

The Bearcats were able to upset Texas Tech thanks to a number of plays by MJ Cannon. He’s a big corner at 6’3”, 213 pounds, but does his best work in coverage rather than at the line of scrimmage. While he isn’t very fluid, he does react quickly to the play in front of him. That lets him breakup passes or limit yards after the catch if a pass is completed. He can also use his play recognition to trigger downhill and make a stop. Cannon’s not a true centerfielder, but can handle any other deep coverage responsibilities. His nine tackles, forced fumble, PBU, and interception were big in Cincinnati’s win.

Which college players caught your eye in Week 8 and could help the Washington Commanders?

item.title: How Giants' defense can recalibrate after season-ending injury to Tremaine Edmunds
item.description: Since losing star linebacker Tremaine Edmunds to injury, the rest of the Giants' defense has stepped up. Who will they rely on as the season progresses?
item.content:encoded:
Giants linebacker Tremaine Edmunds signed a three-year deal worth $36 million during the offseason, and was expected to be one of the key figures to help install head coach John Harbaugh’s defensive system and get everyone on the same page. 

That was his role in the early part of the season, as he racked up 50 tackles, two sacks, and two pass breakups in the first six games to help New York to an NFC East-leading 3-2-1 record.

Unfortunately, Edmunds was the latest Giants star to be ruled out for the remainder of the season, after suffering a torn chest muscle near the end of their loss to the New Orleans Saints in Week 6. With New York already losing starting quarterback Jaxson Dart and star edge rusher Brian Burns, this puts a further dent in their hope of winning the NFC East with the rest of the teams in the division looking vulnerable.

However, just as they did after losing Dart and Burns, the Giants responded well in Sunday’s 27-21 overtime win over the Houston Texans. The Texans, who had played really well in the previous two weeks to get to 2-4, were held to a season-low 15 first downs. Their 153 net passing yards also tied a season low. 

Prior to this game, Edmunds had played 100 percent of the defensive snaps for New York, so how did they cope without him, and is this sustainable over the remainder of the season?

The immediate lineup change was to bring in Micah McFadden as the other starting linebacker alongside rookie Arvell Reese.

McFadden got injured in Week 1 of last season, missing the rest of the year, and had played just two defensive snaps in the first six games of 2026. However, the 26-year old has had some valuable experience in the past. He started 14 games in 2023 and another 14 in 2024, registering over 100 tackles in each season, so he has shown he can be productive.

As for Reese, after some early struggles, especially in coverage, he’s gone from strength to strength over the past few weeks, racking up statistical production and making more and more impact plays as the season goes along. Reese has a team-high 56 tackles and also leads the team in tackles for loss with five. He’s added four pass breakups, 1.5 sacks, and an interception.

Arvell Reese 😤 https://t.co/TAqrIDDScY

— SNY Giants (@SNYGiants) October 4, 2026

Ironically, when Burns was injured, one possibility that was discussed was using Reese in an edge rusher role from time to time by bringing in McFadden more often to line up next to Edmunds and free up Reese. That option is out of the window now, and all of Reese’s focus is going to be on the linebacker position.

Defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson had expressed confidence that Reese can take on more responsibility within the defense, saying ahead of Sunday’s game that he has "all the utmost confidence in that young man in everything he does."

Both McFadden and Reese were in the game for all 61 defensive snaps in Sunday’s win, and McFadden wore the green dot on the back of his helmet for the whole game, signifying that he was the one hearing Wilson’s pre-snap instructions in his headset. However, Wilson believes this is something Reese can handle at some point in the future, noting that he already actively set fronts and was a vocal communicator even while Edmunds was still playing.

The plan worked well on Sunday, as McFadden had a team-high 10 tackles, along with two tackles for loss. Reese added seven tackles and half a sack, while also blowing up a screen pass in the backfield for a loss. Houston gained just 100 net yards after halftime, although 48 of those came on a late, game-tying drive to send the game to overtime.

In overtime, though, McFadden came up big as he stuffed Houston’s first play for no gain and then, two plays later, had a quarterback hit on a third down incompletion. After the three-and-out, New York took the ensuing punt and scored three plays later to secure the win.

However, it’s Reese whom Giants fans will mostly be pinning their hopes on. If he can step up to the challenge of taking on more responsibility — ultimately becoming the linchpin of the defensive unit — then McFadden can play more of a supporting role, which is where he will be most effective.

Edmunds in still under contract for two more seasons and should be available as a sounding board for Reese over the rest of this year. Based on how he’s been performing, though, Reese may have already learned most of what he needs from Edmunds to live up to his intriguing potential.

item.title: Can Travis Etienne fix the Saints’ stagnate run game?
item.description: New Orleans' rushing attack has been so bad without Travis Etienne that his return might not be enough to fix it.﻿
item.content:encoded:
The New Orleans Saints’ rushing attack has been so ineffective without Travis Etienne that it is fair to wonder whether the offense would look much better even if he were healthy.

With Etienne currently on injured reserve due to a hamstring strain, the Saints have been left without one of their most explosive playmaker’s and the focal point of their rushing attack. His absence has been extremely noticeable, but Sunday’s performance against the Pittsburgh Steelers in Paris showed just how serious New Orleans’ problems have become. The Saints managed a measly 18 total rushing yards (five from Alvin Kamara, six from Kendre Miller and seven from Tyler Shough), an unacceptable performance for an NFL offense.

Losing a productive tailback can certainly hurt an offense, but the Saints’ struggles go beyond simply missing one player. When a team cannot consistently move the ball on the ground, it becomes increasingly difficult to keep defenses honest and take pressure off the passing game and Tyler Shough.

Etienne, who is eligible to return Week 9 against the Cleveland Browns, could provide a much-needed boost to a struggling operation. His return will add that explosiveness and home-run play ability to a backfield that desperately needs both. However, expecting one player to completely transform an offense that has struggled this badly would be asking a lot.

The offensive line also has to be part of the conversation. If New Orleans can’t improve their blocking up front and establish a more effective ground game as a unit, Etienne could face many of the same challenges when he returns.

The Saints can’t afford to keep having performances like Sunday’s against. Eighteen rushing yards is not going to cut it, regardless of who is carrying the football.

Etienne’s eventual return should help, but it shouldn’t become an excuse for the team’s broader problems. New Orleans needs to figure out why the game has been so ineffective and make the necessary adjustments before expecting one injured player to provide all the answers.

Until then, it is difficult to feel confident that Etienne alone would be enough to turn things around.

Do you think that Etienne’s return could make a different?

item.title: Lions vs. Packers Song of the Game: ‘Get Over It’ by OK Go
item.description: The next song on our Detroit Lions playlist for the 2026 is an ode to Green Bay Packers fans: Get Over It.
item.content:encoded:
If you’re a Packers fan, you have two ways to think about what happened on Sunday. One way of looking at this game is nothing less than comeuppance, justified retribution for the years of officiating that has benefitted Green Bay in critical moments. The other is that your football team was objectively worse in every which way, and had it not been for fumbles your defense didn’t even cause, Sunday would have been a two-score game at a minimum.

Choose your perspective, and get over it—you have “Thursday Night Football” to prepare for!

Lions vs. Packers Week 7 Song of the Game: “Get Over It” by OK Go

Take a break from your daily grind and come back with me in time—back to the year 2002.

The Playstation 2 is all the rage in the gaming world, and you’ve just ripped the wrapper on your brand new copy of Madden NFL 2003. You’re excited to see how the Detroit Lions stack up against the competition, but after scrolling through the league, it might be easier to rebuild one of the NFL Europe teams in Franchise mode. You wonder how the Lions are always so bad, year after year, but this your cross to bear. There’s no amount of trades you can pull off to improve your team enough and actually enjoy playing the game, so you play God and take control of all 32 teams to carry out your bidding.

(Except Mike McMahon—you and your 77 acceleration can stay under center.)

The soundtrack to your menu scrolling—while stealing Torry Holt from the Rams and Ricky Williams from the Dolphins—brings you so many offerings, from Good Charlotte (ew) to Nappy Roots’ rock remix of “Awnaw” (bop). But there’s one track you can’t get enough of: “Get Over It” by OK Go. You get to the options for EA Trax and turn off whatever Bon Jovi song keeps playing, and you’re listening to “Get Over It” four or five times an hour.

Let’s just cut to the chase: do you know what all of these memories and the Lions’ 20-17 win over the Green Bay Packers on Sunday has to do with one another? Manipulation! Corruption! Cheating!

Oh, it’s such a drag, what a chore
Oh, your wounds are full of salt
Everything’s a stress, and what’s more
Well, it’s all somebody’s fault

Packers’ fans had a rough Sunday and Monday—we’ll see how Tuesday plays out—but it’ll be interesting to see if they continue to spin tales of the officials, the Lions, and the NFL at large conspiring to defeat their beloved team.

Honey, your football team just isn’t very good.

It’s nobody’s else’s fault that Green Bay sports the least efficient and productive rushing attack in the NFL since… 1994. Yes, the Packers 2.9 rushing yards per attempt is the first time a team has been under 3.0 rushing yards per attempt in overthirty years. Green Bay’s deep-passing attack is what we thought it was when it’s not buoyed by immoral and unethical behavior. Detroit’s self-inflicted miscues were the only reason the Packers even had a shot in this one, but at the end of the day, they lost a morally good football game because the better team won.

What a pain, well, it’s all a crying shame
What left to do but complain?
You better find someone to blame

Hey! Get, get, get, get, get over it!
Hey! Get, get, get, get, get over it!
Hey! Get, get, get, get, get over it!

item.title: Titans offense may have finally unlocked something with Tony Pollard
item.description: Tennessee Titans running back Tony Pollard carried the offense in the Week 7 loss to the Cleveland Browns.
item.content:encoded:
The Tennessee Titans suffered a nailbiting loss to the Cleveland Browns, losing 27-24 in Week 7. Both the offense and defense squandered away opportunities to win a contest the Titans once led 14-0. Analyzing the bright side, it was arguably the offense’s best output of the campaign.

The 24 points were the most the Titans offense has scored this season. They collectively scored 26 versus the Colts last weekend, but that included a blocked punt returned for a touchdown. Perhaps Brian Daboll and the offense unlocked something with Tony Pollard moving forward.

The Titans rushed for 141 yards. It was arguably Pollard’s best performance in Tennessee. The veteran back rushed for 129 yards and three touchdowns. Pollard did that while averaging more than 5.0 yards per attempt.

Pollard’s production removed some pressure from young quarterback Cam Ward. Ward still made a few mistakes, but he also made several big-time throws throughout the second half. Surely he appreciated leaning on Pollard.

Entering Week 7, the Titans hadn’t run the football consistently. It was a breakout performance for Pollard in a game where Tyjae Spears and Nicholas Singleton were inactive. It’s worth remembering Pollard and the Titans’ run-game got things going in similar fashion down the stretch of last season. That offensive line also featured Dan Moore, Peter Skoronski, and JC Latham.

Hopefully the offensive line will eventually get Fernando Carmona back. If Daboll’s unit continues running the football effectively, the offense could start scoring 20+ points consistently. They’ve failed to reach that scoring benchmark in four of seven games this season.

The Titans absolutely should have defeated the Browns on Sunday. Pollard and the offensive line did enough to carry the offense to victory. Unfortunately, both the passing attack and defense let the Titans down in crucial moments. Hopefully the offense made progress though.

item.title: The Day After the Day After: Houston Texans fall to the New York Giants of New Jersey 27-21
item.description: Well, that sucked. Let’s get this over with…Houston lost to the Giants at home.
item.content:encoded:
The Day After the Day After…when the raw, immediate emotions from the aftermath of a game diminish into the realm of clarity and the proverbial (or literal) hangover no longer haunts the mind. With that, a review of Week 7

Penalties…YIKES!!! 10 Penalties for 80 yards. After seeing the Giants rush for 188 yards, that is the next number that jumps out at you reading the box score. This game was in Houston, with an experienced team, facing a Giants team that hadn’t looked all that great in their last two games. Of Houston’s flags, 4 were of the mental mistake variety (3 x False Starts, 1 x Encroachment). Additionally, 3 of the penalties were offensive holding, which cost Houston 31 yards of rushing offense. The consistent lack of discipline points the finger squarely at the coaching staff. This with at least 3 flags declined, so the flag numbers could have been even worse. Bad enough when this was in Year 1 with a relatively young team. In Year 4 of the Ryans regime, with an experienced team, and at home…inexcusable, and to borrow the McClain catchphrase “pathetic”. 

If the Defensive Line can’t take control...The driving force for Houston’s defense is the defensive line. With Danielle Hunter and Will Anderson Jr., the theory is that they should be enough to disrupt an offensive line, with the resulting impact aided the rest of the defense. However, the Giants offensive line basically negated their impact. Will Anderson Jr was a practical non-factor. While Houston sacked McCarthy 3 times, only one of those sacks came from the defensive line. Half of that total (1.5), came from defensive backs blitzing, as the final 0.5 of a sack came from a blitzing LB. If you need your defensive backfield be the catalyst of getting pressure/sacks, then this defensive scheme is not having a great day. Additionally, the Texans came into this game with a top 5 rushing defense in yards allowed/game. However, the defensive interior could not lock down the Giants’ rushing attack, especially in the 4th quarter and OT, when Houston surrendered 101 yards on the ground alone. Went from allowing less than 82 yards/game to now allowing over 98 yards/game on the ground.  

Home is not where the heart is: Under Ryans, the Texans entered the 2026-7 season with an 18-8 home record (2-0 in playoff games). In the previous three seasons, Houston lost no more than 3 games at home in a season. They’ve already exceeded that total this year. At best, Houston will end the season at 4-4 at home…at best. They still get all three division rivals at home, along with the Ravens, so there is potential for the home crowd to get something for their money. This will be Houston’s worst home record since 2022 (0-7-1), but unlike that time, Houston should be able to win at least one home game…right?  

THE CRITICAL PLAY: 

8:23 in OT; NYG Ball @ NYG 28; 2nd and 1; RB Cam Skattebo 42-yard run up the middle. 

Perhaps it was inevitable. The Texans had momentum coming into the extra frame, having just tied the game, as well as just missing out on a possible INT ball on the Giants’ final regulation drive. However, the Texans went a quick 3-and-out, punting the ball back to the Giants, who set up shop at their 19-yard line. A quick McCarthy pass got the Giants to a favorable 2nd and 1. The Giants lined up in a run formation, and McCarthy went with the handoff to Skattebo. The Giants line, aided by FB/TE Ricard, who lined up as the 2nd TE on the right side of a 3-TE set on the Giants’ right side of the line, blasted through the defensive front of the Texans. The Texans did not have a body covering the second level beyond the DL, and Skattebo had perhaps the best running lane of his pro career. From there, it was a foot race between Skattebo and the Texans’ secondary. Lassiter finally brought him down, but by then, the Giants were well within FG range. Even with their struggling kicker, it is hard to imagine that they would miss. Since Houston busted on its first OT possession, the Giants were likely going to win. Singletary’s nifty 30-yard run on the next play resolved the questions about how the Giants would clinch. 

FUN WITH NUMBERS: 

2-0: JJ McCarthy’s record at NRG/Reliant Stadium: Combining his college and pro career, he’s played two games in Houston. This past Sunday, and when he was the starting QB for Michigan when they won the 2024 National Championship over Washington. Still has never thrown at TD in Houston, but he’ll take the combined 30 for 46 for 392 yards with no INTs and no loses. 

7: Number of NFL teams since 2002 that started 2-5 and made the playoffs: If you still hold out hope, you can look to this. One of those was the 2015 Texans, who started 1-4 and 2-5, and managed to win the AFC South with a 9-7 record. They hosted another team that season (Kansas City) who also started 2-5. It did not go well. 

GAME BALLS: 

WR Xavier Hutchinson: All of the WRs on the Texans’ roster, and the most versatile one in this game ended up being Xavier Hutchinson. On the final drive, he ran for a 1st down on a jet sweep-type play, was slated to throw a WR pass and then caught the game-tying TD pass. Go figure. His final line: 3 receptions for 17 yards and 1 TD, 2 rushes for 12 yards, 3 kickoff returns for 74 yards. 

WR Tank Dell: Not bad when your first game action in almost 2 years after a devastating injury saw you take a pass you weren’t the primary for 43 yards to set up a tying score late in the 1st half. Also sparked the 4th quarter tying drive with his 14-yard punt return. Final line: 1 reception for 43 yards, 1 rush for 2 yards, 1 punt return for 14 yards. 

Giants FB/TE Patrick Ricard: He followed Harbaugh from Baltimore to East Rutherford. Good pickup. He logged no stats in the standard box score, but his blocking from the FB and the TE positions sprang the three biggest runs of the game for the Giants: the fake tush-push 3rd Down run from Skattebo for 19 yards, and the two big runs in OT combining for 72 yards and clinching the win. This game needs to lead off his future contract negotiations. 

SHOULD BE FORCED TO LISTEN TO JOHN MCCLAIN RAMBLE ON ABOUT THE BAYLOR COACHING SEARCH WHILE DROPPING HIS TRADEMARK “PATHETIC” DESCRIPTION ABOUT THE TEXANS ON REPEAT ALL WEEK.  

DC Matt Burke/Defensive Backs Coach Dino Vasso. Words I would not have uttered to start the year, but this pair might be sacked come Black Monday. The secondary once again was picked apart, this time by a known mercurial QB. Yes, Pitre and Blankenship were out for this game, but the communication between DBs in respective zone coverages seemed lacking, with the Giants able to rack up some explosive plays in the Texans’ defensive backfield. It is far too late in the season to be suffering comms break-downs. Throw in a defensive line that could not take advantage of a newish QB and LBs that allowed themselves to be shut down by Giants’ blockers, and you have a recipe for what you saw Sunday. Yes, Ryans is calling the plays, but whatever is going on in practice is either not translating onto the field (bad), or the performances from practice are translating to what is happening on the field (worse). 

OC Nick Caley/HC DeMeco Ryans:Actually, let’s put the offensive coaches as well as the overall coaching staff on this one. The offense was a bit too stubborn trying to get Marks going with the running game when turning Stroud loose might have worked out better, even given some of the pressure the Giants put on him. Ryans, well, this game had all the hallmarks of a trap game (back from big overseas win with a bye week coming), and he let the team step right into it without hesitation. 

Giants PK Dominic Zvada: Lost in all the hubbub about Skattebo and McCarthy was the fact that the Giants PK did not have a very good day. He missed two FGS in the 1st Half which might have salted this game away well before OT. Even accounting for one being a 56-yarder, the kicks were in a stadium with the roof closed. Zvada has been mercurial at best this season, and this game won’t help his cause. 

At 2-5, the Houston Texans now enter their bye week. Not sure how restful or fun it will be, but it is on the schedule. Will everyone on the roster at the end of this game make it to the game in two weeks? Stay tuned.

item.title: Broncos at Cardinals: The No Bull Review
item.description: The Denver Broncos got right against the Arizona Cardinals. No Bull thoughts, opinions, and analysis on the decisive win
item.content:encoded:
Let this be a lesson to all of you out there in Broncos Country: don’t trust the talking heads with narratives about this team or its players. 

Last week all we heard about was how terrible and inept Bo Nix was. No one in the mainstream media was talking about the quality of defenses the Denver Broncos were facing or the lack of a competent run game. Most of them took their turns dumping on Bo Nix because none of them thought he was going to do anything coming out of the draft. He was mislabeled as a check-down merchant in Oregon, and that label will likely follow him every time he has a match-up against an excellent defense.

Not to worry, Broncos Country. This team is who we here at the No Bull Review thought they were. This is darn near the same script we saw last season. Sit back and enjoy the ride for the rest of this season as the Broncos hit their stride.

Offense

Sean Payton continues to tweak the offense as he keeps the team growing and moving toward a better version of themselves as the season wears on. He gave a ton of snaps to young Jonah Coleman, signaling that he’s not satisfied with the best a back can gain on average is 3 yards. He had more plays for Mims in this game and designed a multitude of shots downfield to multiple receivers. 

There was still a nice balance of run (26) vs. pass (29). The big difference in this game was in explosive plays. The offense had 5 plays of 20 yards or more.

There are still many things for them to clean up. Receivers had drops, linemen blew blocks, and the quarterback can place the ball better in spots for sure. I’m not saying that the offense is a group of world-beaters. I am saying this team played up to their potential and showed what they are capable of doing.

Quarterbacks

Bo Nix can throw downfield, in case you didn’t know. He attacked deep early and kept it up through the game. He had an absolutely masterful run for a touchdown. He threw a 27-yard pass to Waddle that was a laser.

I’m going to reiterate that everyone in the media has misread the ankle injury completely. People keep mentioning it as if it is still an issue. The issue is not the ankle from a health standpoint. As we saw on his nearly 20 mph run to the promised land, the ankle is working just fine.

The issue with the ankle injury comes from him getting back into his groove as a passer. His accuracy has been lacking early this season (much like it did last season). I think we’re seeing Nix rounding into form as the season wears on. He’s getting work each week finally, and as he settles his footwork down, his throws are only going to get better and better.

Line

I largely liked what I saw from the line this week. They only gave up one sack. The run game was blocked up well enough. Sure, we saw McGlinchey miss a stunt and block no one to give up a big pressure. We also had a couple of illegal formation penalties that should never happen.

This line has had a rough start to the season. With a more efficient runner toting the rock, I’m optimistic about their progress and ability to round into form much like Nix.

Running Backs

A healthy Jonah Coleman is just what the doctor ordered for this ailing Broncos run game. He was in on 50% of the snaps for the team. He showed a runner who has vision, burst, and power. 

I loved his ability to cut back and head north when his designed holes were closing up. That seems simple enough, but we’ve seen far too many runs go for nothing because backs aren’t cutting when the play is smothered. He averaged 6 yards per carry on 9 runs for 54 yards. He also caught two passes for 15. Coleman is versatile in anything we ask the position to do in this offense. I’m excited to see what this rookie does with the rest of his season.

R.J. Harvey is a home-run hitter. He took a screen pass to the house early in the 3rd quarter. It was a perfectly timed and executed play that had multiple blockers running free downfield to help Harvey jet into the end zone. He was pretty rough as far as output goes outside of that one play. His other 4 touches were plays for 2-3 yards each. 

JK Dobbins had 6 carries for 23 yards. On one hand, that’s an improvement over what we’ve seen from him in the past few games. On the other hand, there’s a reason he only saw 23% of the snaps in the game. One of his carries was a touchdown that he earned fighting through a tackle to lunge the ball over the goal line.

Receivers

Let’s give some love to Marvin Mims for getting more involved with the offense this week. He had a gain of 47 yards off a busted coverage play to the sideline. He’s another guy on this offense who is a threat to house the ball if they can just find ways to get him the ball in space.

Cortland Sutton got the party started with an in-breaking route across the middle for a big gain of 20 yards. He’s still looking like a player who has lost a step, but his size and great route running open up plays for Nix.

Jaylen Waddle had a couple of really nice catches in this game. He caught a low throw on a 14-yard out that was way tougher than it needed to be. Late in the game, he caught a 27-yard back shoulder downfield while taking a big hit from a closing safety. He ended the game with 4 catches for 48 yards.

Troy Franklin was ice cold in this game, missing both of his targets. What I loved from him was his blocking for the Nix run. He blocked two guys to help Nix get into the end zone.

Defense

The Broncos defense again held the opponents to under 20 points. That’s excellent in today’s NFL. Vance Joseph didn’t have an answer for Trey McBride (he threw everything and the kitchen sink at him coverage-wise). Sometimes you can’t hold down a great player (just ask JSN).

I want to say that Joseph had his defense playing inspired football to close out the game. The Arizona Cardinals got the ball down to the 1-yard line and the defense held them out for 7 straight plays. The effort never dropped even with a two-score lead. 

Front 7

Malcolm Roach, to me, was the defensive player of the game. He was absolutely killing it up front all game long. He had a sack, a tackle for loss, 4 quarterback hits, and a batted pass to seal the big goal-line stand at the end of the game.

Alex Singleton stacked up another really solid game. It wasn’t a shut-out for him, as he had a couple of coverage plays with shaky coverage, including a 14-yard crossing route that got by him. He had an impressive 19-tackle game with a tackle for loss, 2 quarterback hits, and a sack on the day.

Sai’vion Jones had the most impressive sack of the game, with a guy draped over him using one arm. He also had a tackle for loss and a quarterback hit.

Secondary

Riley Moss got flagged for pass interference for executing perfect pass defense to deflect a pass as it was caught. I’m honestly sick and tired of referees throwing a flag when they see Moss in coverage. The replay made me want to puke, honestly. Riley had a pass defense later in the game with far more contact than we saw on the pass interference penalty.

Kris Abrams-Draine continued to impress me with his play this week. He had an excellent open-field tackle to keep a pass bottled up on a 2nd and 5. On a 4th and 13 play out to his side, he did a superb job not biting as the receiver lateralled the ball to a guy behind him. KAD recognized what was happening and kept himself in line to stop the play.

Brandon Jones on 3rd and 2 got the defense off the field with smothering coverage on McBride. He gave a huge pass interference call up by being too handsy and also had a couple of missed tackles. 

McMillian darn near had 3 interceptions in the game. They all go down in the stat sheet as a pass defense, but my soul weeps a bit to see so many passes hit his hands and not get picked.

Barron got a bogus PI call as well for playing perfect coverage. He got another PI in the end zone that was within 5 yards and was just a contested catch.

Special Teams

Adam Prentice got a big time punt block to help put the team in scoring position. He made a great effort to focus on the ball and not just flail his arm into the punter’s leg to avoid a penalty.

Marvin Mims Jr. got back involved with kickoff returns and made an impact with a 38-yard return. He also should have gotten an unnecessary roughness foul drawn from the Cardinals as he was hit 1 yard out of bounds and thrown to the ground, but that went unflagged.

Final Thoughts

The Broncos had another bonus home game in Arizona. It was impressively loud at times when the Cardinals had the ball. That’s Broncos Country showing up strong and proud for our team.

The Broncos have easily the most important game of the season next week at home against the Chiefs. They can and should take over the AFC West with a victory. This win against the Cardinals should go a long way to helping boost the confidence of the offense as they prepare for the big showdown.

item.title: 10 thoughts on the Cowboys win over the Eagles
item.description: Our thoughts on the Cowboys win over the Eagles
item.content:encoded:
The Dallas Cowboys’ losing streak is over as they came away with a 38-21 win over the Philadelphia Eagles on Monday night. While the final scoreboard suggests they ran away with this one, it ended up being a little more troublesome than one might’ve thought.

The Eagles were short-handed, and they actually had the lead early before Dallas finally pulled away at the end. Here are 10 thoughts on this much-needed Cowboys victory.

1. Restored rushing attack

The ground game finally decided to show some life and give the offense some balance. The blocking upfront was outstanding, and the holes were plentiful. The Cowboys racked up over 200 yards rushing, with 155 coming courtesy of Javonte Williams, who finished the game with over six yards per carry, including the game’s final touchdown. It was a positive step forward for a rushing attack that had been missing in action over the previous few weeks.

2. Stars a shining

While Williams set the tone on the ground by running the ball, Dak Prescott did a good job of distributing the ball. He finished the game with three touchdown passes. Two of those scoring strikes found the hands of CeeDee Lamb, while the other went to George Pickens. That touchdown grab by Pickens was amazing, as he adjusted his body, hauled down the pass, and kept both feet in bounds. He’s so incredible at bringing in difficult catches that very few receivers in this league can do.

3. Welcome back, DeMo

DeMarvion Overshown made his return to the lineup and provided an immediate spark for the defense. He was flying around, filling gaps, and tracking down ball carriers with authority. He filled the stat sheet, leading the team with five solo tackles, but his biggest play came when he dropped back in coverage and stepped in front of a Dallas Goedert pass and hauled in the interception. That was essentially the game-ender.

4. Impactful Q

Quinnen Williams has been a disruptive force recently, and Monday night was no different.  He was a complete nightmare for the opposing blockers, consistently blowing up plays before they could develop. Williams finished a dominant performance with a sack and three tackles for a loss, routinely collapsing the pocket. He almost added another highlight by making what initially looked like a fourth-down stop, but he lined up a little too close to the center and got flagged for a penalty.

5. The Goodson

The team continues to roll without their All-Pro kick returner, who is recovering from a rib injury, but his absence hasn’t hurt the team. Backup running back Tyler Goodson has filled in nicely. While his return touchdown didn’t count, he showed some good explosiveness and has slowly put himself into the conversation as a useful tool for this team, on offense or even on special teams.

6. Aubrey pinning them deep

Brandon Aubrey continues to prove that his value extends beyond making field goals by weaponizing his kickoffs. He appears to have dialed in his dirty kicks, lining driving the ball to perfect locations and forcing difficult return situations. Three separate times during the second half, the Eagles’ returners failed to handle the ball cleanly, allowing the Cowboys coverage unit to swarm. Because of his precision, the opposing offense was forced to start their drives inside their own 20-yard line.

7. Third-down disaster

Third downs have become so nightmarish for the Cowboys defense. Every time third down rolls around, we can hear the cryptic Michael Myers Halloween music in our heads. Something bad is about to go down. It’s frustrating, because this dysfunctional group can play somewhat well on early downs. They just can’t close the deal and get off the field.

8. Penalty problems

Getting stops on defense is hard enough, but it becomes almost impossible when you are constantly fighting your own mistakes. The Cowboys’ defense spent a large part of the night shooting themselves in the foot with penalties that wiped out would-be stops. The peak of this frustration came on a fantastic kickoff return from Goodson that had fans out of their seats, only to slowly sit back down as it was nullified by a holding penalty. This stupid team, sometimes.

9. Run defense struggles

While the defense eventually settled down and started making stops, it was still weird how much they struggled stopping the run, considering that’s really all the Eagles could do. Quarterback Tanner McKee wasn’t going to hurt them. Despite knowing this, they still couldn’t stop the Eagles’ rushing attack. The Cowboys caught a break that Saquon Barkley wasn’t at full health because he ran for nearly nine yards a carry, but could only muster seven rushing attempts.

10. Clock mismanagement

We were graced with a little bit of excitement toward the end of the first half when it looked like the Cowboys offense was flying down the field. With just over a minute left in the second quarter and the ball on their own 13-yard line, the Cowboys marched down the field quickly.

However, instead of finishing with a touchdown, they had to settle for a field goal thanks to poor clock management. Brian Schottenheimer chose not to use a timeout after a completion to Lamb with 44 seconds left, allowing precious time to come off the clock. They struck again on the very next play, getting down inside the Eagles’ 10-yard line, but they only had 12 seconds left, ultimately limiting how many shots they could take at the end zone.

item.title: The Chiefs’ defense struggled to get stops in Seattle
item.description: A closer look at why Kansas City was unable to get off the field in key moments on Sunday night.
item.content:encoded:
In the 20-3 loss to the Seattle Seahawks, the Kansas City Chiefs’ defense played the bend-don’t-break style that coordinator Steve Spagnuolo has sharpened throughout his time in Kansas City. Through Week 7, the Chiefs still allow the second-fewest points per game in the NFL (17.2).

The defense kept the team in this game — a better kick from 45 yards by Harrison Butker would have brought the game to within a score in the fourth quarter — but regardless of the point total, the Seahawks’ offense stayed on the field.

Seattle converted 11 of 16 third downs and sustained five possessions for nine or more plays. The Seahawks ran 19 more plays than Kansas City and held possession for nearly 12 more minutes.

The three longest drives were key turning points, and each featured third-and-longs the Seahawks converted:

  • 1st half: 15 plays and 96 yards for a field goal
    • 3rd & 9 and 3rd & 7 converted
  • Second quarter: 10 plays and 66 yards for a touchdown
    • 3rd & 6 and 3rd & 9 converted
  • Third quarter: 13 plays and 62 yards for a field goal
    • 3rd & 9 and 3rd & 10 converted

Let’s take a closer look at why the Chiefs couldn’t get off the field when it needed to in Seattle:

Man coverage lapses

Early on, Spags deployed man coverage on third downs, and quarterback Sam Darnold targeted slot cornerback L’Jarius Sneed regardless of the matchup. On the opening drive, he allowed a chains-moving third-down catch out of the slot, but the Chiefs eventually forced a punt.

Third-and-9 on the second drive: With wide receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba, the reigning NFL Offensive Player of the Year, as the primary threat on a pass down, the Chiefs have near-safety help over the top. Here, safety Chamarri Conner brackets Smith-Njigba with cornerback Mansoor Delane in trail-man coverage, taking away a throw at the sticks.

However, slot receiver Cooper Kupp — who goes in pre-snap motion to identify Sneed as his man-coverage defender — will receive the pass with a quick pass over the middle. Kupp sets Sneed up outside and beats him back across; there’s no help over the middle because linebacker Nick Bolton is in the pass rush.

Darnold’s quick release was a theme of the game, especially in the first half. He averaged 2.45 seconds to throw, the third-fastest time of his career according to NFL Next Gen Stats. He completed 13 of 14 passes when throwing in 2.5 seconds or less.

Third-and-7 on the same drive: In a similar man-coverage setup, it’s now Sneed who is manned up on Smith-Njigba, with safety Alohi Gilman anticipating an out-breaking throw at the sticks in help coverage. However, Sneed loses the inside leverage by overdoing his jam at the line of scrimmage. Gilman cheating outside opened the floodgates for the 33-yard catch-and-run over the middle, and Conner’s poor angle on the missed tackle didn’t help either.

The Seahawks relentlessly attacked the Chiefs’ man coverage over the middle until Spags adjusted.

Not finishing the play

When the Chiefs turned to zone coverage, typically when closer to or in the red zone, it wasn’t as easy for Darnold to find an option to move the chains. Kansas City held Seattle to a field goal on the previously discussed possession by playing tight zone coverage on the ultimate third down.

Third-and-6 from late in the first half: The Chiefs dropped seven into zone coverage with a four-man rush, and Darnold rolls to his right after not his initial reads are taken away. That sets up defensive end George Karlaftis to wrap him up for a game-changing sack, leaving Seattle on fourth down and deciding to kick a roughly 60-yard field goal.

Instead, Darnold jukes Karlaftis and outruns defensive tackle Chris Jones to the sticks. It was one of the first times the Chiefs’ defensive lineman had a chance at a sack, and No. 56 in particular couldn’t come through. A few plays later, Darnold delivered a perfect pass in rhythm to Smith-Njigba, who caught the touchdown down the sideline through tight coverage by Delane on third-and-9.

Third-and-9 in the third quarter: Another four-man rush with zone coverage forces Darnold out of the pocket, and without a throwing option, cornerback Nohl Williams and linebacker Nick Bolton can’t react in time to stop him from crossing the marker. A late fake by Darnold fools Bolton.

Third-and-10 from the same drive: Zone and a four-man rush work once again, with a stunt by Karlaftis dissuading Darnold from a downfield throw and forcing a checkdown. Yet Bolton and Williams are again too passive in rallying to the ball, allowing the running back to gain the first down.

Edge rusher R Mason Thomas’s visible frustration after the play, in which he pressured Darnold, reflects how many in Chiefs Kingdom felt. Nothing seemed to go Kansas City’s way on third-and-long in Seattle.

The bottom line

Despite a frustrating night, the Chiefs’ defense was close to having a winning formula. The problem is, we say the unit is “close” way too often when analyzing negative plays, whether it’s the pass rush or coverage. On the flip side, it suggests that the players on the field simply need to perform better.

However, there need to be personnel wrinkles, including at slot cornerback. Sneed (14 snaps) seemed to see his playing time decrease as the night went on, and that should continue as Chris Roland-Wallace rises in that same position.

Another wrinkle that the Chiefs teased on Sunday night was second-year linebacker Jeffrey Bassa playing a Quarterback-spy role. He was in on two third-down red-zone stops as part of a unique defensive formation that deployed just two pass rushers, flooding coverage with as many defenders as possible.

Look out for Bassa on the field as a spy moving forward, especially against mobile quarterbacks like the Buffalo Bills’ Josh Allen.
