item.title: Detroit Lions film breakdown: The trained eyes of Jared Goff
item.description: Jared Goff showed why his pre and post-snap coverage reads are elite vs. the Green Bay Packers.
item.content:encoded:
Last week, a few people pointed out a great answer from Detroit Lions offensive coordinator Drew Petzing about what makes Jared Goff special as a play-action quarterback. Here’s the transcript of Petzing’s answer below. I’m going to highlight the key points:

“One of the things that makes him so elite in that is his process. It’s uncomfortable and you don’t do it a ton in college anymore where you turn your back to the defense. And you have to take in a ton of information pre-snap, and you have to know where your eyes need to go and who you need to locate on their side of the ball and on our side of the ball. And I think that’s a huge part of the action game. And it’s one of the reasons you see defenses try to disguise and try to show different looks so that when you do turn your back, you’re turning around and seeing a different picture. And he’s done it at such a high level that I think even when that happens, he’s able to calibrate quickly, figure out what’s going on and make the proper decision almost every time. And that’s really one of the main reasons I think he’s excelled in that area.”

Here’s the video:

In short, play-action can be really tough for quarterbacks, because in today’s NFL, defense’s are so good at disguising coverages that the look you see before you turn your head to fake the run could be completely different than the look you see when you turn back around to look at the defense.

The Green Bay Packers are one of those teams that have been expertly disguising coverages. With three stellar safeties at their disposal, there’s so much they can do. That’s why their pass defense was one of the best in the league going into Sunday’s matchup with the Lions. They ranked third in passer rating allowed (73.9), third in yards per attempt (5.9) and second in DVOA.

But Goff had no problem dissecting the defense, particularly early in the game, and a lot of that had to due with Goff’s elite ability to identify coverages both pre- and post-snap. On play-action passes, Goff went 8-of-11 for 140 yards against the Packers. His +0.55 EPA/dropback on play-action passes was third-best of the week, and his 145.1 passer rating was second.

One particular play shows exactly the skills Petzing was talking about.

It’s the tail end of the first quarter and the Lions are kicking off their second series of the game. As Goff is ready to snap the ball, the Packers are showing a pretty ordinary cover-2 look.

Both safeties are back pedaling at the snap, while the Packers are just widening their zones with Amon-Ra St. Brown’s motion—clear zone indicators.

However, at the snap—literally the moment Goff turns his back for play-action, the right side safety—All-Pro Xavier McKinney (#29)—aggressively runs toward the line of scrimmage to play a shallow zone, leaving the other safety, Evan Williams, as the single high.

So when Goff finally turns around, the coverage is MUCH different than it looked before the play-action. But Goff immediately clocks it, drawing his eyes to the safeties before even looking at his receivers:

So he knows that McKinney has vacated the left-middle part of the field, where Amon-Ra St. Brown’s leak route just so happens to be brilliantly designed to attack—while Jameson Williams takes the play-side cornerback out of the play.

Despite the Packers doing a great job not tipping their coverage design, Goff immediately identified it, found where the weakness was, and exploited it for a huge gain.

Here’s it all working together in harmony:

Aided by strong protection from the offensive line, this is Jared Goff making the remarkable look unremarkable. And against a team like the Minnesota Vikings who will do everything they can to disguise things and confuse Goff this upcoming Sunday, it’s when having someone like him at quarterback is also extremely valuable.

item.title: Don’t call Blake Corum Rams’ RB1 just yet
item.description: Blake Corum had a great Week 6 and more NFL news
item.content:encoded:
Blake Corum had a fine game for the Los Angeles Rams in Week 6, and fumble aside, so did Kyren Williams. There is the notion that Corum will get more work for the Rams, and he could take over as the RB1, but before Corum is anointed, he has to actually become the RB1.

Corum seems to have the talent, he appears to be learning Sean McVay’s playbook and Corum has shown a willingness to block as hard as he’ll run. But, to be the Rams RB1, you have to be consistent. Can Corum handle the true workload as the featured running back for L.A.? Can Corum stay healthy? Can Corum stay productive? We don’t know that, yet.

We know Williams can handle it. Fumbles aside, he’s been amazing for the Rams as a fifth-round pick who plays like one of the best running backs in the league, and has been one of the most productive.

The future for Corum looks bright, but for now, he’s not the RB1. That’s seems like it’s Williams’ job to keep, or lose.

Rams Week 7 snap counts: Corum’s role grows, WR2 still unclear (ramswire)

“Kyren Williams still played more snaps than Corum, but just barely. He had 37 plays compared to 32 for Corum, and five of those snaps were on the final drive when the Rams were just milking the clock. Corum’s 32 snaps were a season-high and his 44% snap share was his second-highest.”

Rams Top PFF Performers in Week 7 Victory Over the Raiders (sports.yahoo)

“Here are the top five players on offense and defense via Pro Football Focus (PFF).

Offense

  • RB Blake Corum: 87.4
  • WR Puka Nacua: 86.8
  • RT Warren McClendon Jr.: 75.2
  • RB Kyren Williams: 72.3
  • QB Matthew Stafford: 70.5

The Rams returned to a split-carry situation with both Kyren Williams and Blake Corum having strong days.“

Rams Player Grades: Running Game Leads the Way in Week 7 Win Over Raiders (si.com)

“Running Backs: A-

The engine of the Rams’ offense on Sunday against the Raiders was the running game. They rushed 33 times for 192 yards and had a touchdown. Blake Corum and Kyren Williams became the first Rams running back duo since Marshall Faulk and Trung Candidate in 2001 to each have 90 rushing yards in the same game. Williams did have a fumble, which continues to be an issue. However, outside of the fumble, Williams and Corum were fantastic. 

  • Blake Corum PFF Grade: 83.6
  • Kyren Williams PFF Grade: 70.4

Wide Receivers: B

There continues to be a significant drop-off at wide receiver behind Puka Nacua and Davante Adams. With Adams out, Konata Mumpfield and Tutu Atwell rotated as the second wide receiver. Mumpfield had one catch for 15 yards while Atwell had nothing. If the Rams make a trade at the deadline, it needs to be for a wide receiver. “

Rams RB duo passes legend Marshall Faulk’s 25-year-old record (sports.yahoo)

“Williams, 26, led the way as the starter, recording 99 rushing yards and a touchdown on 16 carries. Corum, 25, complemented him with an equally impressive performance, finishing with 93 yards and a touchdown on 17 carries.

Their combined production gave the Rams a balanced rushing attack that helped them pull away from Las Vegas and secure an important victory.

The achievement recalls the days when Faulk was one of the NFL’s most dynamic offensive weapons. During his time with the Rams, Faulk established himself as a central figure in the franchise’s success, making the comparison particularly notable for the current backfield duo.“

Puka Nacua cracks top 10 of Rams’ all-time receiving list in just 49 games (ramswire)

“If Nacua adds another 722 yards this season, he will finish the year ranked seventh all-time, eclipsing Hall of Famer Tom Fears for the spot. Despite his incredible output, Nacua has only played in 49 games for the Rams so far, but his averages of 7.3 receptions per game and 95.4 yards per game lead the franchise by a significant margin.

Cooper Kupp is ranked second for receptions per game with 6.1, while Torry Holt averaged 80.1 yards per contest.“

Rams Captain Quentin Lake Says Your Body Is Your Résumé (sports.yahoo)

“”Your body is your résumé, and your best ability is availability,” Lake says.

He admits he did not fully understand that principle when he entered the league. Now he treats recovery as an investment in his career. His routine can include massage, chiropractic work, acupuncture, compression boots, and individualized strength work designed to address differences in mobility and strength between each side of his body.

“You have to reinvest the money that you make into yourself so that you can put your best product out there,” Lake says.“

Davis Allen showed he can do more than block in Rams’ win over Raiders (ramblinfan)

“There seems to be another consistent theme running throughout the Rams roster. LA has accumulated talented players whose greatest challenge is getting enough work in to make a difference. Allen is one such example.

Now in Year 4, Allen has been targeted a mere 71 times, catching 50 passes for 425 yards and six touchdowns. That’s a catch rate of over 70 percent. And yet, he has only been targeted 14 times this season.

Over the course of his career, he has only cracked 100 receiving yards once in a season. with his two-score performance in Week 7, he now has two seasons with multiple touchdowns.“

Sean McVay & Colby Parkinson discuss Week 7 win over the Raiders, tight end depth, playing resilient & more (nfl.com)

“Los Angeles Rams head coach Sean McVay and tight end Colby Parkinson recap the Rams’ Week 7 win over the Las Vegas Raiders. Watch them discuss standout performances, tight end depth, playing with resiliency & toughness, and more.”

Rams Deliver Myles Garrett Update as Roster Decision Looms (heavy.com)

“The Los Angeles Rams are uncertain about Myles Garrett’s immediate future. The same is true of second-year tight end Terrance Ferguson, according to Rams head coach Sean McVay during his day-after press conference.

“I’m not sure yet. Have not decided on those things,” McVay told reporters on October 26 when asked about opening their 21-day practice windows from IR, per the LA Times’ Gary Klein.“

Comment of the day:

“Yes, he had a pretty good, not great, rookie season. However, in 2025, Thomas missed three regular season games, he was targeted 91 times, caught 48 for 707 yards and two touchdowns. That’s a 52.7% reception rate, no bueno, to say the least. So far, in 2026, he has caught 9 passes out of 19 targets, less than 50%, he has 105 yards, and 1 touchdown. Trevor Lawrence is just not throwing him the ball any longer, and we can see the reason why. Hard pass for me, and no way is he worth a 2nd round pick. If we could get him for a 5th or 6th I might, and I do mean might, consider it.”-BradleyS
